lawyer:
Mr. Mostafa Zaman Islam, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner 
Mr. Shasti Sarker with Mr. Ellius Ahmed, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Md. Mokbul Hssain
Vs.
Md. Umar Ali and others
full_judgment:
Md. Mamtaz Uddin Ahmed, J: The Rule was issued at the instance of the pre-emptee calling upon the opposite party no. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order complained of in the petition moved in court should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The pre-emptor instituted the preemption Misc. Case no. 11 of 2006 in the court of Assistant Judge Bhuringamari, Kurigram for preemption of the schedule property made in the preemption case.

3. The case of the pre-emptor is that the land was recorded and published in S.A. Khatian No. 30 and 55 in the name of Kalu Sheikh who died leaving sons namely Mokbul Hossain, Abul Kashem, Quader, Sabed and daughter Hazera Khatun and the land was recorded rightly in new dhiara khatian in their names. The pre-emptor is the brother of the seller, opposite party no. 2 who transferred the case land on 17.11.2002 to the pre-emptee opposite party no. 1 by a registered deed. The preemptee is a stranger of the case land. No notice was served upon the pre-emptor regarding the transfer of the case land. The pre-emptor came to know about the sale on 03.03.2005 from the local people and thereafter, obtained the certified copy on 5.3.2005 of the sale deed and then instituted the case.

4. The pre-emptee opposite party no.1 contested the case by filing a written objection denying the material allegations made in the preemption application and stated that the case is not maintainable in the present form and manner and the same is liable to be dismissed. He further stated that he is a businessman, dealing with paddy and doing business using the disputed land covering plot nos. 697, 696 and 486 where he established a Husking Mill and chatal. In order to extend his existing chatal, he purchased the land to the knowledge of all concerned including the pre-emptor. The disputed land was a fellow/ditch land and developed the land investing of Tk. 1,50,000/-. The preemptor was aware of the sale and development of the land. The value of the land has increased now and for the purpose of the illegal gain and benefit, the pre-emptor filed the case which is liable to be dismissed.

5. The pre-emptor examined 2 witnesses and the pre-emptee examined 3 witnesses including himself and the Advocate Commissioner also examined as witness.

6. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties, perusing the evidence of the parties and the record allowed the preemption case by his judgment and order dated 22.4.2007.

7. The preemptee being dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 22.4.2007 preferred preemption Misc. Appeal No. 29 of 2007 in the court District Judge, Kurigram and eventually, the learned Additional District Judge Kurigram heard the appeal and after hearing the parties, and considering the material evidence dismissed the appeal by his judgment and order dated 26.9.2007 and thereby, affirmed the judgment and order dated 22.4.2007 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge and allowed the preemption Misc. Case no. 11 of 2005.

8. The pre-emptee having being dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 29.9.2007 passed by the Additional District Judge, Kurigram has preferred this revisional application before this court and after hearing the learned Advocate this court issued the Rule as stated above.

9. Mr. Mustafa Zaman Islam, the learned Advocate with Mr. Syed Kamrul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the preemptee petitioner has placed the judgment and order of the courts below and submitted that the preemption case is barred by limitation in as much as, the case land was sold by registered deed dated 17.11.2002 but the preemption application field on 5.3.2005 having knowledge on 3.3.2005 but the pre-emptor has not been able to prove his alleged date of knowledge. on the other hand, the learned Advocate submits that the pre-emptor being PW.1 stated in the evidence that he came home after 7 days of the sale and the preemptor, has not produced any witness to corroborate his alleged date of knowledge though in the application for preemption as well as in his evidence stated that he came to know from the local people and none of the local people was produced to corroborate his evidence, but the courts below did not at all consider this material aspect of the case and upon such non consideration allowed, the preemption case which is an error resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He contended further that the courts below quoted the evidence of the OPW.1, pre-emptee without discussing the evidence of PW.1 (preemptor), his witnesses has allowed the preemption beyond the scope of the principle of law and thereby, committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submitted that the courts below did not consider the evidence of the witnesses cited by the pre-emptee in as much as the evidence of OPW.1, 2 and 3 and also the evidence of Advocate Commissioner, where from it would be evident that the pre-emptee had developed the land at a substantial expenditure within the sight and knowledge of the preemptor for about 2 years 4 months from the date of the execution of the deed but the courts below did not consider those evidence and allowed the preemption case and thereby, upon misconstrued the evidence committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further contended that the preemptor of the case, ignored the transfer for about 3 years but filed the case after statutory period of limitation and in such circumstances, heavy burden lies on the preemptor to discharge the onus of proof about his knowledge of the transfer of the case land but in this particular case failed to discharge the initial onus in not producing witness as to knowledge from among the local people from whom he allegedly came to know about the transfer to corroborate his evidence and such uncorroborated evidence of PW.1 (pre-emptor) being interested witness cannot be relied but the courts acted under misconception of law as to question of onus of proof regarding knowledge of sale and ignoring such legal aspect of the case have allowed the preemption case which is an error resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. To support his contention he has referred to the decision in the case of Abdul Mazid Howlader and another Vs. Lahajuddin Howlader and others reported in 48 DLR(AD) 160 wherein their Lordships observed in paragraph 11:-

"On a careful consideration of the evidence of PW.1 Lehajuddin (pre-emptor) it appears that he for the first time came to know about the transfer from PW.2 Sekander Ali, uncle of PW.1 Lehajuddin who lives in the same mess with the pre-emptor. PW.2 Sekander Ali deposed about the date of knowledge as instructed by his uncle PW.1 Lehajuddin. PW.2 Sekander Ali stated that he disclosed about the date of knowledge to PW.1 before OPW.3 Mobarak Ali. But OPW.3 denied of any such disclosure about the talk of kabala in his presence. Thus it is palpably clear that Lehajuddin could not adduce any disinterested and reliable witness to prove his alleged first date of knowledge. Further, there is material contradiction between the evidence of PW.2 Sekander Ali and OPW.3 Mobarak Ali with regard to the disclosure of the first date of knowledge. On the other hand, the six OPWs. proved the possession of the pre-emptees in the suit land for the last 13/14 years. Further, OPW.2 Ayub Ali son of Tozamber Ali , the vendor of Bolaram Sil, testified that he and his father used to barga cultivate the land after it was sold to Balaram Sil. On a total non-consideration of the aforesaid material evidence of all the witnesses of the appellants the lower appellate Court wrongly arrived at a finding that the pre-emptees were possessing as bargaders and that the application for pre-emption was not barred by limitation. There being a total non-consideration of all the witnesses of the pre-emptees, the learned Single Judge acted wrongly in refusing to exercise his revisional jurisdiction in a case where due to non-consideration of the material evidence on record an erroneous decision has been arrived occasioning a grave failure of justice".

11. Another decision in the case of Madinullah Miah Vs. Md. Abdul Mannan and another reported in 54 DLR(HCD) 507, wherein their Lordship held in paragraph 20:-

"A single Bench of this Division was severely criticised by the Appellate Division in Abdul mazid Howlader and another Vs. Lahajuddin Howlader and others, for not interfering with the decisions of the lower appellate Court, which was arrived at without considering the evidence of the witnesses of the-pre-emptee. The case is reported in 48 DLR (AD)160. There is a similarity of facts of the present case and the facts of that case. Like the pre-emptor of the present case, the pre-emptor of that case too pleaded 7 years of ignorance of the transfer of the case land to the pre-emptee. The Appellate Division observed,

"In this case admittedly the application for pre-emption was after 7 years of transfer and a heavy burden lies on the pre-emptor to discharge the onus of proof that he filed the case within four months from the date of his knowledge. The pre-emptor having failed to discharge the initial onus by adducing cogent and reliable evidence the learned single Judge ought to have held that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation." In the present case the preemptor opposite party has claimed to have knowledge of the transfer of the case land to the pre-emptor petitioner after six and half years of the transfer. He referred no explanation for such a late knowledge of the transfer of a piece of land, which is contiguous to the land held by him and situated next to his baithak khana and the vendor of the land was not a total stranger to him. Nor did he explain the source of his knowledge of the transfer. So his claim is not credible. As against this, there is in the file the contrary evidence of the vendor and the purchaser of the case land, both of whom categorically stated that the pre-emptor was aware of the transfer of the case land immediately after its transfer. They narrated the circumstances in which the pre-emptor had come to know of the transfer. The trial Court found no wrong with their evidence. So, he should have relied upon their evidence and dismissed the pre-emptor's case on the ground of limitation."

12. The learned Advocate further contended that the pre-emptee having being in possession on the strength of the deed had developed the land by filling earth and thereafter, established husking mill and made the chatal for the purpose of paddy business and such case has been proved by producing disinterested witnesses such as OPW.2, 3 and Advocate Commissioner, but the learned judges over looking those evidence allowed the preemption case holding that the development so made, made during the pendency of the preemption case and such findings are vague being not based on evidence on record and as such, the courts below committed error of law in allowing the preemption case without giving development cost and the same being an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

13. On the other hand, Mr. Shasti Sarker, the learned Advocate with Mr. Ellius Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the preemptor opposite party has also taken me through the judgments and also the evidence and submitted that admittedly the preemptor is brother of the seller and a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding and on the basis of such fact the preemption was allowed on the concurrent findings and in view of such position of law, this court needs not interfere as the issues has been settled upon proper consideration of the evidence of the parties. He further submitted that pre-emptor himself proved the knowledge but such evidence could not be shaken by cross examination by the pre-emptee and a solitary witness can be relied as he is a credible witness and having regard to the provision of section 134 of the Evidence Act have allowed the preemption case and thus, the courts below committed no error of law. He further submitted that the Trial Court thoroughly examined the evidence and the Appellate Court also examined the evidence in its own way and arrived at his own conclusion having regard to the object of provision of order 41 Rule 31 and since the facts settled by the final court of facts cannot be disturbed in revision and as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. To substantiate his contention he has cited a number of decisions different Counts:-

(a) "In the case of Sona Mia Vs. Abdul Khaleque reported in 10 BLD(AD) 209, wherein their Lordships observed that this being a finding of purely of facts does not warrant interference in revision. The High Court Division rightly refused interference."

(b) In the case of Most Rokeya Begum Vs. - Md. Abu Zaher and others reported in 20 BLD(AD) 90, paragraph 28: wherein their Lordships held:-

"The Appellate Division in the case of Sona Mia Vs. Abdul Khaleque reported in 10 BLD 209 has held that on consideration of the evidence and circumstances the appellate court reversed the trial Court's findings and this being purely on fact cannot be interfered with in revision. It has further been held by the Appellate Division in the case of Kurshid Ali and others Vs. Noorjahan Bewa and others reported in 15 BLD 82 that when the appellate Court as final court of fact decide questions of fact and records it findings on consideration of the evidence on record the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with the finding of fact unless the High Court Division is satisfied that the said findings of the appellate court are perverse. "

(c) In the case of Jafar Ali Vs. Hushiar Ali and others reported in 46 DLR(AD) 187 pars 5 wherein their Lordships held: "The positive case of the pre-emptor is, that he filed the earlier pre-emption case before the registration of the kabala and hence withdrew the same. According to the pre-empotor, he came to know about the registration of the kabala on 4.2.1975 and, after obtaining the certified copy of the same exhibit 1, filed the present case on 12.2.1975. The pre-emptor led evidence with regard to his date of knowledge of the registration of the kabala. The pre-emptee did not adduce any evidence to show that the pre-emptor was aware of the registration of the kabala prior to alleged date of knowledge. There being no evidence on record by the pre-emptee challenging the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor, all the courts below believed the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor and held that the case was not barred by limitation. This being a finding of fact on assessment of evidence on record, Mr. Mohammad Habib Ahmed, learned Advocate's contention that the application is barred by limitation is untenable in law. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

d. In the case Md. Belayet Hossain Vs. Shah Alam Parvez and others reported in 19 BLD(HCD) 359 wherein their Lordships held that order 26 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for holding local investigation on specified grounds when the court finds a local investigation necessary and proper for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute but the court has no power to delegate to the authority to the commissioner for ascertaining facts which are required to be decided by him alone on taking evidence and that the pre-emptee has to prove improvement bona fide for the beneficial development of the case property.

e. In the case Shishir Kanti Pal and others Vs. Nur Muhammad and others reported 54 DLR 440 wherein his lordships observed in para no. 13 that the Trial Court discarded the evidence of PW.2 on the ground that he was sold the solitary witnesses as in the possession of the suit land in support of the plaintiffs case of possession since 1963, completely overlooking the provision of section 134 of the evidence Act and the further fact that the plaintiff possession was never denied by the contesting the defendant.

f. In the case Nur Mohammad and another Vs. Sultan Ahmed and another reported in 40 DLR (HCD) 369 wherein their Lordships held that failure of a party to cross examine the witnesses of its adversary on material evidence. Effect of the Rule of cross examination is not merely " a technical rule of evidence" but it is as well " a rule of essential justice" because it is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses as has been expressed in the most authoritative observation of Lord Chancellor Herschel] in the case of Browne V. Dunn, (1983) 6. R. 67. (paragraph No. 8)

14. It appears from the judgment of the Trial Court that the Trial Court discussed the evidence of PW.1 and recorded findings:-

“সুতরাং দেখা যাচ্ছে জেরায় পি ডব্লিউ-১ এবং ২ এর কাছে তেমন কোন প্রতিকুল তথ্য উতঘাটনে প্রতিপক্ষ সক্শম হন নাই। জেরাতেও প্রার্থী স্বীয় মোকদ্দমা প্রমানে সদা সচেষ্ট ছিলেন।” and discussed the evidence of the pre-emptee opposite party no. 1 and quoted the suggestion given by the petitioner and also OPW. 2 and 3 but did not discuss the evidence of Advocate Commissioner and finally, drawn conclusion that the petitioner is a co-sharer and further held the development so made during the pendency of the suit and as such, the opposite party preemptee is not entitled to the cost of the development and allowed the pre-emption case.

15. The Appellate Court, it appears that has discussed the evidence of PW.1 and held that he was not cross examined as to the knowledge of transfer and discussed the evidence of OPW.1 quoting from the suggestion and drawn conclusion that upon consideration of the evidence the date of knowledge was found to be correct and also held that the opposite party has not produced any document in support of the development cost and he has not proved the alleged development by producing any independence witness and thereby, affirmed the findings taking into consideration of the decision reported in 34 DLR 177 and 180 along with other decisions and relied the decision reported in 30 DLR 75 as to improvement cost and allowed the preemption concurring with the findings of the Trial Court.

16. In view of the submissions and counter submissions and having regard to the law regarding the concurrent findings of fact, it is necessary to look at the evidence of the preemptor who is under legal obligation to prove his case and since, the preemption case was not filed after the execution of the deed and as well as after registration under section 60 of the Registration Act rather admittedly, the case was filed after 2 years and 6 months of the execution of the deed and 1 year 4 months after the registration of the deed. The preemptor in the application for pre-emption stated to have knowledge from the local people in as much as “পরস্পর হতে জানিয়ে” and in the evidence also he has stated “লোক পরস্পর ২৩.৩.২০০৫ নোটিশের বিষয়টি প্রথম জেনে জাবেদা তুলে.....জেনেছি” and during cross examination, he stated “নালিশী জমি বিক্রি করবে কিনা সময় ভাইয়ের কাছে আমি তা শুনিনি। বিক্রির সপ্তাহ খানেক পরে বাড়ী এসেছি। এসে তাকে/ভাইকে এর বিষয় জিজ্ঞেস করিনি। কিন্তু আমি নালিশী জমিতে ও মাটি কাটতে কাউকে দেখিনি। তাতে আদৌ মাটি ভরাট করা হয়েছে কিনা জানিনা।”  and the preemptor has not produced any witness as to his knowledge on 23.3.2005 to prove his contention.

17. PW.2 has been examined to deny the development to have made by the preemptee.

18. From the above evidence of PW.1, it would be evident that he got the knowledge from the neighbor but such person or persons were not examined to corroborate his alleged knowledge. In this case, it has been found that the preemptor is co-sharer and such finding of the courts below appear to have based on documentary evidence exhibit-1 and 1(a) and I am also of the opinion that in coming to such conclusion, the courts below committed no error of law.

<u>19. The petitioner admittedly filed the case 2 years and 6 months from the deed of execution of the deed and 1 year 4/5 months after the registration of the deed under section 60 of the Registration Act and as such, burden heavily lies on the pre-emptor to prove his knowledge but the findings and conclusion have made based on solitary witness, the pre-emptor himself who is an interested witness. It is not necessary to seek, corroboration always from independent sources but in the instant case the preemptor himself stated to have knowledge from the (লোক পরস্পরে), in view of such evidence and since the petitioner filed the case beyond 4 months of the deed of registration of the deed and in such, circumstances the preemptor has to prove the knowledge in order to obtain the preemption by corroborative evidences by disinterested witnesses. It is true that under section 134 of the Evidence Act even on the testimony of the solitary witness judgment can be passed provided his credibility is not shaken but in this case, it is on evidence that the preemptor is the full brother of the seller , resides in the same house, and visited the house within 7 days after execution of the deed and continued to ignore the transfer of the case land to the pre-emptee for such a long period and in view of such evidence on record, it appears that the preemptor had failed to discharge initial onus by producing cogent and reliable evidence as to the knowledge by corroborating evidence. But such disability of proving the case has not been considered at all by the courts below and as such, I am of the view that the application for preemption is barred by limitation. There being a total non consideration as to knowledge by the courts below on this point, the findings and decisions arrived at by the courts below being perverse are not sustainable in law due to non consideration of the material evidence on record. It would be evident from the cross examination made by the pre-emptee as to knowledge the PW.1 admitted that he visited his village home frequently and at first he visited the house after 7 days of the execution of the deed, so it would baffle my comprehension that the preemptor could not have knowledge during a long period from execution of the deed as well as from the date of registration of the deed from his brother though the case land was developed and constructed but and chetal over the case land. It is found further from the evidence of OPW.2, 3 and Advocate Commissioner that the preemptor along with the PW.2 who stated that “নালিশী জমি উচু তবে এখন বাড়ী আছে।” that the pre-emptee after purchase improved the land substantially which was a nul (cultivable) land, but the courts below as it appears did not consider those evidence to its true perspective and arrived at wrong conclusion in not disallowing the pre-emption. It is also evident from the record that the petitioner did not file any objection against the report of the Advocate Commissioner and during cross examination the Advocate Commissioner specifically stated as to the development of chatal but such evidence also was not properly considered by the courts below.</u>

20. Upon over all consideration of the evidence, it appears that the courts below have misread the evidence. I have had the opportunity to go through the decisions referred by both the parties. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the decisions referred to above by the above petitioner reported in 48 DLR and 54 DLR appears to be very much applicable in this particular case, in as much as, the pre-emptor-petitioner had ignored the transfer of the case land made by his full brother for about 2½  years and in such circumstances, I am also of the opinion that the preemptor has failed to discharge the initial onus by producing witness to prove the knowledge which is essential in order to get pre-emption case. As there is no corroboration of testimony of the PW.1 regarding the knowledge, in such circumstances, on the basis of such solitary witness, the pre-emptor the courts below allowed the pre-emption which is not at all safe and a corroboration is a must. The principles laid down in the decisions referred to above by the preemptor opposite party cannot be disputed, but we cannot use those decisions profitably in this particular case as the preemptor petitioner failed to prove the knowledge.

21. In view of my discussions made above, I find sufficient substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the preemptee-petitioner and the courts while allowing the preemption have committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. I find merit in the Rule.

22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order of the courts below are set aside. Consequently, the preemption application is disallowed. The pre-emptor is at liberty to withdraw the money suit, so, deposited along with the compensation.

23. Send down the lower courts record immediately.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. T.H. Khan with Mr. Subrata Chowdhury, ------ for the petitioners. 
Mr. Hasan Ariff with Mr. Borhanuddin and Mrs. Khaleda Zaman.------ for the opposite party.
parties:
Subash Das Chowdhury and others
Vs.
Sheikh Reazuddin Ahmed Siddique, B. L. Waqf State
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin, J: This rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 25.11.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 97 of 1997.

2. The Opposite Party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 97 of 1997 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong against the present petitioners and others for declaration of title and possession of the Waqf Property in the suit land and for declaration of possession and also for injunction and recovery of possession after evicting the tenants and also for declaration that the judgment and decree in Mortgage Suit No. 2 of 1991 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat no. 2. Chittagong is void and illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff. During pendency of the suit the pre-sent petitioners who were defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the suit filed an application under Order 7 Rule 11 and section 151 C.P.C. praying for rejection of the plaint mainly on the ground that the suit is barred under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 and also under section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ordinance, 1969. The plaintiff filed written objection against the prayer for rejection of the plaint and the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer for rejection of the plaint.

3. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order rejecting the prayer for rejection of the plaint the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as petitioners moved this court and obtained the present rule.

4. Heard Mr. T.H. Khan with Mr. Subrata Chowdhury, the learned advocates appearing for the petitioner and Mr. Hasan Arif, with Mrs. Khaleda Zaman, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party No. 1. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 is an implied bar in taking cognizance of this suit and the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not holding that the suit is barred under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance. He further submits that the other prayers made in the plaint are dependent on prayer No. A and therefore a decision as to prayer A will suffice for the decision as to the maintainability of the suit in respect of other prayers. In support of his contention that the suit is barred under section 50 of the Wakf Ordinance Mr. T.K. Khan, the learned advocate has referred to section 50 itself of the Waqf Ordinance and also the case of Syed Masud Ali and others vs. Md. Asmatullah and others reported in 31 DLR(AD)249 and also the case of Syed Shah Mohammad Osman Ghani vs. Bangladesh, through Secretary M/O. Public Works and Urban Dev. and others reported in 39 DLR.451. On the other hand Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1 submitted that the case reported in 31DLR(AD). 249 has no manner of application in this case. He next submits that the case of Osman Ghani reported in 39 DLR,451 is also not applicable in the present case. He next submits that the case of Osman Ghani even if found applicable in this case this is no authority on the question whether section 50 of the Ordinance provides a bar in the institution of the suit of the present nature. Section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance provides an implied bar for cognizance of Civil Suit for any decision as to whether the particular property is Waqf Property or not. Mr. Hasan Arif has referred to the various sections of the Wakf Ordinance and submits that the Wakf Ordinance like any other statute should be interpreted as a whole. He lastly submits that the suit as framed by the opposite parties is clearly one under section 83 of the Wakf Ordinance. 1962 and the trial court has rightly rejected the prayer for rejection of plaint.

5. In order to appreciate the submission of the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party it is necessary to quote the prayer portion of the plaint of Title Suit No. 97 of 1997 which runs as follows:--

“(ক)নালিশী সম্পত্তি ও তৎস্থিত যাবতীয় গৃহাদি মরহুম শেখ রেয়াজ উদ্দিন ছিদ্দিকী বি,এল,ওয়াকফ এস্টেটের স্বত্তীয় দখলীয় সম্পত্তি হয় এবং ১/২নং বিবাদী তপশীলোক্ত সম্পত্তিতে অবৈধ দখলকার হয় মর্মে ঘোষনামূলক ডিক্রী হয়।

(খ) নালিশী সম্পত্তি স্থিত দালানের ৩য় ও ৪র্থ তলায় বাদীর দখল স্থিরতর তাহা হইতে বাদীর ভাড়াটিয়া ১৭নং বিবাদীকে গায়ের জোরে উচ্ছেদ না করার জন্য এবং তৎ ভোগ দখলে বিঘ্ন সৃষ্টি না করার জন্য ১/২নং বিবাদীকে বারন করিয়া প্রথমে অস্থা��ী ও পরে স্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার ডিক্রী হয়।

(গ) নালিশী তপশীলোক্ত সম্পত্তি হইতে ১/২নং বিবাদীকে এবং তাহাদের কথিত ভাড়াটিয়া ৪-১৬নং বিবাদীকে উচ্ছেদ ক্রমে বাদী বরাবরে খাস দখলের ডিক্রী হয়।

(ঘ) আদালতের নির্দিষ্ট মেয়াদ মধ্যে ১/২ নং ও ৪-১৬ নং বিবাদীগন আপোষে দখল ছাড়িয়া না দিলে আদালত উপলক্ষ্যে বাদী বরাবরে খাস দখল প্রদানের ডিক্রী হয়।

(ঙ) চট্রগ্রাম ২য় অর্থঋন আদালতের বন্ধকী মামলা ২/৯১ এর রায়ডিক্রী বে আইনী ও তৎ দ্বারা বাদী ও নালিশী সম্পত্তি বাধ্য নহে মর্মে ঘোষনামূলক ডিক্রী হয়।

(চ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ বিবাদীগনের বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রী হয়।

(ছ) আদালতের ন্যায় বিচারে বাদী আর যে যে প্রতিকার পাওয়ার হকদার হয় তাহা দেওয়ার ডিক্রী।”

6. From a close reading of prayer portion in paragraph-15 as quoted above it is apparent that the plaintiff in the suit has prayed for a declaration that the property described in the schedule of the plaint and the houses standing thereon belong to the plaintiff Wakf Estate having been in possession of the Waqf Estate and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are trespassers therein. In other words the plaintiffs are seeking for declaration of right, title and interest of the Waqf Estate in the suit properties and for a declaration that the defendant. 1 and 2 are mere trespassers therein. Section 83 of the Wakf Ordinance runs as follows:

"83. Administrator may Institute Suit or proceeding regarding Waqf. If there is no mutawalli or the mutawalli refuses or neglects to act in the matter, within a reasonable time, the administor may, in his own name, institute a suit or proceeding in a Court against a stranger to the waqf or any other person-

(a) for the establishment of right, title and interest in a waqf property or

(b) for confirmation of possession in a waqf property, or

(c) for the recovery of any waqf property wrongfully possessed, alienated or leased, or

(d) for having any waqf property discharged of an encumbrance or obligation wrongfully created, or

(e) for the recovery of any money belonging to waqf, or

(f) for any other relief in the interest of waqf he may consider necessary.

<u>7. Thus it appears that for establishment of right, title and interest and for confirmation of possession and for recovery of possession of the waqf property wrongfully possessed, by any person or for having any waqf property discharged of an encumbrance or obligation wrongfully created. it is the duty of the Mutawalli to institute a suit for those reliefs and if the Mutawalli refuses or neglects to do so the administrator may in his own name, can institute a suit for those reliefs as mentioned in section 83 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962.</u>

8. Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 submits that the prayer as made in the plaint are actually in the nature of the prayers and reliefs as contemplated by section 83 of the Ordinance and therefore the learned Subordinate Judge committed no error of law in rejecting the prayer for rejection of the plaint.

9. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner has drawn our attention to the prayer portion as made out in the suit of Osman Ghani's case as mentioned in paragraph-5 thereof and submits that the prayer in the present suit and in that suit is all the same. The prayer in Title Suit No. 304 of 1975 as mentioned in Osman Ghani's case in paragraph-5 runs as follows:-

"That a decree be passed declaring the property in the schedule to be a waqf property".

10. It clearly appears that in that suit a declaration was sought for to the effect that the schedule property of that suit is a waqf property whereas in the present suit the prayer is in respect of the title, confirmation and recovery of possession and eviction of the trespasser after declaring them to be a trespassers and a further declaration that certain judgment and decree passed in mortgage suit is not binding upon the waqf estate. Mr. T.H. Khan has referred to section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance which is also reproduced in Osman Ghani's case in paragraph-3 of the reported judgment. At the very outset it appears that the quotation as given in paragraph-3 of the Osman Ghani's case started as follows:- "Direction if a property is waqf Property" Whereas in the government publication it appears that there is no such heading before section 50, rather there is a marginal note that speaks of 'decision' only. Therefore the title as shown in the Osman Ghani's case in section 50 of the Ordinance and section of the DLR Publication of the Waqf Ordinance r addition of 1998 are very much misleading. There is no such title or a marginal note which Mr. T.H. Khan terms as 'Rubric' in section 50 either saying of declaration or direction. It is true that this marginal note found printed at the side of a section in an Act is sometimes used as an aid to the construction but the weight of authorities is to the effect that they are not parts of the statute and so should not be considered. Reference may made of the case of Sutton Vs. Sutton reported in (1883) 22 Chancery Division 511 and in the case of Chandler and others and Director of Public prosecutions reported in 1964 (A.C) page 763.

11. Thus we hold that since there is no mention of any declaration either in the section 50 itself or in the marginal note thereof, Waqf Administrator has no power of giving any declaration either in respect of right to property belonging to the Waqf Estate or right to any office under Waqf Ordinance.

12. Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 has referred to the preamble of the Waqf Ordinance of 1962 which speaks of purpose as to consolidate and amend laws relating to determination and management of the Waqf Property in Bangladesh and submits that the Waqf Ordinance has nothing to do with the establishment of the right, title and interest in the Waqf Properties or right to any office under Waqf Ordinance. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Dildar Ahmed Chowdhury Vs. Farroque Ahmed Chowdhury and another reported in 27 DLR(SC) 138 wherein it was held-"It could not be shown from any provision of the E.P. Waqf Ordinance that a suit even if it be of a civil nature would not lie in a civil court of ordinary jurisdiction". Mr. Hasan Arif has referred to para-11 of Dildar Ahmed's case which runs as follows:-

"11. It is to be mentioned that there is a dispute in the present case regarding the character of the waqf. The appellant contends that it is a public waqf while the respondents allege that it is a private waqf. It is a question of fact which is to be resolved on evidence. In view of a disputed question of fact involved regarding the character of the waqf on which no opinion can be expressed at this stage and which is connected with the contention raised, it is neither necessary nor is it possible to come to a finding on this contention"

13. Mr. Hasan Arif, the learned advocate appearing for the respondent No. I submits that although in that case their Lordships of the Appellate Division found that a question as to the Waqf character was very much involved even then their Lordships found the suit maintainable as because the suit of civil nature was made out in that suit as contemplated by section 9 of the C.P.C. But in the case of Syed Masud Ali and others reported in 31 DLR(AD)249 this decision was not brought to their Lordships notice. Moreover the other sections of the Waqf Ordinance particularly sections 6(six), 27(e), 47(5) and chapter-II as a whole were neither brought to their Lordships notice nor considered in that case.

14. Similarly Mr. Hasan Arif argued that in Osman Ghani's case as well section 50 of the Ordinance was considered in isolation of the other section of the Ordinance. In Osman Ghani's case a wrong heading of the section, namely, 'declaration of a property or wakf property' was supplied to their Lordships which is not there in the law. Moreover section 35 of the Wakf Ordinance was misread and it was presumed that under section 35 of the Ordinance a person aggrieved may submit a petition to the District Judge for declaration that the suit property is or is not wakf property. Whereas under section 35 an aggrieved party can only seek before the District Judge that the suit property is not waqf property. He submits that their Lordships in Osman Ghani's case found that the Waqf Ordinance is a statute confirmatory of a pre-existing right and it is reenacting or affirming a right already existing in common law and gives a special and peculiar form of remedy different from the remedy which existed before the enactment of the statute. It is well settled in respect of such statutes that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to deal with the matter is excluded unless the statute says so expressly or by necessary implication and having found that there is no express bar of suit in the ordinance proceeded under a wrong reading of section 35 assuming a power that the aggrieved person can even file a petition before the District Judge for declaration that certain property is waqf property although there is no such power in section 35 of the Waqf Ordinance. He submits that it is no authorized under the law to read in something in a section which is not there, obviously because function of the court is interpretation and not legislation. If a reference is needed case is of Md. Ismail and others Vs. The State reported in 21DLR(SC) 161. Mr. Hasan Arif Next argued that in a proceeding under a supposition that A and B are going to the Civil Court and going to the waqf Administrator it was not spelt out whether both are going for the same relief or for different relief's. He contended that A may go to Administrator for a decision that particular property is waqf property. If his prayer in the affirmative is rejected he has no remedy under section 35 of the Waqf Ordinance and therefore both A and B may not be going for the same relief. He submits that the court proceeded on the submission at the bar that the jurisdiction of the civil court and that of the Waqf Administrator is parallel, identical and alternative whereas it is not so in fact. He lastly argued that section 50 has not created an independent forum for resolution of the question regarding the waqf character of the property. Section 50 has not given waqf administrator any power to entertain an application from the parties nor it has provided for any procedure for filing of the application or the method of decision on the application. Referring to section 6 of the Ordinance he submits that the Waqf Administrator while causing a survey for waqf properties is receiving a report from the surveyor or any person appointed for the purpose and he can pass necessary order under Chapter IV of the Ordinance and therefore while deciding a report of the surveyor under section 6 of the Ordinance or any body submitting a report to him the Administrator may be called upon to decide whether the property is a waqf property or not. Again under section 40 of the Ordinance Mutawalli may be asking for opinion, advice or direction of the Administrator in respect of any Waqf Property and while giving opinion, advice or direction administrator may be called upon to give decision as to the waqf character of the property involved and again under section 47 of the Waqf Ordinance Administrator while receiving application for enrolment of the Waqf as per section 47 sub-section (3) and in the manner as provided by section 47 subsection (3) nad in the manner as provided by section 47 subsection (8) Administrator may be called upon to decide whether a property is in fact waqf property or not and therefore he submits that section 50 is not all an independent section giving independent power to the Administrator. It is an enabling power of the Administrator to decide the waqf character while functioning under any of the sections preceding section 50 as mentioned above. It is to be also considered that in the same statute while providing express ouster under section 102 of the Ordinance is it not absurd that legislature had the intention to provide for implead ouster also under section 50. It is universally accepted principal of interpretation that whenever a legislature intended to take away jurisdiction of the court it did so by express provision.

15. Mr. Hasan Arif submits that this aspect of the Waqf Ordinance has neither been discussed or decided either in Osman Ghani's case or in Sayed Masud Ali case reported in 31 DLR(AD)249. Therefore the case reported in 31DLR(AD) has no manner of application in this case.

16. In the present suit the plaintiff has not prayed for a declaration that suit property is not a waqf property rather the plaintiff is asserting that the suit property belong to the Waqf Estate and defendants No. 1 and 2 are trespassers therein. The prayer Ka in paragraph-15 of the plaint is so drafted that one part of the prayer cannot be isolated from the other because unless it is declared that the property belongs to the Waqf Estate it cannot be declared that the defendant nos. 1 and 2 are trespassers and since the prayer made in the present suit is altogether different from the prayer as mentioned in Sayed Masud Ali Case, we hold that decision has no manner of application in the present case.

17. So far the infirmity as pointed out by Mr. Hasan Arif in the case of Osman Ghani, if a decision is at all called for by this court in order to dispose of this revision surly this court will decide the various submission at the bar but we find that this civil revision can be decided even without disagreeing with Osman Ghani's case. It may not be necessary in this case to answer all the submissions of Mr. Hasan Arif on the interpretation of section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance.

18. In view of the prayer as made in the plaint in the present suit before us it is obvious that the plaintiff of the present suit is praying for a decree for the establishment of right, title and interest of the waqf estate in the schedule property. Therefore we hold that it is a suit in respect of right to property of the waqf Estate which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Administrator to decide and the jurisdiction of the Administrator is connected with the control and management of the Waqf Estate and the Waqf Administrator cannot entertain a case of the present nature as is before us. If a person goes to the Administrator for removal of a mutawalli in a petition and if the Administrator refuses the prayer he has no remedy before the District Judge under section 32 of the Ordinance and he is to go to the civil court for the relief as has been found in the 27 DLR case as referred to above and section 32 is not exhaustive similarly section 50 read with section 35 of the Waqf Ordinance is also not exhaustive inasmuch as a person aggrieved by the order of the Administrator refusing to decide if particular property is waqf property cannot go to the District Judge under section 35 because section 35 provides that aggrieved person can seek for a declaration that the property is not waqf property and therefore the present plaintiff had no occasion to go to the administrator because he is not aggrieved by any decision of the Administrator rather he is asserting that property in question belong to the waqf estate. For such purpose section 50 is no answer nor section 35 is an answer. This view of ours is supported by a decision in the case of 1. Makhulal Haq Khan vs. Administrator of Waqfs Estate Pakistan, Dacca. 2, Ekramul Huy, Inspector of Waqfs, Noakhali reported in 17 DLR, 30 wherein it was held that "In an appeal tinder section 35 against a decision taken under section 34, the Mutawalli or any person claiming any interest in the property can only agitate that the property in question is not a wakf property within the limits stated in the petition of appeal". Similarly in the case of Yar Ali Khan Chowdhury Vs. Administrator of Wakfs, Government of Pakistan and others reported in 20 DLR, 535 it was held-"The Administrator has no power to fix rent of a wakf property and for such a purpose the administrator must take resort to section 83 of the Waqf Estate. With regard to the bar under section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ordinance, 1969 the finding of the trial court relying on the case of Chaina Arjuman Banu Vs. Rupali Bank Limited and others reported in 14 BLD, 321 is based on sound principle of law.

19. In view of our discussions and findings as above we find that the present suit as has been made out in the plaint is maintainable and section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance is no bar in taking cognizance of by the civil court and by the impugned order the trial court has not committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and therefore the impugned judgment and order does not call for any interference by this court.

In the result this rule is discharged without however any order as to costs.

End.

Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, Mr. Mahmudul Islam, Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud ------- for the applicants. 
Mr. Manzill Murshed ------- for the petitioners.

parties:
Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh and Others
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and Others
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This is an application for direction/modification at the instance of Heidel Hergeement Bangladesh.

(i) The applicant is represented by Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, a learned Advocate of this Court.

2. Licence/permission for construction of use of jetty as a semi pucca structure on the river Shitalakkhya was given by BIWTA by a memo dated 22.9.1998 to M/S. Scancem Bangladesh Ltd. subject to payment of necessary fees. After that, three companies, namely, (1) Scan Cement Bangladesh (2) Scancem International Ltd. and (3) Chittagong Cement Clinker Grinding Co. Ltd. were merged into the name of Chittagong Cement Clinker Grinding Co. Ltd. The name of Chittagong Cement Clinker Grinding Co. Ltd. was changed to its present name, Heidel Berg cement Bangladesh Ltd. The applicant is one of the multinational conglomerates of the world. The applicant's factory has been established upon huge foreign investment. At present it employs 300 employees.

3. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud submits that the applicant's jetty is situated on the river Shitalakkhya and is crucial for smooth and continued operation of its factory. He further submits that in its judgment, this Court directed removal of unauthorized structures but not any authorized structure built under the licensee of BIWTA. He also submits this the notice, Annexure-X to the application, is defective. He then submits that the applicant being a licensee under the BIWTA, its authorized constructions cannot be demolished. He lastly submits that BIWTA stated that the interest of its lessees should be protected. We shall address the submissions of the learned Advocate later.

(ii) This is an application for direction at the instance of ACI Salt Limited. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, a learned Advocate of this Court, represents this applicant. The applicant prays for directing the respondents not to evict the applicant from the foreshore land covered by its licence.

4. The applicant is a private company limited by shares. The applicant constructed a hi-tech factory on its land. The applicant applied to the conservator of BIWTA to construct jetty and use foreshore land adjacent to the land of the applicant. Pursuant to a year-to-year licence first granted on 29.1.2005 the applicant constructed a jetty and other structures on the foreshore land.

5. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, learned Advocate for the applicant, submits that admittedly, the applicant is a licensee under the BIWTA and that the jetty and other structures were constructed under the licence of BIWTA and as such, those structures of the applicant cannot be demolished. He further submits that the judgment speaks of illegal construction, and not of any legal construction and as such, the applicant's structures are protected and that the respondents cannot evict applicant therefrom.

(iii) This is an application for direction at the instance of Kamal Vegetable and two others.

6. The applicants are represented by Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, a learned Advocate of this Court.

7. Applicant No. 1 is a limited company having an industrial undertaking for refining of vegetable oil and applicant Nos. 2 and 3 are its Managing Director and Director respectively.

8. Applicants Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed and Ms. Yeasmin Alam purchased the land covered by S.A. Khatian No. 76, S.A Plot Nos. 658 ,659, 660, 661 and 662 of Mouza-Dapa Indrakpur, Fatudlah on 2.10.2010. Those applicants also acquired the shares of Kamal Vegetables Oil Mills. The applicants got their names mutated in Mutation Khatian No. 1897 in respect of land measuring 2.35 acres of which .09 acre is occupied by a graveyard. The applicants have been enjoying the land by establishing vegetable oil refining factory. The Roads and Highways Department tried to demolish the structures of the applicants but could not succeed because of a direction made by this Court in Writ Petition No. 3120 of 2007. Applicant No. 1 also obtained licence for 494 square meter of land from BIWTA on the basis of lease for one year. The lease has since been renewed from year-to-year. The joint survey was conducted beyond the knowledge of the applicants who purchased the land and established oil refining industry investing about Tk.100 crore.

9. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, learned Advocate for the applicants, submits that the joint survey was conducted beyond knowledge of the applicants and the notice for eviction is illegal and without jurisdiction.

10. We shall address this point later.

(iv) This is an application for review of the judgment and order dated 24 and 25 of June, 2009 and the order dated 24.1.2010 at the instance of Mollah Salt (Triple Refined) Industries Ltd.

11. The applicant is represented by Mr. Abdul Baset Mujamder, a learned Advocate of this Court.

12. The applicant is a private limited company engaged in production of refined edible salt by establishing an industry on the bank of Buriganga of Narayangonj Port. The applicant applied for licence to BIWTA and obtained year-to-year licence for construction of jetty as evidenced by Annexure-B series.

13. Mr. Abdul Baset Mujamder, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the applicant is a licensee under the BIWTA and as such, it cannot be designated as unauthorized occupant and cannot be evicted therefrom and as such, the judgment should be reviewed.

(v) This is an application for direction made by applicant No. 1 City Sugar Industries Ltd, (2) City Vegetable Oil Mills Lt, (3) Deepa Food Products Ltd and (4) Fazlur Rahman who is the Managing director of applicant Nos.1 to 3.

14. The applicants are represented by Mr. Mahmudul Islam.

15. Applicant No.1 set up its industry and made an application to BIWTA for construction of a semi pucca jetty on the eastern side of the bank of Sitalakkahya river. Licence was granted in favour of applicant No. 1 for one year. Applicant No.2 obtained similar licence for construction of semi pucca jetty and setting up a pipe line of oil on the foreshore on the eastern side of the river Shitalakkhya. Their licenses are being renewed from year-to-year. Applicant No. 3 set up its industry and made an application to respondent No. 7 for construction of RCC jetty on the same river. Licence was granted to the applicant, which was renewed from year-to-year. On 14.10.2010, the applicants received two notices both dated 9.2.2010, Annexure-F series, directing the applicants to remove their structures by 20.2.2002. The applicants filed Writ Petition No. 1393 of 2010 on 16.2.2010 challenging those notices. The Writ Petition was summarily rejected on 23.2.2010. The applicants filed Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal 148 of 2010 before the Appellate Division. On 24.2.2010 the learned chamber Judge fixed the matter for hearing on 1.3.2010 in Court No. 1 and the matter appeared in the list on 4.3.2010. But their lordships refused to pass any order of stay. The applicants were directed to file regular Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal.

16. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that the four jetties constructed by the applicants were authorized and legal and as such, the notices were illegal. He further submits that the respondents cannot issue the notices as they were not authorized to do so under Article 102 (2) (a) (i) of the Constitution. Referring to section 10 to the Port Act, Mr. Islam submits that only the Conservator can issue such notices but not the respondents mentioned in the notice.

(vi) This an application for direction not to remove or evict the two jetties and conveyor belt of the applicant, Akij Cement Company Limited.

17. This applicant is represented by Mr. Rafique-ul Huq.

18. The applicant is a private limited company by shares. The applicant purchased 5.92 acres of land from the Government of Bangladesh. The applicant constructed a cement factory on the land investing Tk.200 crore. The applicant obtained two licenses for construction of two jetties from BIWTA for one year. The licenses have since been renewing from year-to-year. By amending the licenses, BIWTA allowed the applicant to construct larger jetties.

19. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq has made similar submissions as made by him before.

20. It is contended that the judgment speaks of unauthorized constructions and not of authorized ones. The judgment Must be considered as a whole and not in isolation.

21. Paragraph 17 of the judgment passed in the case of Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh and Others Vs. Government of Bangladesh, (2009) 17 BLT (AD) 455 deals with the change of course of rivers and with alluvial land. This paragraph states about long term lease and not of year-to-year licence.

22. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Advocate, has referred to 4 lines from paragraph 17 of the judgment in the case of Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh and Others Vs. Government of Bangladesh and Others, (2009) 17 BLT (AD) 455.

যদি সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্তৃপক্ষ কর্তৃক আইনানুগতভাবে, বিলিবন্দোবস্ত করণ ব্যতিরেকেই কেহ দখলদার থাকেন তাহা হইলে সরকার তাহাকে উচ্ছেদ করিবার জন্য যথযথ আইনানুগ পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করতঃ উক্ত ভূমির দখল অবিলম্বে পুনরুদ্ধার করিবেন।

23. Having gone through the four lines, we find that their Lordships were of the opinion that the persons, who are possessing the land within the territory of the four rivers without valid permanent lease, were liable to be evicted. The four lines referred to above do not appear to be of any avail to these applicants.

24. Paragraph 20 speaks of the measures to be taken after completion of the survey. We would like to quote a few lines from paragraph 20 as under:

‘‘একই সঙ্গে নদীগুলির চিহ্নিত সীমানা অভ্যন্তরে অবস্থিত সকল স্থাপনাগুলি ব্যতিক্রমহীনভাবে ভাঙ্গিতে হইবে ও অপসারণ করিতে হইবে। নদীর অভ্যন্তরে অবৈধ মাটি, বালু বা স্থাপনা থাকিলে তাহাও অপসারণ করিতে হইবে। ইহার সম্পূর্ন খরচ সরকার পিডিআর আইন এর এর মাধ্যমে অবৈধ দখলদারগণের নিকট হইতে আদায় করিতে পারিবেন। অবৈধ দখল সংক্রান্ত অপরাধের জন্য তাহাদের বিরুদ্ধে সরকার ফৌজদারী দন্ডবিধি অনুসারে প্রয়োজনীয় পদক্ষেপও গ্রহন করিতে পারিবেন”।

25. From the above, we find that paragraph 20 of the judgment deals with the action to be taken after completion of the survey and the lines referred to above in no uncertain terms stated that all structures within the territory of four rivers be demolished without any discrimination after completion of the survey. The words "সকল স্থাপনা গুলি" shall mean and include both legal and illegal structures. The word, `তাহাও' used in the sentence " নদীর অভ্যন্তরে অবৈধ মাটি, বালু বা স্থাপনা থাকিলে তাহাও অপসারণ করিতে হইবে" makes this sentence independent of the sentence" একই সঙ্গে নদীগুলির চিহ্নিত সীমানা অভ্যন্তরে অবস্থিত সকল স্থাপনাগুলি ব্যতিক্রমহীনভাবে ভাঙ্গিঁতে হইবে ও অপসারণ করিতে হইবে।"

26. We would like to quote paragraph 21 as under:

‘‘এখানে উল্লেখ্য যে, বর্তমানে ৪টি জেলার সংশ্লিষ্ট নদীগুলির অভ্যন্তরে অবৈধ দখলদার কর্তৃক নির্মিত নির্মানাধীন সকল স্থাপনা অপসারনের যে কার্যক্রম চলিতেছে তাহা অব্যাহতভাবে চলিতে থাকিবে। আরও উল্লেখ্য যে, নদী অভ্যান্তরে অবৈধ স্থাপনা অপসারণের ব্যাপারে কোনরুপ ব্যতিক্রম চলিবে না। অবৈধ স্থাপনা তাহা যাহারই হউক না কেন এবং তিনি যত বড় শক্তিশালীই হউন না কেন বা তিনি যে গোষ্ঠীরই হউন না কেন, বৈষম্যহীন এবং ব্যতিক্রম ছাড়া তাহা অপসারণ করিতে হইবে”।

27. Having gone through the entire paragraph 21, we find that this paragraph stated about the drive that was going on the date of pronouncement of the judgment against the illegal occupants within the territory of four rivers. The words "যে কার্যক্রম চলিতেছে তাহা অব্যাহতভাবে চলিতে থাকিবে" used in this paragraph are very significant. Their Lordships stated about the drive that was going on at the relevant time but not about the action to be taken after completion of the survey. Therefore, the word ‘অবৈধ’ occurring in this paragraph is not of any help to the applicants. Paragraph 21 in no way speaks about the structures to be demolished after completion of the survey. Consequently, this paragraph is of no assistance to the applicants.

28. It is also stated that in directive (ga) the word `অবৈধ' was not wrongly mentioned. Having analyzed paragraphs 17, 20 and 21, we find that this contention does not have any substance.

29. It is contended that notice under section 5(1) and (2) of the Ordinance 1970 is defective. The eviction drive is being carried out according to the directions of the judgment pronounced in Writ Petition No.3503 of 2009. Therefore, what form was used for issuance of notice upon the applicants is immaterial. Admittedly, the applicants are year-to-year licensees under BIWTA. After obtaining licenses from BIWTA the applicants made permanent jetties within the rivers and their foreshore land. The photographs annexed to some of the applications show that massive R.C.C. constructions were made within the rivers not to speak of the foreshore land of the rivers. What prompted BIWTA to allow the applicants, who are year-to-year licensees, to make huge constructions within the territory of rivers including the rivers is shrouded in mystery. Construction of massive jetties within the rivers and their foreshore land impedes the normal flow of the rivers and encourages others to intrude within the territory of the rivers. In addition to above, survival of the four rivers surrounding Dhaka City is linked to the survival of the capital city Dhaka. The structures made by the Government organizations within the rivers and their foreshore land only for public utility service shall remain intact and those structures do not tentamount to encroachment on the rivers.

30. It is contended that the notices served upon the applicants stated about illegal structures and not of legal structures and as such, the structures of the applicants cannot be demolished.

<u>31. The judgment speaks of all sorts of structures meaning thereby both authorized and unauthorized and as such, the word ‘অবৈধ’ used in the notices cannot protect the structures of the applicants.</u>

32. Mr. Manzill Murshed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that a company made a floating jetty in one of the rivers and that no notice was served upon that company for removal of the floating jetty. By referring to section 10 of the Ports Act 1908, it is contended that only the Conservator can issue notice under section 10 of the Ports Act for removal of the structures of the applicants. We have already found that the eviction drive is being carried out according to the directions given in the judgment delivered in Writ Petition No. 3503 of 2009 and as such, the contention does not stand to reason.

33. In order to implement the judgment, year-to-year licenses granted to the applicants can not stand on the way.

34. We would like to quote a few lines of paragraph 6 of the judgment delivered in the case of Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra Vs. U.P and Others, AIR 1985 SC 652 as under:

"This environmental disturbance has however to be weighed in the balance against the need of lime-stone quarrying for industrial purposes in the country and we have taken this aspect into account while making this order."

35. Paragraph 8 of the above judgment as under:

"We would also give the same direction in regard to the lime-stone quarries in the Sahasradhara Block even though they are placed in category B by the Bhargav Committee. So far as these stone quarries in Sahasradhara Block are concerned, we agree with the Report made by the Working Group and we direct that these lime-stone quarries should not be allowed to be operated and should be closed down forthwith. We would also direct, agreeing with the Report made by the Working Group that the lime-stone quarries placed in category 2 by the Working Group other than those which are placed in categories B and C by the Bhargav Committee should also not be allowed to be operated and should be closed down save and except for the lime-stone quarries covered by mining leases Nos. 31, 36 and 37 for which we would give the same direction as we are giving in the succeeding paragraphs in regard to the lime-stone quarries classified as category B in the Bhargav Committee Report. If there are  any subsisting leases in respect of any of these lime-stone quarries they will  forthwith come to an end and if any suits  or writ petitions for continuance of expired or unexpired leases in respect of any of these lime-stone quarries are  pending, they too will stand dismissed".

36. Having gone through the paragraphs quoted above, we are of the opinion that in the instant case nothing including year-to-year licenses shall stand on the way of implementation of the judgment.

37. In this connection it is important to note that on February 5, 2010, a special forest Bench of Indian Supreme Court headed by Chief Justice Balakrishnan stayed mining in Maghalaya Forest. Prior to the order of stay, Lafarge was mining in Meghalaya to carry

limestone to its cement plant in Bangladesh over a 17 Km conveyor belt. (The Daily Star dated 31.3.2010).

38. Indian Supreme Court passed the order of stay for protection of a forest not to speak of a human habitation like its capital city. We have already stated that survival of the four rivers is linked to the survival of the capital city, Dhaka.

39. It is wroth mentioning the case of M.C. Mehta V. Union of India, AIR 1997 SC 734, popularly known as Taj Mahal Case. In order to protect Taj Mahal from environmental pollution, the Supreme Court of India passed directions to 292 industries located and operating in Agra to change-over within fixed time schedule to natural gas as industrial fuel or stop functioning with coal/coke and get relocated.

40. The judgment further reveals that the 212 industries which did not respond to the notice and failed to take any step towards installing the pollution control devices were closed by the order dated August 27, 1993 with immediate effect. The closure order was to operate till the time necessary pollution control devices were to be set by the industries concerned.

<u>41. Applicant No. 1 City Sugar Industries Ltd., (2) City Vegetable Oil Mills Ltd., (3) Deepa Food Products Ltd and (4) Fazlur Rahman, who is the Managing Director of applicant Nos. 1 to 3 filed Writ Petition No. 1393 of 2010 on 16.2.2010 challenging the notices annexed to the present application. The Writ Petition was summarily rejected on 23.2.2010. The applicants tiled Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 148 of 2010 before the Appellate Division. On 4.3.2010, the Appellate Division instead of passing any interim order of stay directed the applicants to file a regular Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal. Therefore, it appears that the Appellate Division is in seisin of the eviction notice issued by the respondents.</u>

42. Additional stand is taken in the application of Kamal Vegetable and two others that they were not aware of the survey and that no notice was served upon them prior to the survey. The survey was conducted according to the direction of this Court to determine the territory of the four rivers surrounding the capital city, Dhaka. The survey revealed that the applicants encroached upon the territory of the river. Therefore, the applicants are also liable to be evicted. These applicants also take the stand that there is a graveyard on .09 acre of land. A graveyard within the territory of the river is also not protected.

43. In the applications it is stated that BIWTA has taken the stand to protect the interest of the licensees. BIWTA is a party to this Writ Petition as respondent No. 7 and it should have challenged the judgment before the Appellate Division. Instead of doing that the present stand of BIWTA is unfortunate.

44. In the judgment their lordships also observed as under:

আরও উল্লেখ্য যে, এই রীট মোকাদ্দমায় প্রদত্ত বিভিন্ন নির্দেশনা সম্পর্কে কোন সংশয়ের উদ্দেক হইলে দরখাস্ত কারী বা অন্য পক্ষ বা অন্য যেকোন প্রতিবাদী হাইকোর্ট বিভাগের সংশ্লিষ্ট বেঞ্চের নিকট নির্দেশনা প্রার্থনা করিতে পারিবেন।

45. Therefore, we are of the view that the present applications filed by the applicants are maintainable. Some of the applicants also filed applications for addition of party. The lines quoted above show that such an addition is not necessary.

46. The learned Attorney General submits that if any immediate step is taken for demolishing the jetties, there may be price hike in market.

47. Having considered all aspects of the case, we are also of the opinion that in order to enable the applicants to go to the Appellate Division, a reasonable time should be given to them. In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any substance in these applications filed by the applicants.

48. Accordingly, all the applications are rejected on merit.

49. The respondents are directed not to demolish any structures of the applicants for a period of 1(one) month so that the applicants may move the Appellate Division in the meantime, if so advised.

50. The applications for addition of party filed by the different applicants be kept with the record.

End.
