full_judgment:
Faruque Ahmed, J.: This rule at the instance of the plaintiff petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree complained of in the revisional application should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Short facts of the case are as follows:-

The petitioner, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Madhukhali, Faridpur against the defendant (Opposite Party) for recovery of possession by evicting the defendant in respect of 5 decimals of land more fully described in the schedule of the plaint.

3. The defendant (Opposite Party) field a written statement and contested the suit.

4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Madhukhali, Faridpur decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 25.05.1999, holding that the defendant had not been in possession of the disputed land earlier and the plaintiff had been able to prove her case.

5. The defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 before the District Judge, Faridpur, and the same was transferred to and heard by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Faridpur who set aside the aforesaid judgment and decree and sent back the case on remand to the concerned lower court for fresh trial (trial afresh) with the observation,

“বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালতকে বাদী রেসপন্ডেন্টকে আরজি সংশোধন পূর্বক নালিশী দাগের জমিতে স্বত্ব সাবস্ত্য পূর্বক বন্টনের ও খাস দখলের প্রার্থনা করার লক্ষ্যে আরজি সংশোধনের সুযোগ দিয়া এবং আরও সাক্ষ্য প্রমাণ উপস্থাপনের সুযোগ দিয়া এবং বাদী রেসপনন্ডেন্টের আরজি সংশোধনের প্রেক্ষিতে বিবাদী আপীল্যান্ট যদি অতিঃ বর্ননা ও সাক্ষ্য প্রমান দিতে চায় উহা দেওয়ার সুযোগ দিয়া মুল মোকদ্দমাটি অল্প সময়ের মধ্যে নিষ্পত্তি করিতে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল। আর যদি বাদী রেসপন্ডেন্ট আরজি সংশোধন না করিয়া মুল মোকদ্দমাটি তুলিয়া লইতে চায় তবে আইনানুযায়ী বিধি মত ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের জন্য বিজ্ঞ আদালতকে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল।”

6. After remand of the case, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Madhukhali after hearing both the parties dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 04.05.2003.

7. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff petitioner preferred Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 before the District Judge, Faridpur, and the same was heard on transfer by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Faridpur, who dismissed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 18.09.2005.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid appellate judgment and decree, the plaintiff petitioner obtained the present rule.

9. Mr. A.B.M. Matiur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner placed the revisional application, the impugned judgments and decrees and submitted that the original suit being a suit under Section 9 of Specific Relief Act there was no provision for filing an appeal against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 and as such the filing of Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 by the defendant opposite party was a nullity in the eye of law and therefore the order of remand dated 08.08.2001 passed by the learned appellate Court was also nullity and the subsequent rehearing of the suit after remand and the subsequent judgment and decree dated 08.05.2003 passed in the said suit as well as the subsequent Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 preferred against that decree and that the judgment and decree dated 18.09.2003 passed in the said appeal by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court Faridpur (the impugned judgment and decree) which are nullity and non existent in the eye of law and as such are liable to be set aside and the original judgment and decree dated 25.05.1999 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Madhukhali, Faridpur in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 should stand good and remained unaffected. The learned Advocate further submitted that when there is no provision for appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, the subsequent filing of appeal by the defendant opposite party, the remand order passed in the said appeal including the order for amending the plaint, subsequent judgment and decree passed in the said suit and subsequent appeal No. 49 of 2003 also are illegal and nullity as there was inherent lack of jurisdiction by the appellate Court.

10. None appears to oppose the rule.

11. On perusal of the impugned judgments passed by the learned Courts below, it appears, the learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record by his judgment and decree dated 25.05.1999 once decreed the suit directing the defendant to vacate the suit land within 45 days, against which Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 was filed before the District Judge, Faridpur which was allowed by judgment dated 08.08.2001 sending the case on remand to the learned trial Court with direction to the plaintiff for amendment of the plaint and that after remand order the learned trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 04.05.2003 dismissed the suit. Against which, Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 was filed by the plaintiff petitioner which was also dismissed by judgment and decree dated 18.09.2005, against which the present revision has been filed by the plaintiff petitioner.

12. The only question to be decided now whether the filing of Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 and subsequent Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 were in accordance with law. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that since there is no provision for appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, the filing of said appeals and the judgment and decree passed in those appeals all are nullities. In order to appreciate the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner let me consider the provision of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act which reads as follows:-

"9. Suit by Person Dispossessed of Immoveable Property: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immoveable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.

Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.

13. No suit this section shall be brought against 9[the 10Government]

"No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed."

14. Thus a close reading of the said provision of section 9 shows that no appeal lies from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under said section. So the only remedy lies against such decree/order is the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his submission has referred to several decisions to the effect that though the plaintiff petitioner appeared in those appeals and contested and also complied with the order for amendment of the plaint the plaintiff petitioner can challenge those as nullity. The learned Advocate has referred to the case of Ashiny Kumar Karmaker Vs. Hari Mohan Shil and others reported in 1984 BLD (AD) page 29 wherein their lordships of the Appellate Division held as follows:- "that jurisdiction of Court is created by statutes and that it can neither be conferred nor taken away by agreement or consent of parties to a litigation or of their lawyers". The learned Advocate for the petitioner then referred to the case of Karimuddin and others Vs. Aftabuddin Ahmed and others reported in 14 BLD page 134, wherein it has been held that "any decision arrived at by a Court having no jurisdiction to try the case, is a nullity". It appears in that case the plaintiff filed a suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of possession and at that time the village Court had exclusive jurisdiction for such kind of matters. In the said judgment his lordship held that since the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to try the case the judgment and decree passed by the Civil Court is a nullity. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also referred to the case of SAM Mahbub Elahi represented by Md. Jahangir Alam Vs. Md. Shah Alam and others reported in 8 BLC page 484 wherein a single Bench of this Court held that when a decree has been passed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in favour of the petitioner, it is binding upon the opposite party unless it is set aside/varied by an order passed under revisional jurisdiction and any order passed by the Court of appeal will be without jurisdiction and not sustainable in law. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly referred to the case of the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Shafiuddin son of late Md. Asuruddin reported in 10 BLT (AD) page 50 wherein it was held that:- "it is by now well settled that consent or waiver cannot give jurisdiction where there is inherent lack or absence of it and in that case the order is a nullity".

15. Thus from the aforesaid decisions it is clear that the proper remedy was by way of filing a revisional application in the High Court Division instead of filing an appeal before the District Judge against the judgment and decree dated 25.05.1999 passed in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998, but in the present case the defendant first time filed Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 which was allowed vide judgment dated 08.08.2001 sending the case on remand to the learned trial Court. After remand the trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 04.05.2003 dismissed the suit. Against which the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 which was also dismissed vide judgment dated 18.09.2005. Against which the present revisional application has been filed by the plaintiff petitioner.

<u>16. A question may arise that the plaintiff petitioner having not raised the objection as to maintainability of the appeal filed by the defendant (for the first time) and the plaintiff himself subsequently having filed the appeal (for the second time) in the wrong forum whether the plaintiff can now raise this question. In reply it can be said that the questions of jurisdiction may be of 2 kinds one is the question of territorial/pecuniary jurisdiction, and another is the question of lack of inherent jurisdiction. When a question comes or is raised that a Court has exercised its territorial jurisdiction or pecuniary jurisdiction though that Courts has/had no such jurisdiction, it has been held by our apex court that in that case the objection to be raised by the parties is a material one, and if no objection is raised, and the case is tried/heard by a Court having no pecuniary or territorial jurisdiction, then that judgment will not by a nullity, but when a case is tried by a court having no territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction then it can be said to be a case of total lack of inherent jurisdiction and the judgment will be a nullity.</u>

17. In the case referred to above in 10 BLT (AD) 50 it has been held that by now it is well settled that consent or waiver cannot give jurisdiction where there is inherent lack or absence of it, and in that case the order is a nullity. So in the present case the learned appellate Court had no jurisdiction, in other words, there was inherent lack of or absence of jurisdiction of the learned appellate Court to entertain this kinds of appeal, and as such, in my opinion, the learned appellate court committed error in law occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree which are liable to be set aside.

18. Accordingly, the rule is made absolute, without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 49 of 2003 as well as in Title Appeal No. 244 of 1999 are set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court dated 25.05.1999 in Title Suit No. 25 of 1998 are restored and maintained.

19. The order of injunction at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated.

20. Send down the L.C. Records immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Mamnoon Rahman, J: In an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 7.9.2008 passed by the Joint District Judge, Court No.2. Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No.38 of 2008 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 27.3.2008 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge Sadar Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Case No.53 of 2007 (Pre-emption) rejection an application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No.1 as pre-emptor instituted Miscellaneous case being No.53 of 2007 on 15.8.2007 under section 96(1) (III) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Dinajpur against the petitioner and others opposite parties for pre-emption.

3. The case of the pre-emptor is the transfer the case property by title deed dated 24.11.2005 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor and subsequently the pre-emptor came to know about the alleged transfer and filed the case on 15.8.2007.

4. The petitioner purchaser entered appearance and filed an application under order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the miscellaneous proceeding on the ground that the pre-emptor has no locus standi to file a pre-emption case as contiguously land owner because of the provision laid down in Act 34 of 2006 and since the proceeding is barred by law the pre-emption application itself is liable to he rejected. The opposite party contested the same by filing written objection and the trial Court after hearing the parties and considering the facts and circumstances rejected the application.

5. Being aggrieved the opposite party moved before the District Judge by way of appeal being miscellaneous appeal being No.38 of 2008 and the same was heard and dispose of by the Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dinajpur who vide the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the judgment and order passed by the trial Court. rejecting the prayer for rejection of the miscellaneous application.

6. Mr. Abdul Quiyum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that both the Courts below without applying their judicial mind and without considering the facts and circumstances and specially the provisions of law most illegally and in an arbitrary manner rejected the application thereby the Courts below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. He submits that the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a miscellaneous proceeding is very much maintainable in view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred the decisions reported in 13 BLD (1993) (AD) 57. By placing the Act 34 of 2006 he submits that the aforesaid provisions of law came into force with effect from 20.9.2006 and from than a contiguous land owner cannot invoke the provision of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption and in the case in hand since the transfer is after promulgation of the aforesaid Act, the miscellaneous proceeding is hopelessly barred by law and thus attract the provision of order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the miscellaneous case is liable to be rejected. The learned Advocate by referring section 60 of the Registration Act submits that in numerous decision this Court as well as our Apex Court came to a conclusion that for the purpose pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act transfer means transfer as per section 60 of the Registration Act not the date on which the sale deed was executed. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 123, and 3 BLT (1995) (AD) 134. He further submits that there is no ambiguity in the present case in hand and as such on the question of law the miscellaneous case can be rejected which is apparent on the face on record i.e. Act 34 of 2006. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred a decision reported in 1 ADC 254. Regarding the question of maintainability of the appeal as raised by the learned Advocate for the opposite party. He submits that there is a Specific provision for preferring appeal and in view of the specific provision in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the petitioner preferred appeal otherwise the petitioner would have preferred the procedure laid down in section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Mr. Serajul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party vehemently opposes the Rule. He submits that both the Courts below on proper appreciation of the facts and circumstances, provisions of law has rightly refused to entertain an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure thereby the Courts below committed no error of law occasioning failure of justice. By referring the judgment passed by the Courts below he submits that both the Courts below on concurrent finding of fact and law came to a clear conclusion that the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable and in view of the concurrent finding of fact this Court sitting on revision cannot interfere in such proceeding. By referring the decisions reported in 57 DLR (AD)18, 56 DLR (AD) 210 and 56 DLR (AD)179 he submits that while dealing with an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Courts below cannot go beyond the plaint in any manner and the Courts below is to confine itself within the four corner of the plaint and in the case in hand the Courts below committed no illegality as because the Courts below considered the application by confined themselves within the plaint itself. By referring the decision reported in 58 DLR 110 he submits that the very filing of the appeal is not maintainable as because in the aforesaid decision the parties preferred revision and the same was maintained by the appellate Court.

8. I have perused the impugned judgment and order, judgment and order passed by the trial Court, revisional application, grounds taken thereon, annexures, provisions of law, decisions as referred to and heard the learned Advocates for the contesting parties. On perusal of the same it appears that the opposite party No.1 as pre-emptor filed a miscellaneous case for pre-emption claiming himself as a contiguous land owner of the case property. The present petitioner who is the pre-emtee purchaser filed an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the miscellaneous case as the same is being barred by law. The Courts below rejected the application for rejection of the miscellaneous case.

9. In numerous cases this Court as well as our Apex Court came to a conclusion that the provisions laid down in the Code of Civil procedure is very much applicable in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950. In the case reported in 13 BLD (AD) 57 their Lordships held;

"This submission has no legs to stand. Section 141 C.P.C. provides that the procedure provided in the C.P.C. in regard to suits shall be followed as far as it can be made applicable in all proceedings in any Court of civil jurisdiction.

10. In view of the aforesaid decisions it appears that an application under order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be maintained in a miscellaneous proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act since the proceeding is a miscellaneous one.

<u>11. In the case in hand it appears that the pre-emptor instituted the case on 15.8.2007 and the alleged kabula was executed on 24.11.2005. It appears that the legislature amended the provision laid down in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with effect from 20.9.2006 vide Act 34 of 2006. By the said amendment the legislatures debarred a contiguous land owner from invoking the right of pre-emption. In the case in hand the pre-emptor opposite party No.1 invokes under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as contiguous land owner.</u>

12. Section 96(18) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (as - amended) by Act 34 of 2006 runs as follows;

"Nothing in this section shall apply to any transfer of any portion or share of a holding of a raiyat or any application under section 96 of this Act, made prior to coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006."

13. So it appears that the aforesaid amendment is applicable from the date of its operation and any transfer may before operation of the new amendment the subsequent amendment shall not applicable.

<u>14. It appears that in the case in hand though the sale deed was executed on 24.11.2005 but the case was filed on 15.8.2007 i.e. the sale deed was executed before the amendment and the case was filed after the amendment. The pertinent question raised in this case is whether the transfer "is made before or after amendment."</u>

<u>15. Section 60 of the Registration Act deals with the provisions regarding issuance of certificate. The question of transfer in a miscellaneous proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act raised time and again and this Court as well as of our Apex Court came to a conclusion that the transfer in the case of pre-emption is the transfer as per section 60 of the Registration Act, not the date of the execution of the sale deed.</u>

<u>In the case of Abdul Motalib vs. Iman Ali Molla and ors. reported in 42 DLR (AD) 123 their Lordships held as follows;</u>

16. We that a long line of decisions of the erstwhile Dhaka High Court has followed the principle that when registration is compulsory, the date of accrual of the right of pre-emption is not the date of execution of the deed of sale or any earlier date or the date of presentation for registration but the date on which the deed of sale is registered and the title effectively passes. The earliest case is that of Noab Mian Bhuiyan V. Golam Hossain, 13 DLR 889. In the case of Muhammad Meher Ali Mondal V. Muhammad Karam Ali Laskar, 17 DLR 365, J.Sayem (as his Lordship then was) delivering the Division Bench judgment, pronounced as follows.

17. It is section 60 of the Registration Act which supplies the answer to the question as to when a document is considered to be registered. In our view, the language of section 60 admits of no doubt that it is the certificate in compliance with the provision of this section that makes a document a registered document. The document can not be regarded as registered before the certificate is endorsed thereon and signed, sealed and dated in terms of section 60, nor has it to wait for acquiring the character of a registered document till after compliance with the other provisions that follow section 60. Their Lordships of the privy Council having had an occasion to refer to this section in the case of Muhammad Ewaz V. Birj Lal (ILR 1 All 465) observed that, "that certificate is that which gives the document the character of a registered instrument.

18. To the same effect is the case of Ajimuddin pramanik V. Najemuddin Mondal. 17 DLR 231. Azimuddin Bhuiyan V. District Registrar, Dhaka 20 DLR 355 and Abdur Rahman V. Baser Ali, 21 DLR 599."

19. In the case of Md. Moslemuddin and another vs. Md. Abdul Hakim and others reported in 1995 (III) BLT (AD) 134 their Lordships held as follows;

"Dr. Ahmed Husain, learned Advocate for the petitioner has urged before us the ground of limitation only. He has questioned the view of the High Court Division that for the purpose of preemption the date of transfer will be the date of registration of the kabala, whereas under section 47 of the Registration Act, a transfer takes effect from the date of execution of the kabala. This is a question which has been long settled by a series of decisions to the effect that transfer within the meaning of section 96 of the state Acquisition Act, is completed when a certificate is issued by the registering officer that the document has been registered. Registration is a process which is completed on the dated this certificate is issued. This has nothing to do with the date from which the transfer takes effect. For the purpose of filing an application for pre-emption, it is the date of registration which is of material importance. The next question urged by the leaned Advocate is that in this case the respondents knew of the transfer long before the date of registration, and as such limitation will start form the date of this knowledge. There is hardly any substance in this argument for, the right to preemption accrues on the date the kabala is registered, and from this date, the application for preemption in this case was filed within the prescribed time."

<u>20. So it appears that the transfer for the purpose of pre-emption is not the transfer by execution of sale deed but the transfer as per section 60 of the Registration Act which is admittedly in the case in hand after promulgation of Act 34 of 2006. Since before Registration of deed of sale under section 60 of the Registration Act the law came into operation as such the pre-emptor in the case in hand is barred by the said Act 34 of 2006 claiming the right of pre-emption as a contiguous land owner. Admittedly as per the decision reported in 1 ADC 254 in there is any doubt or allegation regarding the nature of transaction the Court requires to examined the case on merit and admittedly there is no scope to go beyond the plaint while dealing in an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code. But in the case in hand it is apparent on the face of the new law namely the amended under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the pre-emption case is hopelessly barred by law. The Courts below ought to have considered this aspect by applying their judicial mind and by interpreting the law in its true perspective.</u>

<u>21. Regarding the question of revision or appeal it appears that all the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure is to be followed in any proceeding in the absence of any specific provision. But on perusal of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it appears that the same contained a specific provisions for filing of appeal and as such the petitioner committed no illegality in filing the appeal before the lower appellate Court below.</u>

22. Considering the facts and circumstances, I find sufficient reasons to interfere. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order passed by the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment and order passed by the trial Court is hereby set aside. The application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure preferred by the petitioner is hereby allowed. The miscellaneous case is rejected.

23. Communicate this order at once.

End.

Mr. Shafique Ahmed, Senior Advocate with Mr. Mahbub Shafique, Mr. Golam Mohiuddin, Mr. Saifuddin Md. Aminur Rahim, Advocates ------ For the Respondent Nos. 4, 6 and 7
