full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed, J: This Application under Section 81 read with Section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 ("the Act") is being considered in conjunction with Rules 8 and 263 of the Companies Rules, 2009 ("Rules"). At the time of admission of this Application on 6.1.2015 an Order of Stay was granted staying the operation of Form XII submitted on 9.12.2014 (Annexure-`GG') and Form XII submitted on 22.12.2014 (Annexure-TP(1))'. A direction was concomitantly issued upon the Respondent Nos. 4, 6, 7 and 8 preventing them from representing themselves as the Managing Director ("MD"), Chairman or Directors of the Respondent No. 2 Company ("Company") and desist from interfering in the peaceful holding of the 77th Board of Directors ("BOD") Meeting of the Company scheduled for 7.1.2015 as well as subsequent BOD meetings until further Orders.

2. It no transpired, however, that on 19.1.2015, and at the very heels of the orders and directions as above cited, a prayer was made on behalf of the Respondents that, and pursuant to the 10th Annual General Meeting ("AGM") held on 20.12.2014, the Company was somehow constrained to credit 15% bonus shares by 20.1.2015 to avoid being otherwise listed as a "Z" category company. It was in that exceptional context, and notwithstanding anything contained in the Order of Stay of 6.1.2015, that this Court ordered for such 15% bonus share to be credited "in CDBL/concerned account, as prayed for".

3. The Petitioners before this Court are shareholders-directors of the Respondent No. 2 Company, Shurwid Industries Ltd. presently a public limited company, incorporated under the Act. Indeed, the Company was incorporated on 163.2004 initially as a private limited company. The share-structure of the Company, as evident from the Application itself, had already undergone several changes when on 24.3.2010 the Company vide a Special Resolution adopted at an Extraordinary General Meeting ("EGM") changed its name from "Shurwid Industries (Pvt.) Ltd." to "Shurwid Industries Ltd.", converted from a private to a public limited company, increased its authorized share capital and wholly overhauled its Articles of Association. The Respondent No. 3 Bangladesh Securities & Exchange Commission ("BSEC") vide Memo No. SEC/CPCPLC-237/10/231 dated 26.7.2010 is further noted to have accorded its consent to an increase in the paid-up share capital of the Company pursuant to which the Company proceeded with a further allotment of shares.

4. Notably, in 2013 the complexion of the BOD was as follows:

Sl. No.	Name of Directors	Designation	Change

1. 	Mrs. Syeda Sayma Akhter 	Director  Petitioner No. 3	Existing as a Director from 24.12.2011

2. 	Md. Anis Ahmed	Chairman Petitioner No. 1	Existing as a Director from 24.12.2011 as well as Chairman

3.	Mr. Zahedul Hoque	Managing Director Petitioner No. 2	Existing as a Director from 24.12.2011 and Managing Director for 2 (two) years from 04.2.2012.

4.	Mahmudul Hasan	Director Respondent No. 4	Existing as a Director from 22.12.2012

5.	Ahmed Kabir Majumder	Director	Retired and re-elected as a Director on 27.12.2013

6.	R.Y. Sharnsher	Director	Existing as a Director from 22.12.2012.

7.	Syed Golam Wadud	Director	Existing as a Director from 22.12.2012

8.	Daedal Merchant Alliance Ltd. Nominee Director its Delwar Hossein Titu	Nominee Director	Retired and re-elected as a director on 27.12.2013

9.	Eurodesh Consumer Products Ltd. Nominee Director its Alim Al Razy 	Nominee Director	Retired and re-elected as a Director on 27.12.2013.

5. The BSEC at that juncture vide Memo No. SEC/C1/1P0-146/2011/255 dated 21.4.2014 accorded its consent for the Company to go for an Initial Public Offer (WO). The Company's enlistments with the Dhaka and Chittagong Stock Exchanges followed duly in September, 2014.

6. The 63rd BOD Meeting of the Company proves a convenient starting point for this case. At this meeting the BOD vide resolution dated 6.2.2014 elected the Petitioner No. 1 Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed as Chairman for the year 2014. It is also at this meeting that the Petitioner No. 2 Mr. Zahidul Hoque was appointed as MD subject to approval at AGM.

7. At the 64th BOD meeting held on 27.3.2014, the Respondent No. 4 Mr. Mahmudul Hasan raised a suggestion to appoint Mr. Zahedul Hoque as acting MD till 31.10.2014, but it appears that a majority of the directors approved Mr. Hoque's appointment as a regular Managing Director instead.

8. Though the matter of reappointment of the MD was broached at the 70th BOD Meeting of 1.10.2014 the Board did not deviate from its decision taken at its 63rd Meeting to the effect that the MD had been appointed for two years subject to approval at AGM. Thereafter, on 27.10.2014 the 1300 at its 71st Meeting fixed 20.12.2014 for holding the Company's 10th AGM for the calendar year 2014 as well as for holding 4th EGM. In the meantime the BOD at its 72nd Meeting of 5.11.2014, by a majority decision, appointed Mr. Zahedul Hoque as MD from 21.12.2014 to 31.12.2016 deciding further to place such appointment before the ensuing AGM of 20.12.2014 for approval.

9. This, therefore, proved to be the immediate context against which the Company proceeded to hold its 10th AGM on 20.12.2014. The events that transpired on that date, by the Petitioners' contention being wholly disruptive of the due holding and transaction of the Company's business at the AGM/EGM and necessitating the filing of this Application, are described by the Petitioners thus:

"...thereafter on 20.12.2014, shareholders of the respondent No. 2 company started attending at the registered office of company at Gazipur to participate in the AGM and EGM. The directors of the company also took their seats at 10 am at the podium. But before starting meeting, the respondent No. 4 showing a document started screaming aloud and stated that the petitioner No. 1 was Chairman until 19.12.2014 and on 20.12.2014 he not being chairman he cannot preside over the meetings and also there being no Chairman, the respondent No. 4 (Mr. Mahmudul Hasan) claim that no meeting can be continued The said respondent No. 4 distributed a Particular of Directors (Form-XII) dated 09.12.2014 wherein 0 is seen that the tenure of petitioner No, 1 as Chairman expired on 09.12.2014. This PD dated 09.12.2014 is signed by the respondent No. 4, which is false and fabricated. At this stage, the hooligans rented out by the respondent No. 4 started vandalism at the meeting place and the petitioners were compelled to postpone the said AGM and EGM

... the petitioner No. 1 immediate vide email dated 20.12.2014 at 12.41 p. m sent scan copies of letters dated 20.12.2014 (two letters) to Bangladesh Securities & Exchange Commission. In the said letters dated 20.12.2014 the petitioner No. 1 informed that due to vandalism perpetrated by some unruly shareholders and outsiders, the petitioner No. 1 as Chairman postponed the 4th EGM and 10th AGM In effect, the said actions of postponement were cancellation of the said 4th EGM and 10th AGM, since no meeting can be postponed sine die without fixing time, date and place of the adjourned meeting.

.....the following the Company Secretary of the respondent No. 2 company vide letters dated 21.12.2014 (two letters) informed BSEC that the meetings of 4th  EGM and 10th AGM have been postponed, and provided the video CD of the same along with the said letters

……further on the same date the Secretary of the respondent No. 2 company vide letter dated 21.12.2014 informed BSEC that the declaration of postponement of 4th EGM and 10th AGM in the Daily Shamokal dated 21.12.2014.

...the Company Secretary of the respondent No. 2 company vide letter dated 21.12.2014 also informed RJSC that the said 4th EGM and 10th AGM have been postponed

....on the other hand the respondent No. 4 in a very criminal manner sent a letter dated 21.12.2014 to Dhaka Stock Exchange and Chittagong Stock Exchange Ltd. stating that the said 4th EGM and 10th AGM were held duly.

...the Dhaka Stock Exchange vide Memo No. DSE/Listing/504/2014/11691 dated 23.12.2014 and Memo No. CSE/Com-LD/Shurwid/AGM/2014 dated 24.12.2014 of Chittagong Stock Exchange Ltd. asked the respondent No. 2 company as to actual status of the said meetings.

...the company secretary of the respondent No. 2 company vide letter Nos. SIL/BSEC/2014/50 and SIL/BSEC/2014/51 both dated 24.12.2014 explained the whole situation to Dhaka Stock Exchange and Chittagong Stock Exchange respectively."

10. Thereafter, Mr. Mahmudul Hasan and the Respondent No. 6 Mr. Md. Tuhin Reza, Nominee Director, are alleged to have manufactured a Schedule-X dated 20.12.2014 and filed the same with the Respondent No. 1, Registrar, Joint Stock Companies And Firms ("RJSC"). Messrs Hassan and Reza are also alleged to have manufactured the minutes of the 4th EGM dated 20.12.2014 and a Form XII dated 22.12.2014, showing themselves as MD and Chairman respectively, both of which they are stated to have submitted with the RJSC on 30.12.2014.

11. At the same time, the Petitioner No. 1 Chairman Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed on 30.12.2014 issued a notice for holding the 77th BOD Meeting for discussing the following agenda:

"AGENDA

1. To elect Mr. Anis Ahmed, Director as Chairman of the company as per Article 90(b) for five years from 2015 to 2020.

2. To elect Mrs. Syeda Sayma Akhter as new Managing Director.

3. To appoint two independent directors.

4. To appoint a committee consisting of three members to coordinate business in the factory and market under the supervision of the Managing Director.

5. To take decision in respect of fake Particulars of Directors (Form-XII) and fake minutes of purported 4th Extraordinary General Meeting prepared and submitted by Mr. Mahmudul Hasan and Mr. Md Tuhin Reza.

6. Miscellaneous"

12. The Petitioners contend that due to vandalization perpetrated by Messrs Hassan and Reza, the 4th EGM was not held but the Respondent Nos. 4 and 6 nevertheless manufactured and fabricated the Minutes of the said EGM of 20.12.2014 which now requires to be set aside by this Court. The prayer is also for both the Schedule-X and the Form XII of 22.12.2014 as above noted allegedly falsely prepared and submitted to be set aside by this Court.

13. Learned Advocate Mr. Mahbub Shafique has appeared in this case for the Respondent Nos. 4, 6 and 7. He submits that the Petitioners' Application is inadequate in a lack of justification for invoking Section 85(3) of the Act. No explanation, he submits, is found in the Application of the nature of impracticability that this Court must address. That shortcoming, Mr. Shafique deduces, places an onerous responsibility on the Petitioners to rebut the presumptions of regularity and validity attaching under Section 89(3) of the Act to the calling and holding of company meetings and to transactions therein. Drawing on these contentions, Mr. Mahbub Shafique paints a picture of an intractable situation created further by this Court's Order of 19.12015 permitting 15% bonus shares to be credited as above noted. Mr. Shafique would at the end of the day have this Court appreciate that the 4th EGM and 10th AGM, ostensibly held upon fulfilling the quorum requirement, ultimately stand the test of law. He asks, therefore, whether, given such circumstances a finding on impracticability may reasonably be made to undo the consequences flowing from such meetings.

14. This Court's intervention in this Matter is predicated at the very outset in its reading of Section 3 of the Act as defines the contours of its jurisdiction and the treatment of the same in various judicial pronouncements. This Court finds that Section 3 incorporates the essence of the exclusivity of this Court's jurisdiction under the Act subject, however, to the proviso therein. Evidently, the Government till date has had no cause to invoke its power under the proviso to empower any District Court to exercise any jurisdiction under the Act retaining intact, therefore, the exclusivity of this Court's jurisdiction under Section 3 (Moqbul Ahmed vs. Ahmed Impex reported in 48 DLR (AD)(1996)82, paragraph 11 at page 84). That being the case this Court fully subscribes to the view of Mr. Justice K.M. Hasan, as he was then, in Abdul Muhit vs. SIBL reported in 54 DLR (2002), 306, in paragraph 19 at page 309 thus:

"I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates, perused the applications, affidavits-in-opposition and papers annexed to them. It is settled by a long line of decisions reported in 19 DLR 735, 20 DLR (SC) 335, 28 DLR (SC) 101, 44 DLR 452, AIR 1936 (Allahabad), (Full Bench) 830, 79 Company Cases 830, AIR 947 Madras 322 that unless jurisdiction is provided in the Companies Act the petitioners cannot come to this Court for violation of any provision of the Act. The Company Court has a special company jurisdiction and that jurisdiction has to be found from specific provisions of the Act. Some of the specific provisions giving this court jurisdiction may be found in sections 12, 60, 43, 81, 85(3), 156, 197, 233 and 241. The "Court" referred to in these sections has been defined in section 2(d), according to which the "court" means court having jurisdiction under this Act. Section 3 (1) of the Act while giving jurisdiction to the court states "The court having jurisdiction under this Act shall be the High Court Division."

15. It is that special "Company Jurisdiction" that constitutes the starting point of considering the maintainability of this Application as raised by the Respondents along with the more substantive grounds raised by both parties. Indeed, this special statutory jurisdiction as attaches to this Court by reference to certain very specific provisions of the Act, inclusive of Section 81 and indeed 85(3), came to be endorsed in Abdul Mobil Major (Red) Dr. Rezaul Haque vs. Social Investment Bank Ltd. reported in II ADC (2005) 492. The Appellate Division's findings on the exclusivity of this Court's statutory jurisdiction under the Act, therefore, paved the way for and anticipated the provisions of Rule 9 of the Rules. Locating such jurisdiction within the perimeter of Section 85(3) has also led this Court to delve into the maintainability of this Application given that this is a case not of an ordinary general meeting or EGM not held but rather of meetings held and business transacted therein allegedly without conformity to law. The question posed, therefore, is with regard to this Court's authority to deliberate on matters already transacted at the said meetings of 20.12.2014. The response to that perceived dilemma comes through a catena of decisions of which Satish Chandra Banik vs. Dhaka Jute Mills Ltd. reported in PLD 1968 (Dac) 610 as well as in 19 DLR 280 and Ghyasuddin Ahmed vs. Faruque reported in 38 DLR(AD)(1986)296 are most noteworthy.

16. These authorities affirm this Court's ample powers under Section 85(3) to give ancillary directions to call hold and conduct meetings in such manner as it deems fit and expedient. The ratio decidendi of these two cases has notably been the basis for this Court's decision in A.B.M. Khaliquzzaman & ors. vs. United Commercial Bank Ltd. & another reported in 2LCLR [2013] Vol. 2 HCD,101 as well as 28 BLD HCD (2008) 635 as affirmed by the Appellate Division in Reazaul Karim vs. ABM Khalequzzaman reported in 62 DLR (AD)(2010) 411.

<u>17. Furthermore, in revisiting these cases in Mazakat Ali Harun vs. EXIM Bank Ltd. reported in 18 BLC (AD) (2013) 68 the Appellate Division in reaffirmation of its pervious judgment in the Reazaul Karim Case, confirms this Court's entrenched authority to revisit the proceedings of any AGM or any company meeting to examine the legality of business already previously transacted therein. Any finding of illegality in such a context has been found as ground enough for this Court to nullify any transaction and require and direct meetings to be held afresh regardless of the fact of a previous meeting. The Appellate Division in the Mazakat Ali Harun Case delved extensively into a catena of precedents to arrive at the following decision at paragraph 17 at page 77 thus:</u>

<u>"Thus this Division has already laid down the law that even if AGM of a company is held and f it is found that any business was not transacted in accordance with law the Company Court can very much given ancillary directives in the matter of holding AGMs under section 85(3) of the Act, 1994 including the power to order a meeting of the company to be called, held and conducted in such manner as it thinks fit and expedient."</u>

<u>18. This Court, in the facts and circumstances, finds no reason to digress from that finding of the Appellate Division in the Mazakat Ali Harun Case. Having, accordingly, found no constraints in the law in the exercise of this Court's jurisdiction in this case, it is the law itself that must, therefore, constitute the starting point of the consideration of not only the substantive issues involved but also the issues of the Petitioners' standing and of an ostensibly intractable situation consequent especially upon this Court's Order dated 19.1.2015.</u>

19. Noting Mr. Mahbub Shafique's reservations on treating the Petitioners as directors by reason variously of the Respondents' invocation of Sections 91(2), 108(1)(c) and 110(2) of the Act, this Court finds nothing in this case to deny the Petitioners their status as directors-shareholders of the Company. Such status, especially as shareholders as is not disputed, amply qualifies the Petitioners under Section 81(2) read with 85(3) to place an application as this before this Court.

<u>20. A perusal of the Application and a consideration of all documents brought on record attests to an unusual set of circumstances converging at a point in time, thereby, signifying a marked break in the chain of events ensuing from the 63rd DOD meeting of 6.2.2014 down to the issuance of the notices dated 29.11.2014 for the 4th EGM and the 10th AGM. Materials on record, including video recordings of the meetings viewed by this Court, are in evidence of an adjournment of proceedings very early on in the course of the 4th EGM for reasons making it impracticable for the Company to transact business as per the agenda in the notices of 29.11.2014. Any purported conduct of business at any time immediately thereafter in supposed continuation of the same proceedings is viewed by the Petitioners to be shorn of all legal basis. On the other hand, issue is taken by the Respondents that this Application stops short of expressly raising the spectra or ground of impracticability of conducting business further at the 4th EGM and 10th AGM in conformity with the notices of 29.11.2014. The Respondents argue that it shall, accordingly, not now be open to the Petitioners, through oral submissions made as an afterthought, to make out a case meriting judicial intervention under Section 85(3). That stance, this Court finds, is somewhat misconceived given that the source of this Court's power to intervene in such circumstances under Section 85(3) has clearly been located and identified as above. It matters not to this Court that the Application may not bear express reference to the term "impracticability" so long as the focal contention therein and materials on record clearly establish to this Court's satisfaction the elements of impracticability (M/s. Ali Reza vs. Artha Rin Adalat, 2nd Court & Another reported in 15 BLT (AD) 2007, 323 and Col. Md. Hashmat Ali vs. Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR (AD) (1995)1). Indeed, Mr. Mahbub Shafique himself referring to the consequences following upon this Court's Order of 19.1.2015 has raised the spectra of intractability in further governing the affairs of the Company since 20.12.2014. That Order, therefore, is said to have made it impossible for this Court to devise a solution as prayed for by the Petitioners. Indeed, Mr. Shafique here emphasizes the fine line of distinction that any Court under Section 85(3) must draw in distinguishing "impracticability" from "impossibility" in guarding against undue interference in the internal affairs of a company. In response, this Court holds that subject to maintaining that jurisdictional balance and its neutrality, this Court must also explore all avenues feasible to override any issue that stultifies its statutory jurisdiction to Act under Section 85(3).</u>

21. The test in this regard of the feasibility of holding AGMs and the removal of the impediment at the Court's discretion has succinctly been laid down by the Chancery Division in the RE El Sombrero Ltd. Case in the context of the U.K. Companies Act, 1948 thus:

"It is conceded that the word "impracticable" is not synonymous with the word "impossible"; and it appears... that the question necessarily raised by the introduction of that word "impracticable" is merely this: examine the circumstances of the particular case and answer the question whether, as a practical matter, the desired meeting of the company can be conducted, there being no doubt, of course, that it can be convened and held"

22. It suffices at this juncture to note that certain principles do indeed govern the exercise of this Court's authority under Section 85(3) in particular. These principles were perhaps best succinctly laid down by Chief Justice Fazle Munim in the Ghyasuddin Ahmed Case thus:

(1) regard is always to be had to the Articles of Association of the company;

(2) it is incumbent upon the Court to maintain neutrality and not be seen as getting involved in the internal management of the company; and

(3) the court will draw at the outset an essential distinction between "impracticability" and "impossibility" in further calling and holding meetings of the company.

23. These precepts have duly determined this Court's remit to observe and find in this case as hereunder.

24. It has been for this Court to pinpoint the identity of the Chairman of the BOD who on 20.12.2014 was vested with the authority under law and the Articles, to preside over the meetings. That inquiry draws on the minutes 63rd BOD meeting of 6.2.2014 as approved and confirmed the Petitioner No. 1, Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed to continue as Chairman for the year 2014, thereby, raising the presumption that his tenure would last until 31.12.2014. Such approval and confirmation of Mr. Anis Ahmed's continued status until end- 2014 as Chairman appears also to be based on Article 90(b) of the Articles that mandates such election by the BOO. In the period leading to the issuance of the Notice of 29.11.2014, there is no record of any BOD decision endorsing a different management view of any person other than Mr. Ahmed legally or feasibly officiating as the Company's Chairman.

<u>25. A Chairman's status endorsed in law and the Articles is significant in reflecting the authority to preside over the Company's general meetings. Regulation 54, Schedule I of the Act read with Article 65 of the Company's Articles clearly endorses that view. Material on record, both textual and audio-visual, amply establish that at the initial stages of convening and holding the meetings Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed, as Chairman, made an abortive attempt to conduct the same until such time as he was constrained to adjourn the meetings and leave the venue.</u>

<u>26. The Respondents assert that the meetings were revived and continued unhindered to transact assigned business as attested to by subsequent statutory filings concerning election of office-bearers etc. These developments have brought to fore the role played in particular, by the Respondent Nos. 4 and 6 of whom the latter was shown to have been elected as Chairman under Section 85(2) of the Act. Section 85(2), this Court notes, allows for any member to be elected as chairman by the member present at a meeting only in so for as the Articles do not make other provisions in this behalf. The Company's Articles, it is found, regulate stringently the exercise of such extraordinary powers by members by reference to specific Regulations of Schedule 1 of the Act.</u>

27. The power reserved in the members of a company to respond to certain contingencies ensuring, thereby, that their will is reflected at meetings duly called, convened and held is regulated by Regulations 54, 55 and 56, Schedule 1 of the Act. Regulation 54 incorporates the BOD's authority to select one of its members as Chairman with authority to preside at every general meeting. Regulation 55 provides that the absence from any meeting of the Chairman beyond thirty minutes after the time appointed for holding such meeting would entitle the members present to choose someone of their number to be the Chairman. Regulation 56 allows the Chairman, with the consent of any meeting at which quorum is present, to adjourn meetings from time to time and from place to place and prohibits any business to be transacted at any adjourned meeting other than the business left unfinished at the meeting from which the adjournment took place. Additionally, the Company's Articles contains no bar to the application of these Regulations. On the contrary provisions similar to and clearly drawing on Regulations 54, 55 and 56 remain incorporated in the Articles by virtue of Articles 90(b), 65 and 67 thus:

"90(b) Mr. Anis Ahmed shall be a Chairman of the Company to be nominated by the board dissection.

65. The Chairman of the Company shall be entitled to take the Chair at every General Meeting. If there be no Chairman or if at any meeting he shall not be present within fifteen minutes after the time appointed or holding such meeting or is unable to be present due to illness or any other cause or is unwilling to act, the Vice Chairman will preside over the meeting and in his absence or if he is present but not willing to act, the Directors present may choose one of their members to act as Chairman of the meeting and in default of their doing so the members present shall choose one of the Directorates(sic) to take the Chair and if no Director is present or Directors present are not willing to take the Chair, the members present shall choose one of the members to be the Chairman of the Meeting.

67. The Chairman, with the consent of the majority of the members present, may adjourn any meeting from time to time and from place to place."

28. Accordingly, the Petitioner No. 1, Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed clearly authorized by a series of BOD resolutions dating at least from 6.2.2014 to act as the Company Chairman being present at the venue and at the initial stages of the holding of the 4th EGM and having categorically and clearly adjourned further proceedings of the EGM and consequentially the 10th AGM, it is difficult for this Court to see by dint of what residual or inherent authority the said meetings were revived at the heels of such adjournment. Such renewal of the meetings and the appointment and assumption of authority by Respondent No. 6, Mr. Md. Tuhin Reza as Chairman is found to be wholly unauthorized and illegal.

29. There is of course the issue of the Form XII Particulars of Directors etc. submitted on 9.12.2014 being a date falling in between the issuance of the notices of 29.11.2014 and the holding of the meetings on 20.12.2014. This document, one of two documents the operation of which was stayed by this Court's initial Order of 6.1.2015, is of some significance. This Form: XII purportedly reassigns the statuses as Chairman and Managing Director of Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed and Mr. Zahedul Hoque respectively in a manner and extent not anticipated by or resolved upon at any BOD meeting beginning with the 63rd Meeting of 6.2.2014. The altered status of Mr. Ahmed as "Existing As a Director from 24/12/2011 As Well as the Chairman to 19/12/2014" and of Mr. Zahedul Hoque as "Existing As a Director from 24/12/2011 and the period of Managing Director was expired on 4/02/2014" (Annexure-`GG') is not substantiated by any material on record indicating the date, manner and reason for such reassignment in marked departure from the tenor and purport of the BOD decisions adopted from 6.2.2014 onwards.

<u>30. It is to be noted that any Form XII filing presupposes prior changes, in particular, introduced to the status of directors and the filing of the same within a specified period as laid down in Section 115(2) (b) of the Act. Section 115 applied to the facts and circumstances requires a formal act of introduction of such change at a duly convened meeting of the BOD at any time prior to 9.12.2014 as can attest to the veracity and legality of that document's content. By that reason this Court has good reason to question the provenance of this document and indeed the intent behind it. Clearly, therefore, the Form XII in Annexure-`GG', is found to be shorn of all legality from which no legal consequences ensue. The mere fact of it bring already filed with the RISC does not clothe it with any clement of legality in such a case. That leads this Court to conclude that the continuity and effect of the decisions taken at the 63rd, 64th, 70th  71st, and 72nd BOD meetings between 6.2.2014 and 5.11.2014 did indeed, and continue to, constitute the essential legal basis for the notices of 29.11.2014 and pursuant to which an attempt, albeit an abortive one, at holding meetings was made with the Petitioner No. 1 in the chair on 20.12.2014.</u>

31. This Court is also satisfied that the adjournment of such meetings categorically and emphatically made by the Petitioner No. 1 presiding over the same did not consequentially equip the membership body of the Company or indeed the other directors present at the venue, for lack of quorum, to revive the meeting at the heels of such adjournment and transact business in the manner that they did. The veracity of the contents, consequentially, of the Form XII: Particulars of Directors (Annexures- 'PP(1)') of 22.12.2014 as were also the subject matter of this Court's ad interim Order of Stay of 6.1.2015 are, therefore, suspect.

32. Predicated on the above, this Court finds that the juncture at which the 4th EGM and 10th AGM were adjourned on 20.12.2014 by the Petitioner No. 1 as Chairman marks the point at which all agenda of the notices of 29.11.2014 must be presumed in the eye of law to be held in abeyance until such time as it becomes more practicable for the Company to revive the said meetings. It necessarily follows that from such adjournment onwards all business transacted at the purported meetings of the Company are devoid of any legality and constitute a nullity. All consequences stemming therefrom are found to be equally illegal and void. Indeed, the Form XII of 22.12.2014 is equally to be treated as a document from which no legal and substantive effect follows. The bottom line, the final legal reality, is that after the initial adjournment of the meetings by the Petitioner No. 1, Mr. Anis Ahmed as Chairman nothing transpired on 20.12.2014 and nothing followed therefrom.

<u>33. There remains the issue of the seemingly intractable situation resulting from this Court's Order of 19.1.2015 allowing, a prayer to calculate 15% bonus shares by 20.1.2015 and for these to be credited in the CDBL/concerned account in avoidance of the risk of the Company's categorization as a "Z" category company. In line with the findings above this Court also finds the Company's decision to credit 15% bonus share to be equally illegal given that this also constitutes park of the business transacted illegally. Even given the complexity of the interests attaching to such bonus shares now declared a nullity, this Court is convinced, however, that no element of impossibility of this Court's intervention under Section 85(3) is raised by that reason. It is here that this Court has considered the role of a key stakeholder in this case, i.e., the Respondent No. 3 Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC). Abreast with these proceedings, the BSEC and indeed the two Stock Exchanges, DSE and CSE, have kept an account of the events of 20.12.2014 and beyond. Pertinently, the Company Secretary Mr. Saham apprised these bodies of the turn of events of 20.12.2014 putting them on enquiry of the circumstances that contributed to such incidents. BSEC's Enquiry Report of 5.1.2015 comprises of recordings and findings of fact short of arriving at any substantive decision until this instant Matter remains sub judice. As stated in its Affidavit, the BSEC has until now held back at taking necessary punitive and/or rectifying action as necessary in discharge of its statutory duty in deference only to this Court's authority and until such time as this Court is in seisin of finally disposes of this Matter. This Court's "verdict", BSEC submits will be the crucial determinant for it to take "necessary steps/action in compliance of the judgment and order passed by the Hon'ble Court in accordance with law". This stance of the BSEC is also reflected in the minutes of its 5380 meeting held on 10.2.2015. In this context, the BSEC's Affidavit aptly appreciates this Court's authority under the Act and Rules to address directions to the BSEC as indeed was done, for example, in MA. Quasem Member of MAQ Paper Industries Ltd vs. The Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firers and others reported in 34 BLD (HCD)2014, 650. Furthermore, it is not to be lost sight of that Sections 17 to 20A, 21, 22, 23, 24 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 ("Ordinance"), and Sections 8, 17(ka), 17(kha), 18 and 20 of the Securities and Exchange Commission Act, 1993 ("1993 Act"), among others, represent a fairly stringent regulatory regime governing the securities market in this jurisdiction. These provisions that permit the BSEC to take enforcement measures as necessary am further reinforced by BSEC's directives and orders issued at regular intervals of which SEC Order of 30.5.2006 issued under Section 2CC of the Ordinance and gazetted on 20.8.2006 has featured prominently in this case. That Order, addressed to issuers of security as the Company with the purpose of imposing further conditions to consent previously accorded to the issue of capital in Bangladesh obliges the Company, inter alia, to</u>

<u>"make continuous and uninterrupted audio visual recording of the entire proceeding of its annual general meeting" and to "furnish a copy of the same in unedited form within the shortest possible time but not later than three working days from the date of holding of the said annual general meeting to the Commission and the Stock Exchange(s)"(Emphasis added).</u>

34. Evident from the BSEC's Enquiry Report of 5.1.2015 further is that both parties to these proceedings have submitted individual video recordings of the proceedings of the meeting of 20.12.2014. An evaluation of these recordings figure prominently in the Enquiry Report. This Court having also viewed the said audio-visual recordings finds that it is only with regard to an evaluation of the content of such recordings that the BSEC's Enquiry Report comes closest to arriving at a substantive finding. These findings are reproduced herein below for ease of reference:

"Findings:

v) After reviewing the audio visual record of CD of the aforesaid meetings' proceeding sent by S.K Saha, the company secretary of Shurwid Industries Limited, it has been found that huge indiscipline was created by some attendances of the meeting at the very inception (after reciting from Holy Quran) of the meeting; causing the scheduled 4th EGM could not be held and conducted at scheduled time on 20.12.2014, and later on. Mr. Anis Ahmed, Chairman of the meeting adjourned the proceeding of the meeting and left the venue. And. the proceeding of the scheduled 10th AGM could not be commenced at that time.

vi) It is further viewed from the above audio visual record of CD of the aforesaid meetings' preceding that, some attendances were shouting in the name of "Tuhin Reza" and some were shouting in the name of "Anis Ahmed" to be elected as chairman at the meeting.

vii) The enquiry committee also reviewed the second audio visual record of CD of the aforesaid meetings' proceeding sent by Mr. Eng. Mahmudul Hasan.  After reviewing it has been found that, only 02 Directors (namely Mr. Eng. Mahmudul Hasan and Mr. Tuhin Reza) out of 5 (five) directors were present on the 4th EGM and 10th AGM of the company.

viii) Also it has been found that, the CD that submitted by Mr. Eng. Mahmudul Hasan to the Commission was not continuous and uninterrupted audio visual recording the entire proceeding of the meetings." (Emphasis added)

35. The BSEC's role as a key stakeholder in the securities market and its involvement by dint of the gazetted Order of 30.5.2006 in the present case has led this Court to explore BSEC's enforcement role under the Ordinance and the 1993 Act. It is not readily evident, however, if liability is to attach to any party producing any recording that is not "continuous and uninterrupted". It is deemed fit, therefore, to direct the BSEC in full conclusion of its inquiry process already undertaken to probe into the lapses of the Respondent No. 4 Mr. Mahmudul Hasan in this regard. The BSEC is further to consider if any adverse finding shall necessitate any punitive or rectification measures to be adopted.

36. This Court is constrained further to issue a more specific direction to the BSEC. This pertains to determining the justification of the Respondents' prayer on 19.12015 for crediting the 15% bonus shares failing which it was alleged that the Company would risk categorization as a "Z" category company. In doing so, the BSEC shall be well advised to additionally consider whether such prayer, given the juncture at which it was made, constituted any violation of the Ordinance, the 1993 Act or rules and regulations made thereunder and, thereby, an offence within the securities market regulatory regime. In this it would be for the BSEC to take note of this Court's annulment of all Company proceedings in the EGM and AGM of 20.12.2014 post-adjournment of the same by the Chairman Mr. Md. Anis Ahmed. The BSEC shall be at liberty to investigate in this regard and take adequate steps in tandem with measures to be adopted by the Company as per the this Court's directions hereinafter provided:

(a) the Company is, hereby, directed to call, hold and conduct afresh the 10th AGM, and if need be the 4th EGM, upon fresh issuance of notices for both meetings in the terms and incorporating the agenda as reflected in the notices of 29.11.2014;

(b) fix afresh a Record Date falling within a minimum of 15 (fifteen) days but no more than 21 (twenty-one) days prior to the date of the fresh AGM/EGM ensuring due compliance with Regulation 46 of the Depository (User) Regulations, 2003 and ensuring that all shareholders members of the Company whose names are to be found in the list of members as prepared by the CDBL read with the share register of the Company can duly attend the meetings held upon notice issued in keeping with the relevant provisions of the Act; and

(c) as a necessary corollary to the intent and purport of the Securities and Exchange Commission Order dated 30.5.2006 gazetted on 20.8.2006, and without detracting in any way from the declared provisions of that Order, the BSEC shall ensure the attendance of two representatives duly authorized by it to attend the Company's AGM/EGM and monitor and observe the proceedings and report to BSEC duly.

37. This Court also, hereby, directs the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies and Firms to consider as nullified and expunged the Company's filings being, in particular, Forms XII Particulars of Directors of 9.12.2014 and 22.12.2014 and a Schedule X of 22.12.2014 and to accept afresh all requisite returns, reports and documents, including the relevant Schedule-X Annual Summary of Share Capital to be filed by the Company relating to the 10th AGM held as per this Court's Order. Bearing in mind the directives and conditions above, the Company shall hold the 10th AGM, and if need be the 4th EGM, by 30.9.2015 or alternatively positively by 31.10.2015.

38. In light of the above, this Application is allowed subject to the directions and observations above.

39. Let a certified copy of this Judgment and Order be specifically issued and served upon the Respondent No. 3, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission at the cost of the Petitioners.

40. There is no order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Alauddin ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The State ------ Respondents
case_source: (From Judgment and order dated 08.03.2003 passed by the High Court Division in Death Reference No. 2 of 2000 heard along with Jail Appeal No.544 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam, J.:- The condemned prisoner Alauddin, the petitioner in this jail petition, filed this petition from jail against the judgment and order dated 8.3.2003 passed by the High Court. Division accepting the death Reference Case No. 02 of 2000 and dismissing Jail Appeal No.544 of 2000 and thereby affirming the conviction and sentence passed by the learned Additional Session Judge, 4th Court Rajshahi, on 26.1.2000 in Session Case No. 178 of 1998, convicting the petitioner under section 302 of the penal Code and sentencing him to death.

2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that victim Balika was brought up in the house of Islam, her maternal uncle, and she was given marriage to the petitioner three years back. Initially, the couple led a happy conjugal life but after one year, the petitioner started torturing the victim both physically and mentally and at one stage, the petitioner drove the victim out of his house whereupon she took shelter in the house of her maternal uncle. Subsequently, the petitioner filed a case with Bajubagha union perished to get the victim back in his house and at the mediation of the Chairman of the above Union perished the victim again went back to the house of the petitioner. In the year 1998 on the eve of Eid-Ul-Azha, the maternal uncle of victim took her to his house to celebrate Eid and subsequently on 22.4.1998,Moslemuddin the father of the petitioner, along with two sisters of the petitioner, went to the house of the maternal uncle of victim and after having dinner, they brought back the victim to the house of the petitioner, On 23.4.1998, at about 5-00 a.m. Fuljhuri, the wife of the brother of the petitioner, went to the house of informant and informed that the victim Balika could not be traced. The informant then rushed to the house of petitioner along with Ismail, maternal uncle of the victim, and then after search the dead body of victim was found in the mango-garden of Chainuddin, which is situated about 200 yards away from the house of the petitioner. The informant then went to the police station accompanying the maternal uncle of victim and informed about death of his daughter whereupon unnatural Death Case No.13 of 1998 dated 23.4.1998 was initiated. In the meantime the local people, being suspicious, caught the petitioner who was making contradictory statements. Later on, during inquest of the body of the victim, the police noticed black mark on the neck of the victim and it was revealed that the petitioner, in cogitation with other accused persons, in a preplanned manner murdered the victim and i accordingly on 25.4.1998 the informant, lodged F.I.R. with Bagha police Station implicating the petitioner, Mansur the brother of the petitioner and also Rabiya Bibi, wife of Mansur whereupon Bagha P.S. Case No. 9 dated 22.11.1995 was started under section 302/201 read with section 109 of the penal code. Then on 26.4.1998 the petitioner was produced before P.W.8, First Class Magistrate, Rajshahi and before him, the petitioner made a confessional statement admitting that he murdered the victim. The police after investigation submitted charge sheet against the petitioner under section 302/201 of the penal Code. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, 4th Court, Rajshahi framed charges against die petitioner under section 302 of the penal Code which was read over and explained to the petitioner to which the petitioner pleaded innocence.

3. The prosecution examined 11 witnesses and though the defense examined none, from the trend of cross-examination of the prosecution witness's defense case transpires to be that the victim committed suicide and the petitioner was falsely implicated in the case out of previous grudge and enmity. After recording of evidence of the prosecution witnesses the petitioner was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal procedure wherein he pleaded innocence. On consideration of the evidence on record, the confessional statement and the facts and circumstances, the learned Additional Sessions Judge convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid. The High Court Division after hearing accepted the Death Reference Case No.02 of 2000 and dismissed Jail Appeal No. 544 of 2000.

4. It is admitted fact that victim was married to the petitioner and used to live with the petitioner in his house. The fact that the victim Balika last came at the house of the P.W.1 the informant on 22.8.1998 on "নাইয়র" And went back to the house of the petitioner on that day at night was proved by P.Ws. 1 and 2. the fact that on 23.4.1998 at about 5-00 a.m. Fuljhuri the wife of brother of the prisoner went to the house of the informant and informed that victim Balika could not be traced was proved by p.Ws 1-4. The fact that after search the dead body of the victim was found in the mango-garden of Chainuddin, about 200 yards away from the house of the father-in-law of victim Balika, was proved by P.Ws 3,4,5 and 6. the fact that initially no mark of violence were noticed on the dead body of the victim and the informant went to the police station accompanying Ismail and informed the police about the death of his daughter whereupon Unnatural Death Case No. 13 of 1998 dated 23.4.1998 was initiated was proved by p.Ws.1,2 and 11.The fact that at the time of inquest of the body of deceased, black mark was found on the neck of the deceased was stated by P.W.11. The fact that the prisoner made a confessional statement voluntarily was proved by the magistrate P.W.8.

5. Before the High Court Division it was argued on behalf of the petition that the prosecution   could not file any paper showing that accused was produced before Magistrate on 24.4.1998, the confessional statement alleged to have been made by the petitioner was not true and voluntary and during his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal procedure the petitioner denied to have made any confessional statement, all the columns of the from wherein the confessional statement was recorded were not filled up and so in view of decision reported in 17 BLD 352 the confessional statement of the petitioner cannot be relied upon, the Magistrate who recorded down the confessional statement also did not ask the petitioner as to whether or not any pressure was exerted upon him to make the confession, the conviction was based merely on circumstantial evidence and as held in 42 DLR (AD) 31, in such acme the prosecution must prove the motive as held in 15 BLD (AD) 54, when the investigation of a case had already started on an information prior to the lodging of ejahar, subsequent information cannot be treated as the First Information Report and it must be kept out of consideration of the court and accordingly the information on which Unnatural Death Case No.13 of 1998 was started should have been treated as the First Information Report and not the information made on 25.4.1998 and so the information made on 25.4.1998 should have been kept out of consideration of the Court, in view of the principle laid down in MLR (AD) 248, since admittedly there existed hostile relationship between the petitioner and the victim and in his confessional statement the petitioner categorically stated that there was hot exchange of words between him and the victim in the fateful night, ends of justice will sufficiently be met if the sentence of death is commuted to one of life imprisonment

<u>6. On the other hand, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the State contended before the High Court Division that the confessional statement of the petitioner was true and voluntary and the Magistrate who recorded the confessional statement stated in unequivocal terms that he recorded confessional statement after observing all legal formalities required under the law and in the decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 271 it has been held that conviction of an accused based on retracted confession even if uncorroborated is not illegal if the court believed that it was true and voluntary, the motive behind the murder was proved from the confessional statement of the petitioner, admittedly on the night of occurrence the victim was in the house of the petitioner and the petitioner failed to furnish any reasonable explanation as to death of his wife and in view of the principle laid down in the decision reported in 45 DLR 587, 43 DLR 249 and 6 BLC (AD) 1, the victim being murdered while in the custody of the petitioner, he was under an obligation to explain as to how his wife had met with death and though the appellant tried to explain that his wife committed suicide the same was found to be a travesty of truth in view of the evidence of the doctor and in the absence of satisfactory explanation coming from the side of the petitioner and the explanation given having been found to be false, the petitioner is to be held responsible for causing death of the victim, though an unnatural Death Case No.13 of 1998 was initially started on 23.4.1998 but subsequently final report was submitted in that case and then a regular case was started on 25.4.1998 and so the principle laid down in 15 BLD (AD) 54 is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.</u>

7. As it appears, regarding confessional statement, the High Court Division held that the confessional statement was an inculpatory one wherein the petitioner not only stated that he murdered his wife by throttling but also stated some events of their conjugal life in the fateful night which could not be tutored to him and the Magistrate in his evidence in unequivocal terms also stated that he recorded the confessional statement of the accused after observing all legal formalities and the confessional statement was also voluntary, the principle laid down in 17 BLD 352 is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case as there is no interpolation in the confessional statement made by the petitioner and all the columns of the printed form were filled up by the recording Magistrate.

8. Regarding retraction, the High Court Division considered the decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 271 wherein it was held that a conviction of a confessing accused based on retracted confession even if uncorroborated was not illegal if the court believed that it was true and voluntary and the High Court Division having found that the confession was recorded after observing all legal formalities and that the confession was voluntary, believed the retracted confessional statement and upheld the conviction.

9. Regarding the submission that the prosecution must prove motive, the High Court Division found that the petitioner himself in his confessional statement admitted murder and so the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 31 to the effect that where the conviction is based on circumstantial evidence the prosecution must prove motive was no applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

10. Regarding requirement of reasonable explanation from a husband in the event his wife was found killed while living with the husband and sleeping under the same roof as held in the decisions reported in 45 DLR 587, 43 DLR 249 and 6 BLC (AD)1, the High Court Division after discussing the facts of the present case held that since admittedly in the fateful night the victim was in his house, the petitioner was under an obligation to explain how his wife met death and in the absence of any explanation from his side, it seemed that none other than the petitioner was responsible for the death in question.

11. Regarding the submission that the conviction is based only a circumstantial evidence the High Court Division Relying on the case reported in 16 BLD (AD) 261 held that in the present case the prosecution proved a chain of circumstances including making the confessional statement which proved that the petitioner murdered the victim.

12. Regarding the submission that the information dated 23.4.1998 on the basis of which unnatural Death Case No. 13 of 1998 was started should have been regarded as FIR, the High Court Division considered the principle as laid down in 15 BLD (AD) 54 and held that in the case in hand, the information dated 23.4.1998, on which U.D. Case No. 13 of 1998 was started, ended in submission of a final report and so no illegality was committed in filing a subsequent First Information Report on 25.4.1998 for initiating the instant proceeding and regarding the delay in lodging the FIR, the High Court Division also explained the decision reported in 15 BLD (HCD) 205 and held that in the instant case, the question of delay in lodging First Information Report has been duly explained and as such the principle laid down in the above case is not applicable here.

13. Before the High Court Division, reliance was also placed on the decision reported in 1 M.L.R (AD) 248 in support of the submission for commuting the death sentence into imprisonment for life, wherein the Appellate Division commuted the death sentence to imprisonment for life folding as follows:

"This is not a case of inordinate delay in the execution of death sentence. However, this case calls for a commutation of sentence. The murder was not committed by a viscous macho male. Before causing death of his wife the appellant suffered for some time from a bitter sense of being wronged by his wayward wife. In this case ends of justice will sufficiently be met If the sentence of death is commuted to one of life imprisonment. The appeal is allowed. The sentence of death imposed on the appellant is commuted to one of life imprisonment."

14. However the High Court Division, in the criminal misc. petition No. 46 of 2003 are instant case, having found that the petitioner in accordingly dismissed. his confessional statement stated that initial part of the night after meal, had some events of their conjugal life and then when he told her that in the Eid her father did not give him any present, the victim in bad language rebuked him and after quarrelling for some time she went into sleep and so he being very angry, took decision to kill her and subsequently early in the morning before killing her by throttling, he also had some events of their conjugal life and so it was a cold blooded murder.

15. Question arises whether it is against natural human conduct that the petitioner while making confessional statement also stated that before killing her by throttling he made intercourse with her because due to this statement the scope of the petitioner to take the plea of provocation, as was taken in the decision reported in 1 MLR (AD) 248, became narrowed down. However, it has been found by both the courts below that the above confessional statement was voluntary and the High Court Division also found that before murdering his wife by throttling the petitioner stated some events of their conjugal life which could not be tutored to him and the Magistrate also stated that the confessional statement was voluntary. So there is no scope of raising any suspicion about the contents of confessional statement.

16. Further, from the trend of cross examination of the prosecution witnesses the defiance case during the trial appeared to be that the victim committed suicide and no plea was taken to the effect that since the victim rebuked the petitioner in bad language and quarreled with him, the petitioner, on provocation, killed her and this plea of provocation was raised for the first time before the High Court Division.

17. Accordingly, we find no cogent reason to interfere with the Judgment and order passed by the High Court Division.

18. The Jail petition No. 13 of 2003 and criminal Misc. petition No. 46 of 2003 are accordingly dismissed.

End.
