full_judgment:
Md. Rais Uddin, J: These Rules are taken up together to be disposed of by this single judgment as common question of law and the similar facts are involved in the Rules.

2. In fact, these two Rules were issued calling upon the Opposite-party No.1-33 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 7.05.2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Title Appeal No. 216 of 2007 heard analogously with Title Appeal No.221 of 2007 in dismissing the Title Appeal No.216 of 2007 and allowing the Title Appeal No.221 of 2007 with modification and reversing the judgment and decree dated 11.09.2007 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sonargaon, Narayanganj, in Title Suit No.58 of 2005 decreed the suit, should not be set aside.

3. The relevant fact giving rise to this Rule, in short, is that opposite-party Nos.1 to 33 as plaintiffs brought a suit for declaration and partition contending, inter-alia, that one Kadir was the original owner in 0.25 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.36 and C.S. Dag Numbers 271 and 272 and Laskor was the original owner of 1.33 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.48 and in C.S. Dag Nos.115/116/169/198/201/271 and 273. During the ownership in possession of the said C.S. record Kadir died leaving behind his 2(two) sons Sheikh Gafur, Sheikh Pokai and 2(two) daughters Khatimonnessa and Buri. Sheikh Gafur obtained 0.832/100 acres of land from the land of C.S. Khatian No.36, Sheikh Gafur 0.8 ½ acres, Sheikh Pokai 0.8 ½ acres, Khatimonnessa 0.04 acres and Buri 0.04 acres of land obtained by amicably from said C.S. Khatian No.36. On 28.07.1930 Sheikh Gafur during ownership of the said sold 0.10 acres of land by Saf Kabala deed No.2965 to Anjuman Bibi and delivered his possession therein. Thereafter on 27.12.1960 said Anjuman Bibi sold Saf Kabala deed No.11123 to Nurunnessa and Saf Kabala deed No.11122 to Fazlul Hoque and by Saf Kabala deed No.11124 to Amjad Ali on the same date in 0.8 % acres of land. Amjad Ali died leaving behind his 2(two) sons, namely, FazIul Hoque and Bahauddin. On 17.07.1941 Sheikh Pokai sold 0.8 ½ acres of land by Saf Kabala deed to Samiruddin and Samiruddin sold 0.03 acres from said 0.8 ½ acres of land to Abul Hossain. During ownership of daughter of Kader Khatimonnessa in 0.04 acres of land as heir, she died leaving 1 daughter, namely, Rahimonnessa. Rahimonnessa sold 0.02 acres of land on 16.05.1973 by Kabala deed No.2604 and 0.02 acres of land by Kabala deed No.2593 to Samiruddin on the same date and on 11.07.1978 Samiruddin sold 0.04 acres of land by Kabala deed No.5662 to Raza Mia who sold said land on 26.07.1999 vide Kabala deed No.5843 to Aktar Hossain and Nasima. Nasima her shares orally gifted to Aktar Hossain and thereafter he went to foreign and in this way Akter Hossain owned and possessed said 0.04 acres of land. During ownership in possession of 0.04 acres of land died leaving behind one daughter, namely, Jabeda Khatun and one son, namely, Afsar Uddin who died leaving behind his one son, namely, Khaza Mahamood and 4 daughters. Khaza as orally request by his sister owned and possessed their share of 0.04 acres of land and in this way plaintiffs originally owner in 0.25 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No. 36.

4. Laskor was the originally owner in 133 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.48. He died leaving behind one son, namely, Sukur Mohammad and one daughter, namely, Ayesa Begum who obtained 0.44 acres of land from her father. She died leaving behind one son namely, Samiruddin and 4 daughters, namely, Anjuman Bibi, Bahatam Bibi, FeMur and Sahanni and Samiruddin obtained by her mothers who died leaving behind 6(six) sons, namely, Rafiqul Islam, Yousuf Ali, Dr. Shahjahan, Abdul Awal, Nur Mohammad and Monir Hossain. Rafiqul Islam died leaving behind his son namely, Abdul Hoque. Anjuman Bibi died leaving behind one daughter namely, Amina Khatun Baharun who died leaving behind one daughter, namely, Nurunnahar. Falanur died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Chan Mia Fakir, Tahidul Hoque, Aynal Hoque and Sabjana Hoque and Sahanni died leaving behind 2 daughters, namely, Nurjahan and Suju Bann and in this way plaintiffs were owned and possessed in 0.443/10 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.48. Defendants, the heirs of Sukur Mahmud was ownership in 0.8866/100  acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.48 and in 2 Khatians the plaintiffs and defendants were owned as ejmaly and there was no partition by meets and bounds and when on 15.04.2005 the plaintiffs request to the defendants to make partition of disputed property but refused. Hence the suit for partition.

5. The defendant Nos.1 to 11 contested the suit by filling written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter-alia, that one Dengu was the original owner in 0.17 acres and 0.08 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.36 in C.S. dag Nos.271 and 272. Dengu died leaving behind his two sons, namely, Kadir and Madari. When Madari as minor said Kadir did not record in the name of Dengu in C.S. record he recorded his name with collusive but the said two brothers are equally owner and possessing in C.S. Khatian No.36. Madan during his ownership in said C.S. Khatian No. 36 as C.S. dag Nos.271 and 272 he sold on 05.03.1927, 0.08 acres of land from C.S. dag No.271 and 0.02 acres of land from C.S. dag No.272 in total 0.10 acres of land to Sukur Mohammed by Saf Kabala deed No.2276 and delivered his possession therein and Sukur Mohammad with the knowledge of them owned and possessed the said property.

6. One Laskar was the original owner in 1.33 acres of land in 7(seven) dags at C.S. Khatian No.46 and his name was rightly recorded in the C.S. Khatian, died leaving behind one son, namely, Sukur Mahmud during his ownership in C.S. Khatian No.48 by the heir of his father and in C.S. Khatian No.36 by purchase died leaving behind his two sons, namely, Abdul Gani and Idris and two daughter namely, Roymonnessa and Mahitunnessa. Roymannessa died leaving behind one daughter, namely, Fazila Begum and two brothers. Mohitunnessa died leaving behind three sons, namely, Reazul, Shaft, Mafi and three daughters, namely, Khorsheda, Morsheda and Rosy. Roymonnessa and Mohitunnessa obtained their share in C.S. Khatian No.36 and 48 by their fathers heir orally gifted their two brothers namely, Abdul Gani and Idris Ali and delivered possession therein. Abdul Gani died leaving behind one son, namely, Abu Sayed and two daughters, namely, Fatema and Shamsunnahar. Idris Ali died leaving behind his wife Hesenabanu, four sons, namely, Abdul Matin, Halim, Motalib and Nazir and two daughters, namely, Hosne Ara and Rowshan Ara and in this the defendants were owning and possession in 1.43 acres of land in C.S. Khatian No.48 by constructing houses and growing trees and cultivating lands and they prayed for Sahara in 1.43 decimals of land instead of 1.43 acres of land. Hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. At the trial, the plaintiffs examined 3(three) witnesses and the defendants examined 4(four) witnesses in support of their respective cases.

8. The learned judge of the trial Court after hearing the parties, considering the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 11.09.2007. Against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred appeal being Title Appeal No.216 of 2007 and the plaintiffs preferred appeal being Title Appeal No.221 of 2007 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj. On transfer it was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj who after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record allowed the appeal No.221 of 2007 with modification and dismissed the appeal being Title -Appeal No.2I6 of 2007 by his judgment and decree dated 7.5.2008.

9. Against the said judgment and decree the defendants as petitioners moved this court and obtained the instant Rules in Civil Revision No.2715 of 2008 and Civil Revision No.2716 of 2008.

10. Mr. Parimal Chandra Guha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in both the cases has placed the revisional application, pleadings, evidence, judgment and decree of the courts below and submits that the plaintiffs filed the instant suit claiming 69 decimals of land out of which 25 decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.36 and 44 ½ decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.48 in total 6933 decimals of land but the learned Judge of the trial court failed to consider the evidence both oral and documentary thereby passed the judgment and a decree giving 5933/100 decimals of land and accordingly giving saham. He submits that the appellate court on misreading and non-consideration of evidence allowed the appeal of the plaintiffs giving saham 6933/100 decimals of land to the plaintiffs and 8833/100 decimals of land to the defendants thereby dismissed the appeal of the defendants committed illegality and he prayed for to make the rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree of the court below. He lastly submits that the court of appeal below as a last court of fact without properly considering evidence of the parties and without giving independent finding committed error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the appeal. In support of his contention he has referred the decision reported in: (1) 7 DLR, 63, (2)35 DLR, 295.

11. Mr. S.M. Fakrul Islam, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties in both the revisions submits that the learned Judge of the appellate court on proper consideration of evidence and materials on record rightly allowed the appeal of the plaintiffs and dismissed the appeal of the defendants. He submits that the learned Judge of the appellate court found that the possession of the suit land was correctly recorded in the name of the plaintiffs in C.S. Khatian No.36, plot No.271 and as such deemed the suit. He lastly submits that the appellate court being last and final court of facts reached in a decision on assessing the evidence and material on record and there is no reason to interfere by this court in revision since there is no misreading and non-consideration of any evidence and materials on record and he prayed for discharged the rules. In support of his contention he has referred the decision reported in: (1) 10 BLT (AD) 137, (2)30 DLR (SC) 81.

12. In order to appreciate the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the parties, I have gone through the revisional application, pleadings, evidence, exhibits, judgment and decree of the courts below very carefully.

13. Now the question- calls for consideration whether the learned Judge of the court of appeal below has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the judgment and decree.

14. On perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiffs brought the suit for partition with declaration claiming the saham 6933/100 decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.36 and C.S. Khatian No.48 of the suit land by purchase. The defendants claimed 10 decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.36 and 133 decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.48 in total 143 decimals of land.

15. The learned Judge of the trial court decreed the suit giving 5933/100 decimals of land to the plaintiffs and 9837/100 decimals of and to the defendants.

16. The appellate court considering the evidence and materials on record allowed the appeal of the plaintiffs giving 6933/100 decimals of land and 8833/100 decimals of land to the defendants.

17. Now the only question is to be decided in this revision whether C.S. Khatian No.36, Plot Nos.271 and 272 area of land 25 decimals claimed by the plaintiffs and 10 decimals of land claimed by purchased predecessors of the defendants were entitled to get

18. On perusal of the judgment of the trial court it appears that the learned Judge decreed the suit giving 15 decimals of land from C.S. Khatian No.36 to the plaintiffs with finding-

“বাদী ও বিবাদীপক্ষের আরজী, জবাব ও দাখিলীয় কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনা করিলাম। সার্বিক পর্যালোচনায় ইহা প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, সি,এস ৩৬ নং খতিয়ানে দখলী কলামে ২৭১ দাগে মোহাম্মদ গং লিপি আছে। যাহা মাদারীর অস্তিত্বকে প্রমান করে এবং মাদারী কর্তৃক শুক্কুর মাহমুদ বরাবর ১৯২৭ সালের বিক্রয়ের বৈধতা প্রমান করে। ইহা ছাড়া বিবাদীর দলিল ১৯২৭ সনের যাহা বাদীর দলিলের পূর্ববর্তী কাজেই দলিলটি কারযকর হয়েছে এবং ইহা দ্বারা বিক্রীত সম্পত্তি বৈধ।

সুতরাং সি,এস ৩৬ নং খতিয়ানে বাদীপক্ষের দাবী ২৫ শতাংশ হইলেও বাদীপক্ষ তা প্রমান করিতে পারেন নাই। কাজেই সি,এস ৩৬ নং খতিয়ানে বাদীগন ১৫ শতাংশে মালিক দখলকার আছেন।”

19. The learned Judge of the appellate court considering the evidence and materials on record allowed the appeal of the plaintiffs giving 25 decimals of land to the plaintiffs with the finding-

“নিম্ন আদালত ৩৬ খতিয়ানের ২৭১ নং দাগে মোহাম্মদ গং নামে একজনের অস্তিত্ব লক্ষ্য করা যায় বলিয়া এবং তাহাতে মাদারীর অস্তিত্ব আছে বলিয়া যে অবজারবেশন প্রদান করিয়াছেন তাহার এই বক্তব্য সঠিক নয়। কারণ সি,এস ৩৬ খতিয়ান পর্যালোচনা করিয়া দেখা যায় যে, ২৭১ দাগের উত্তর সীমানায় মোহাম্মদ গং আছে। তাহারা ৩৬ খতিয়ানের কোন অংশীদার নহেন। ৩৬ খতিয়ানের ২৭১ ও ২৭২ দাগে ২৫ শতাংশের সি,এস পর্চানুসারে স্বত্ব কাদিরের। এইখানে অন্য কোন ব্যক্তির অস্তিত্ব নাই। ফলে ৩৬ খতিয়ানে বাদীপক্ষের ২৫ শতাংশের স্বত্ব সন্দেহাতীত ভাবে প্রমানিত হইয়াছে।”

20. On perusal of the record it appears that on the basis of claim by plaintiffs submitted C.S. Khatian No.36, exhibit-1 and the defendants in support of their claim submitted certified copy of deed being deed No.2276 dated 5.3.1927 exhibit-Gha. The defendants called volume and examined D.W.4 to prove the deed and thereby the learned Judge of the trial court found the same as genuine deed.

21. On perusal of the judgment of the court below it appears that the trial court decreed the suit an the basis of deed being deed No.2276 dated 5.3.1927 (exhibit-Gha). On the other hand, the appellate court allowed the appeal on the basis of C.S. Khatian No.36, exhibit-1.

22. Now it is pertinent to decide whether the record of right will prevail over the deed or the deed will prevail over the record of right.

<u>23. On perusal of the judgment it appears that the trial court has considered the materials evidence both oral and documentary in details in coming to its findings that Madani sold the suit land in favour of Shukur Mahmud in the year 1927. The appellate court without discussing the evidence properly had abruptly reversed the findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court without controverting the findings and assessing the evidence independently which is not proper judgment of reversal and as such it is not sustainable in law.</u>

<u>24. The lower appellate Court being the last and final court of facts will have to discuss and re-assess the evidence on record independently while either reversing or affirming the findings of the trial Court. In case of reversal it is more incumbent upon the appellate Court to re-assess the evidence to arrive at his own independent findings. The findings of the trial Court should not be easily disturbed as a matter of course and before reversing the findings and decisions of the trial Court the appellate Court should think twice or more than twice. In the instant case I am of the view that specific findings of the trial Court have not been reversed by the appellate Court exercising its power under Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This view finds support in the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners.</u>

25. It appears the record of right is evidence of present possession and registered kabala is an evidence of title. The registered document will prevail over the records of rights and would remain in enforce until and unless, such kabala is cancelled by an appropriate civil court. The registered deed being deed No.2276 dated 5.3.1927 is an old document more than 30 years produced from proper custody presumed under Section 90 of the Evidence Act that it was duly executed and genuine documents.

26. This view which I have taken finds support in the case of:

(1) A.D.C.(revenue) Vs. Md. Reaz Uddin Pramanik and others, reported in 5 BLC (AD)76, wherein their lordships held:

"Once a document more than 30 years old is produced from proper custody under section 90 of the Evidence Act entitles the court to presume that it is a genuine document."

(2) Abdul Mannan Bhuyan and others Vs. Md. Nasir Hussain and others, reported in 18 BLC (AD) 44, wherein their lordships held:

"S.A. and R.S. records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and that the registered document would remain in enforce unless the same was cancelled by an appropriate civil Court."

27. I have gone through the decisions reported in (I) 30 DLR (SC) 81 and (2) 10 BLT (AD) 137 as referred by the teamed advocate for the opposite-parties. I am respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein. But the facts leading to those cases are distinguishable to that of the instant ease and therefore, to that effect I am unable to accept his submissions.

28. In view of the discussions and reason stated above, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below cannot be sustained in law and are liable to be set aside.

29. In the result, the Rules are made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below in Title Appeal No.216 of 2007 and Title Appeal No.221 of 2007 are set aside and those of the trial court are restored and affirmed.

30. There will be no order as to costs.

31. Let the Lower Court Records along with a copy of the judgment be sent at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Shasti Sarker with Mr. Md. Amirul Islam, Advocates ------ For the petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Nurul Amin with Mr. Md. Saidul Alam Khan, Advocates ------ For the opposite-party nos. 1-8.
parties:
Md. Abdul Jabbar
Vs.
Md. Abdul Latif and others
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury, J : On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party nos. 1-8 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment' and order dated 20.10.2002 passed by the District Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 2002 reversing the judgment and order dated 13.03.2002 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1997 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. On 12.10.1997, one Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas, predecessor of the opposite-party nos. 1-8, as pre-emptor instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1997 in the 1st Court of Joint District Judge, Kushtia against the pre-emptee-petitioner and others praying for pre-emption of the case property measuring an area of 01.37 decimals out of the total quantum of land of 16.44 decimals appertaining to S. A. plot no. 82 corresponding to R. S. plot no. 222 and S. A. Khatian No. 746 corresponding to R. S. Khatian No. 706 of Mouza Bahadurkhali, District- Kushtia under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. During the pendency of the Miscellaneous Case, the original pre-emptor Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas died and his legal heirs, that is to say, opposite-party nos. 1-8 ware substituted in his place and as substituted pre-emptors, they prosecuted the pre-emption case against the pre-emptees and others in the Court of first instance. Anyway, the case of the pre-emptors, in short, is that the pre-emptors are co-sharers in the case plot. On 20.08.1997, the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas sold out the case property in favour of the pre-emptee-purchaser Md. Abdul Jabbar for consideration money of Tk. 1,85,000/- by a registered deed and at the time of sale; the pre-emptee-seller sold out some land in excess of his share. The pre-emptee-purchaser is a stranger to the case plot. However, the pre-emptors are entitled to the refund of Tk. 45,916/- for the sale of excess land to the extent of 00.34 decimals. After the purchase of the case property by the pre-emptee-purchaser, he instituted Partition Suit No. 16 of 1997 against the original pre-emptor Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas in the Civil Court and on receipt of the summons of the partition suit, Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas became aware of the purchase of the case property by the pre-emptee-purchaser from the pre-emptee-seller. As the substituted pre-emptors are co-sharers in the case plot, they are entitled to get the case properly by way of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act.

3. The pre-emptee-purchaser Md. Abdul Jabbar contested the case by filing a Written Objection traversing the material allegations made in the case petition. His case, in short, is that the pre-empted-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas got his share in the case plot .(case property) mutated in his name on 10.12.1994 vide Mutation Case No. 12/IX-II/94-95 and while he was owning and possessing the case property, he transferred the same in favour of the preomptee-purchaser by a registered deed dated 20.08.1997. As the jama was separated vide Mutation Case No. 12/IX-II/94-95 the pre-emptors are no longer co-sharers in the case plot. An they are not co-sharers in the case plot, they cannot get the case property by way of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

4. After hearing the parties and on an assessment of the evidence and materials on record and in the facts and circumstances of the case, the trial Court dismissed the Pre-emption Case mainly on the score that the pre-emptors are not co-sharers in the case jote in view of the Mutation Khatian No. 706/1 standing in the name of the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas.

5. On appeal, the learned District Judge of Kushtia reversed the finding of the trial Court and held that the pre-emptors are co-sharers in the case plot and in that view of the matter, he allowed the Miscellaneous Appeal thereby granting pre-emption of the case property to the pre-emptors.

6. Being aggrieved at and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 20.10.2002 passed by the District Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 2002, the pre-emptee-purchaser preferred the revisional application and obtained the instant Rule.

7. The only point for determination in this Rule is whether the Court of Appeal below committed any error of law resulting in any error in its decision occasioning a failure of justice?

8. At the outset, Mr. Shasti Sarker, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptee-purchaser, submits that it is the admitted position that the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas was a co-sharer in the case plot and he got his share mutated in his name vide Mutation Case No. 12/IX-II/94-95 and consequently, a new Khatian being Mutation Khatian No. 706/1 was opened in the name of the pre-emptee-seller and since the jama was separated and a new Mutation Khatian was opened in the name of the pre-emptee-seller on 10.12.1994, the original pre-emptor, that is to say, Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas ceased to be a co-sharer in the case plot and that being so, the substituted pre-emptors are not entitled to get the case property by way of pre-emption. In support of his submission, Mr. Shasti Sarker relies upon the decisions in the cases of Shah Alam -Vs- Shahidur Rahman and others, 55 DLR (HCD) 214; Alfazuddin Ahmed-Vs- Abdur Rahman and others, 8 MLR (AD) 153 and Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan -Vs- Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, being dead his heirs: Amena Khatun and others, 35 DLR (AD) 338.

<u>9. Mr. Shasti Sarker also submits that the kabala under pre-emption refers to the transfer of 01.37 decimals whereas pit is the claim of the pre-emptors that the pre-emptee-seller transferred in excess of his share to the extent of 00.34 decimals valued at Tk. 45,916/- and by that reason, they are entitled to the refund of the aforesaid amount of money and this being the scenario, partial pre-emption of the case property cannot be allowed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In this regard, Mr. Shasti Sarker adverts to the decision in the case of Giri Bala Das -Vs- Basudev Dey and others reported in 32 DLR (HCD) 68.</u>

<u>10. On the contrary, Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the substituted pre-emptors (opposite-party nos. 1-8), submits that the lower Appellate Court did not contrail any error of law resulting in any error in its decision occasioning a failure of justice by holding that the substituted pre-emptors are co-sharers in the case plot and since they are co-sharers in the case plot, they are entitled to get the case property by way of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act albeit there might be a Mutation Khatian in the name of the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas. In order to buttress up this submission, Mr. Md. Nurul Amin draws my attention to the decision in the case of Md. Aminullah and others...Vs...Serajul Huq and others reported in 18 MLR (AD) 131.</u>

11. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin further submits that it is an admitted fact that the pre-emptee-purchaser filed Partition Suit No. 16 of 1997 in the competent Civil Court against the original pre-emptor, that is to say, Md. Lokman Hossain Biswas admitting him to be a co-sharer in the case plot and now the pre-emptee-purchaser, that is to say, the plaintiff of the Partition Suit No. 16 of 1997 cannot turn round and say that the original pre-emptor or for that matter, the substituted pre-emptors are not co-sharers in the case plot.

12. I have heard the submissions of Mr. Shasti Sarker and the counter-submissions of Mr. Md. Nurul Amin and perused the revisional application and the impugned judgment and other relevant materials on record.

13. A reference to the judgment of the Court of first instance indicates that it dismissed the Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1997 mainly on the ground that the jama is separated in view of the Mutation Khatian No. 706/1 standing in the name of the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas.

14. In the decision in the case of Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan...Vs...Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, being dead his heirs: Amena Khatun and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 338, it has been held that the effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding.

15. In the decision in the case of Alfazuddin Ahmed...Vs...Abdur Rahman and others reported in 8 MLR (AD) 153, it has been spelt out that separation of tenancy/jama khatian disentitles the petitioner to the right of pre-emption.

16. In the decision in the case of Shah Alam (Md) -Vs- Md. Shahidur Rahman and others reported in 55 DLR (HCD) 214, it has been held that a co-sharer loses his co-sharership in the tenancy or holding by separating his jama through a mutation proceeding and cannot apply for pre-emption. It has been further held in that decision that separation of jama or sub-division of a holding or tenancy distributing rents, whether in case of agricultural land or non-agricultural land, takes place under Section 117(1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the original co-sharers on such separation cease to be co-sharers.

17. In the decision in the case of Md. Aminullah and others...Vs...Serajul Huq and others reported in 18 MLR (AD) 131, it has been held in paragraphs 12 and 13:

"12. In a case of pre-emption filed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be treated as co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. Therefore, in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian, a co-sharer tenant can file a pre-emption case under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. The words 'one or more co-sharer tenants of such land' occurring in Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act means a co-sharer in the plot and not in the holding as mentioned in Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Such' being the position of law, the pre-emptors are not even required to file an application for amendment to show that they have also interest in R. S. Khatian No. 3838.

.

13. In the case of S. M. Basiruddin -Vs- Z. Islam (1983); 35 DLR (AD) 230, it has been held that the expression 'non-agricultural land' used in Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used in the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act"

18. From the above principle of law, it is crystal clear that a person seeking pre-emption of any non-agricultural land under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act must be a co-sharer in the plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. The R. S. Khatian of the case plot is 706 and the Mutation Khatian No. 706/1 stands in the name of the pre-emptee-seller Md. Abdul Jalil Biswas vide Mutation Case No. 12/IX-11/94-95. It is the admitted position that the R. S. case plot no. is 222 corresponding to S. A. plot no. 82 and the quantum of land of the entire case plot is 16.44 decimals and the land sought to be pre-empted is 01.37 decimals. So it is seen that with regard to the case plot, there are two Khatians, namely, R. S. Khatian No. 706 and Mutation Khatian No. 706/1 and both these Khatians relate to the R. S. plot no. 222 corresponding to S. A. plot no. 82. Following the 'ratio decidendi' of the decision reported in 18 MLR (AD) 131, I am left with no option but to hold that the substituted pre-emptors are necessarily co-sharers in the case plot, though it appertains to two Khatians, namely, R. S. Khatian No. 706 and Mutation Khatian No. 706/1. From that decision, it is also abundantly clear that the expression 'non-agricultural land' used in Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used is the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>19. Indisputably, the  pre-emptee-purchaser (petitioner) filed Partition Suit No. 16 of 1997 against the pre-emptors in the Civil Court admitting them to be co-sharers in the case plot. In this connection, a reference may be made to the decision in the case of Begum Khodeza Akhter...Vs...Hajera Khatun and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 212. In that decision, our Appellate Division has held that admission is, no doubt, a strong piece of evidence against its maker; but it is also open to him to adduce evidence to show that it is not, in fact, an admission but is the result of bonafide mistake of fact. In the absence of any bonafide mistake of fact, the substituted pre-emptors are necessarily co-sharers as admitted by the pre-emptee-purchaser in the Partition Suit No. 16 of 1997. In such a landscape, I hold that the lower Appellate Court did not commit any error of law resulting in any error in deciding that the substituted pre-emptors are co-sharers in the case plot.</u>

20. The decisions referred to by Mr. Shasti Sarker in the cases of Shah Alam (Md) -Vs- Md. Shahidur Rahman and others, 55 DLR (HCD) 214; Alfazuddin Ahmed -Vs- Abdur Rahman and others, 8 MLR (AD) 153 and Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan...Vs...Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, being dead his heirs: Amena Khatun and others, 35 DLR (AD) 338 do not appear to be applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case on the question of loss of co-sharership by separation of jama.

21. In the decision in the case of Giri Bala Das...Vs...Basudev Dey and others reported in 32 DLR (HCD) 68, it has been held that partial pre-emption of the case property cannot be allowed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Reverting to the case in hand, I find that the pre-emptors have not prayed for partial pre-emption of the case property. They have only stated in their pleading that the pre-emptee-seller transferred some land in excess of his sham to the pre-emptee-purchaser and on that count, they have claimed refund of some money; though the claim of pre-emption is with regard to the entire land covered by the kabala under pre-emption measuring an area of 01.37 decimals. Against this backdrop, the submission of Mr. Shasti Sarker that the pre-emptors cannot claim partial pre-emption of the case property stands negatived. So I am of the opinion that this is not a case of partial pre-emption.

22. From the foregoing discussions and in the facts and circumstances of the case, I am led to conclude that the Court of Appeal below did not commit any error of law resulting in any error in its decision occasioning a failure of justice by allowing the Miscellaneous Appeal and granting pre-emption of the case property in favour of the pre-emptors. In the result, there is no merit in the Rule. The Rule, therefore, fails.

23. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

24. Let the lower Court records along with a copy of this judgment be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 29.03.1998 passed by the learned District Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 20 of 1990 reversing those of dated 18.02.1990 passed by the learned Additional Assistant Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Case No.41 of 1989 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite party No.1 as pre-emptor instituted the original Miscellaneous Case being No.118 of 1988 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for getting the case land pre-empted in the 1st court of the then Munsiff, Kushtia. Subsequently the case was transferred to the court of learned Additional Assistant Judge, Kushtia for disposal and re-numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 1989 contending inter-alia that in the S.A. plot No.749, 27 decimals of land appertaining to S.A. khatian No. 1078 under mouza Baradi originally belonged to one Susanto Kumar Saha who died leaving behind 3(three) brothers Narayan Chandra, Gopal Chandra and Debendra Nath. The aforesaid 3(three) brothers sold the case land to the pre-emptee-petitioner on 28.08.1988. The further case of the pre-emptor is such that he is a contiguous land holder of the case plots No.749, 750 and 750/1999. The pre-emptor is the owner of some land in plot No.750 and 750/1999. The case land is outside of municipality and it is a "Bhita" with cultivable land. The purchaser-pre-emptee is a stranger. For the requirement of the pre-emptor knowing about the case kabla he instituted the original case within time for getting the case land pre-empted.

3. The contrary case of the purchaser-pre-emptee in short is thus that the case land is not the agricultural land and that the case is bad for defect of parties and not maintainable. The further case of the pre-emptee is such that he is a contiguous land-holder of the case land and the land appertaining to C.S. khatian No.1078 in plot No.749 in fact originally belonged to one Susanto Kumar who died leaving, three brothers namely Narayan Chandra, Gopal Chandra and Deben Chandra. The three brothers for want of money wanted to sale the property and executed a bainanama in favour of the pre-emptets-petitioner on 02.03.1965. Subsequently they migrated to India. Thereafter the pre-emptee-petitioner Lutfor Rahman filed a Title Suit being No.30 of 1977 in the 1st Court of the then munsiff, Kushtia for Specific Performance of Contract for getting a registered sale deed. The pre-emptee-pettlioner obtained the decree and through Execution Case he obtained the registered sale deed in his favour which is within the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptee-petitioner after his bainapatra constructed his homestead in the case land and planted various trees with an expenditure of Tk.2,84,000/-(two lac eighty four thousand). The pre-emptee-purchaser thus have become the owner of some land of case plot No.750 and 750/1999 and as such he is a contiguous land owner of the case land. The case land as is situated in plot No.749 is a non-agricultural land which is not pre-emptable under section 96 of the State Acquisition And Tenancy Act, 1950. As because; the pre-emptee is a contiguous land owner of the case land, the original case is not maintainable.

4. The learned trial court during trial after examining witnesses from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the case by it's judgment and order dated 18.02.1990.

5. Being aggrieved the pre-emptor preferred a Miscellaneous appeal being No.20 of 1990 in the court of learned District Judge, Kushtia and the learned appellate court hearing the appeal allowed the same reversing the judgment and order passed by the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the pre-emptee-respondent-petitioner Md. Lutfor Rahman have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay.

7. During pendency of the Rule the petitioner died and his legal heirs have been substituted.

8. Mr. Md. Nurul. Amin the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. F.M. Mizanur Rahman, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

9. The learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeal committed illegality and irregularity in holding the view that the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case is maintainable. The case land is a homestead land for more than 100 years and it is being used as non-agricultural land. The learned Advocate further submits that the original case for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties which is overlooked by the learned appellate court illegally and it is the mandatory provisions of Jaw that under section 96(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the vendors shall be made parties to the case but in the instant case the pre-emptor-opposite party did not make them parties. Furthermore; to the western adjacent side of the case land the pre-emptee has land; which was acquired by him otherwise than by purchase and as a result of that the case is barred under section 96(10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The learned Advocate also submits that after bainanama of the year 1965 the purchaser-pre-emptee within the knowledge of the pre-emptor constructing his pucca homestead as dwelling huts residing there for more than 50 years. Under the law Reforms Ordinance, 1976 for the said reason the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case is barred section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thirdly; the learned appellate court without rebutting the conclusive findings of the trial court as to the contiguous land of the pre-emptee-purchaser in two plots 750 and 750/1999 reversed the judgment of the trial court, which is the violation of the provisions laid down in order 41, Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the learned appellate court below in a very evasive manner without any sifting of evidence both oral and documentary and assessment of same decided the merit of the case illegally only on one point which is not in accordance with law. In support of the submissions the learned Advocate referred several decisions of this Court and our Apex Court reported in 32 DLR(AD) 54, 37 DLR(AD) 220, 50 DLR(AD) 97, 20 DLR 1197, 43 DLR 510, 44 DLR 414 and 2 AIR (2013) 462. 10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeal committed no illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptor-opposite parties being the contiguous land owners of the case land are entitled to pre-empt the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case land is not admittedly within the municipality. It is a decided matter that the land which is not within the periphery of a municipality is pre-emptable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned trial court misconstrued the factual aspect and failed to appreciate the actual position of law in holding the view that the case is not maintainable but subsequently the learned appellate court considering the evidence on records correctly decided that the case is maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred two decisions of this court reported in 48 DLR 175 and 49 DLR 74.

11. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case records, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses, impugned judgment and order along with all relevant papers.

<u>12. On perusal of the case records it transpires that admittedly the case land measuring an area of 27 decimals of land in S.A. plot No.749 of khatian No.1078 appertaining to mouza Baradi belonged to the predecessor of the vendors Susanto Kumar Saha. It is also admitted that Susanto died leaving behind three brothers namely Narayan, Gopal and Debendra. These three brothers transferred the case land in favour of the pre-emptee-petitioner by way of a bainapatra on 02.03.1965. Thereafter without execution and registration of the kabla deed while they left this county the pre-emptee-purchaser instituted a suit for Specific Performance of Contract being Title Suit No. 30 of 1977 and in that suit he has obtained a decree and by its execution the kabla deed was registered through court. It is not denied from any corner that the case land after acquisition by way of purchase was developed and the purchaser constructing the pucca homestead started to reside therein. Therefore obviously the case land is being used by the purchaser-pre-emptee-petitioner as his homestead.</u>

<u>13. Having gone through the evidence on record I find that the purchaser-pre-emptee is the owner of some land of case plot No.750 and 750/1999. The case land consists of three plots which are 749, 750, 750/1999. From the C.S. khatians being No.653, 654 and 655 corresponding to S.A. khatian No. 562 it appears that the nature of the case land is homestead. The said khatians makes it clear that from the very beginning the land in dispute is being used as homestead. Furthermore, I have come across from the case records that the learned trial court during disposal of the original suit adverting evidence held that the purchaser-pre-emptee is a contiguous land owner of the case land and he has 11½ decimals of land in plot No.750 and 750/1999 and the pre-emptor as P.W.1 admitted in his deposition that the purchaser-petitioner along with one Suresh Chandra acquired the land of plot No.750 and 750/1999. The pre-emptor subsequently claiming the land of two plots 750 and 750/1999 filed a suit being No.161 of 1970 against the pre-emptee and one Suresh Chandra but failed to succeed. In this way it is obvious from the case records that the learned appellate court without rebutting the findings of the trial court on this very particular pertinent point adverting the evidence on records decided the merit of the appeal.</u>

14. It is a fact that the case land is not situated within the periphery of municipality and it is a decided matter that the land which is situated in the rural area and not within municipality is pre-emptable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned appellate court relying upon the decisions of this Court decided this point rightly in favour of the appellant therein. But the fact remains that in order to obtain an order of pre-emption the provisions laid down in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are to be strictly followed. In a case under section 96 of this Act, 1950 the vendors shall be a parties and section 96(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that the presence of the vendors (transferors) is necessary and their absence is a fatal defect in a Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case. I have also spelt out above that from the documentary evidence it is apparent that the pre-emptee-petitioner acquired some land otherwise than the case kabla which is adjacent to the land transferred and thus he became a contiguous land owner. The findings of the trial court is based on materials on records which is not overruled or reversed by the appellate court and thus the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is well founded with regard to the baring clause imposed in section 96(10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In this context; their lordships in the case of Azimuddin Pramanik and others vs. Sree Satya Narayan Pramanik and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 220 held (vide paragraph No. 4 & 5):

"Sub-section (10) of section 96 provides that a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase, such as, by inheritance, is not pre-emptible. This means, all other co-sharers by inheritance will be debarred from pre-emption by this sub-sec (10). But in the case of transfer to a co-sharer by purchases, it is not so protected from pre-emption, and any other co-sharer, whether by purchase or by inheritance, may claim pre-emption. But it does not mean that pre-emption may be claimed by a contiguous land-holder when the land has been transferred to a co-sharer by purchase.

The appellants need not have joined the pre-emptor-respondent, because to join in the application for pre-emption filed by a contiguous land-holder is unnecessary. The learned Single Judge has relied upon the case of Yakub Ali Mondal v Akher Ali Mondal 6 DLR 130 in which it was held that transfer to a co-sharer by purchase is pre-emptible. This proposition is not disputed; secondly, that case was decided under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act which limited pre-emption to co-sharers only, either by purchase or by inheritance; it did not extend the right pre-emption to a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred. As such the decision relied upon is of no assistance to the instant case where the claim of a contiguous land-holder is involved. The contiguous land-holder comes to the picture only when the co-sharer-tenants neither purchased the land nor claimed it by way of pre-emption but the land is sold to a stranger. Had, in the instant case, pre-emption been sought by a co-sharer by purchase, it would have been incumbent upon the co-sharer-transferee to apply to join in the application for rateable pre-emption. Reading section 96 as a whole it is found that if a land has been transferred to a co-sharer and when no other co-sharer has claimed pre-emption, the transfer is immune, by necessary implication, to a pre-emption, by a contiguous land-holder. The question raised is found to have been correctly answered by the learned Munsif"

15. Before parting, however, I must observe that the land transferred is admittedly as being used by the purchaser-pre-emptee-petitioner as his homestead and he use to reside therein since 1965, Section 6 of the law Reforms Ordinance, 1976 it is a legal embargo in getting the land pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

16. Having regard to the facts, circumstance and decisions referred to above I have the reason to inclined such inference that the teamed appellate court committed illegality in deciding the merit of the appeal and the impugned judgment and order is not passed within the purview of order XLI, Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such the Rule have got every merit to succeed.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order dated 29.03.1998 passed by the learned District Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No.20 of 1990 reversing those of dated 18.02.1990 passed by the learned Additional Assistant Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 1989 is hereby set aside.

18. The order of stay granted earlier by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

19. However; there will be no order as to costs.

20. Communicate this judgment and order immediately and send down the lower court's record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Rais Uddin, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 18.06.2014 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Barguna in Civil Revision No.13 of 2013 affirming the judgment and order dated 21.07.2013 passed by learned Assistant Judge, Barguna in Title Suit No.91 of 2012 rejecting the application for amendment, should not be set-aside.

2. The relevant fact giving rise to this Rule, in short, is that the Opposite-parties as plaintiffs brought a suit praying for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering into the plaintiff’s peaceful possession of the scheduled land.

3. The defendant Nos.5-9 appeared and filed written statement to contest the suit and the defendants-petitioners tiled an application for amendment of the written statement. The learned Judge of the trial court after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record rejected the application for amendment by his order dated 21.07.2013. Against the said judgment and order the defendants preferred Civil Revision No. 13 of 2013 under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned District Judge, Barguna. On transferred it was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge who after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record rejected the revisional application by his judgment and order dated 18.06.2014.

4. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and order the defendants as petitioners moved this court and obtained the instant Rule.

5. Mr. M. Mainul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners has placed the revisional application, pleadings, judgment and order of both the courts below and other materials on record before this court and submits that the learned judge of the courts below has committed in an error of law in deciding that by the proposed amendment nature and character has been changed. He submits that both the courts below failed to consider that by the proposed amendment the nature and character has not been changed rather by the proposed amendment it will be convenient and helpful for the court to decide the real question in controversy.

6. In support of his contention he has referred the decisions, in the case of: (1) Jadav Chandra Mali, being dead his heirs: Kusumbha Mali and others Vs. Abdul Khaleque and others, reported in 27 DLR AD) 114, (2) Abdul Motaleb Vs. Md. Ershad Ali and others, reported in 18 DLR (AD) 121, 3) Managing Committee, N.M.C. Model High School and others Vs. Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury and others, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 133.

7. Mr. Fahima Barrin, the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 4-6 opposed the rule and submits that both the courts below rightly rejected the amendment application observing that by the proposed amendment new contradictory and inconsistent facts has been incorporated. She further submits that the amendment may be allowed when real question in controversy will be resolved, rather, by the proposed amendment new, inconsistent facts has been incorporated and as such she prayed for discharged the rule.

8. In support of her contention she has referred the decisions, in the case of: (1) Abul Kalam Azad and another Vs. Sunhar Ali and others, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 130, (2) Abul Kashem Al-Asad Vs. Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land & others, reported in 57 DLR, 51, (3) Afzal Khan (Md) Vs. Md. Azmal Khan and others, reported in 59 DLR, 43.

9. In order to appreciate the submission made by the learned advocates for the parties, I have gone through the revisional application, pleadings, judgment and order of the courts below and other materials on record very carefully.

10. Now the question calls for consideration whether the learned Judge of the revisional court below committed any error of important question of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and order affirming the judgment of the trial court.

11. On perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiffs instituted a suit for permanent injunction. In the suit the defendants-petitioners appeared and filed written statement to contest the suit. The defendants-petitioners filed an application for amendment of their written statement.

<u>12. Amendment of pleading may be allowed in such a manner and terms and as such amendment shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties. The amendment sought for by the petitioners introducing a new story by taking new stand reversed to the original written statement and by such amendment a completely new and alternative facts will be introduced in the written statement. The amendment of pleading should not be refused unless; first, the pleading is wholly displaces by the amendment and secondly, the amendment introduces a different new story and inconsistent case.</u>

13. Since the instant Rule is obtained against an order, I need not enter into the merit of the case and suffice it to say that the learned Judge of the revisional court below on considering the materials on record and relevant provisions of law has rightly rejected the application filed by the petitioners and affirmed the judgment and order of the trial court has not committed any important question of law rather, are well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case and law.

<u>14. The courts are always inclined to allow amendment so as to enable the parties to bring all the points relating to dispute between the parties before the court in order to avoid multiplicity of the proceeding but the instant case by the proposed amendment the new and inconsistent facts has been introduced by taking new stand reversed to the original written statement. This view of mine find supports in the decisions, reported 46 DLR (AD) 130, 59 DLR 43, 57 DLR 51, wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"The defendant would not be allowed to introduce an alternative and completely different kind of defence both in terms of content and from which will have the effect of introducing a new controversy between the parties which, in fact, did not exist before."</u>

15. It appears to me that the decisions reached at by the revisional court below having been rested upon considerations and discussions of the materials facts on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspect involved is the case.

16. Moreover, the impugned judgment and order of the revisional court below in its entirety are well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. Therefore, grounds urged and the contentions advanced by the learned advocate for the petitioners are not correct exposition of law. However, I have gone through the decisions reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114, 10 DLR (AD) 121 and 31 DLR(AD) 139 referred by the learned advocate for the petitioners. I am respectful agreement with principles enunciated therein. But the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case and therefore, to that effect I am also unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the legal pleas taken by the learned advocate for opposite party prevail and appear to have a good deal of force.

17. In view of the discussions, decisions and reasons stated above, I am of the new that the impugned judgment and order of the court of revisional below suffers from no legal infirmity which calls for no interference by this court in exercising revisional power under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thus, I do not find any merit in the Rule.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and order dated 18.06.2014 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Barguna in Civil Revision No.13 of 2013 is hereby affirmed.

19. There will be no order as to costs.

20. The order of stay granted earlier by this court stands vacated.

21. Let the Lower Court Records along with a copy of the judgment be sent at once.

End.

lawyer:
