parties:
Sheikh Mohmmad Zafor and another... Defendant-Appellant-Petitioners
Vs.
Samela Bibi Sheikh and another....Plaintiff-Respondent-Opposite Parties*
full_judgment:
Kashefa Hussain, J: This is an application by the Defendant-Appellant-Petitioners for review of judgment and decree dated 05.12.2010 passed by this Division in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998. Upon filing of the instant Review Application, Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 05.12.2010 passed in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 by the High Court Division should not be reviewed and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts of the case in a nutshell, are that the appellants filed First Appeal No.177 of 1998 before the High Court Division being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 09.10.1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Court, Khulna in Title Suit No.79 of 194 decreeing the suit. In the First Appeal, the appellant's contention inter alia was that the Respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.79 of 1994 before the aforesaid Court seeking partition of the land and that it belonged to one Hossain Sheikh. The plaintiff stated inter alia, that Hossain Sheikh died leaving behind one son Akam Uddin and a daughter Samela Bibi who was plaintiff in the Samela Bibi as per the plaint inherited 1/3rd share to the land under partition and the rest 2/3rd was inherited by Akam Uddin and Akam Uddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdul Hakim Sheikh and Abu Zafor Sheikh one wife Chutu Bibi and a daughter Romesa Khan', Akam Uddin created a registered deed of patta dated 29.11.1927 showing settlement of 5.27 acres of land in his favour measuring 14 annas share in the property of Hossain Sheikh and 2 annas were left out of settlement.

3. It is the plaintiff's case that the patta was a unilateral patta and was not registered by both the parties and since both Samela Bibi and her brother Akan, Uddin were both minors at the time such patta was void. The plaintiff further stated that there were several previous litigations and the parts deed was cancelled. But the plaintiffs names in the suit property was not recorded as per her 1/3rd share and this compelled her to file the partition suit claiming 1/3rd sham of the suit land.

4. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alia that Hosain Sheikh had lawfully settled the suit land in favour of Akam Uddin by a registered patta deed dated 29.11.1927 and that after the settlement there remaining only 2 annas share to be divided between the heirs accordingly to their proportionate shares, Akam Uddin started possessing 4.60 acres of land and died leaving behind 2 sons and his legal heirs inherited the suit land proportionately and in this manner the defendant No. 2 inherited 1/5 share in the suit land. Abdul Hakim being in possession transferred 1.54 acres of land by registered kabalas deed dated 04.04.1984 in favour of defendant Nat. During possession the defendant Nos.1 and 2 also purchased lands by a number of kabala deeds and the defendant No.1 disclosed that they are in possession of the entire land except 20 decimals of such land.

5. During trial six issues were fronted, the P.Ws and D.Ws were duly examined and exhibits were duly produced before the Court and after conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Jude, 1st Court; Khulna decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 09.10.1997 ascertaining the share of the plaintiff to the extent of 1.60 acres and ascertaining the share of Akam Uddin to the extent of 2/3rd shares.

6. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree dated 09.04.1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 79 of 1994, the defendant Nos. l and 2 preferred First Appeal being No.177 of 1998 before this division and after hearing both sides and upon scrutiny of materials on record, this division allowed the appeal mainly on the ground of defect of parties and the requirement of the suit land to be brought into the hotchpotch of the suit. Although the appeal was allowed yet the appellants preferred this review application before us arising out of First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 on a specific ground of law. The petitioners in the review petition stated that due to unavoidable circumstances beyond their control they could not file an appeal against the judgment passed by the High Court Divisions and by the time they were ready to file an appeal, time for filing an appeal before the Appellate Division had already expired. They also stated in their review petition that the plaintiff-respondent in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 after dismissal of their suit filed a new suit afresh in the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna and summons of such suit was received and only after obtaining the certified copy, of the judgment the engaged Advocate from the Khulna Bar for the first time pointed out that there was an adverse finding on law points in the judgment of the High Court Division. But due to circumstances beyond their control there was no time to file an appeal before the High Court Division and due to such unavoidable circumstances the review application was also filed with a delay of 445 days and such delay was wholly unintentional.

7. Mr. Abul Kalam Mainuddin with Mr. M Shamsul Haque the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the review petitioners while Mr. M. Qumrul Haque Siddique with Mr. Tusher Kanti Roy, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the respondent-opposite-parties to resist the Rule.

8. Mr. Abul Kalam Mainuddin, the learned Advocate for the, review petitioner while making his submissions mainly cast his thrust upon the issue of amendment of Section 107 of the Transfer Property Act particularly the date of the amendment. He takes us through the judgment passed in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 and points out that this Division in its judgment made an error in law in not taking into consideration the fact that the pasta deed in question was executed on 29.11.1927 which was before the subsequent amendment of Section 107, which amendment came in 1929 only after the execution of the deed on 29.11.1927. He agitated before us that therefore the amended version of Section 107 requiring a patty deed to be executed by both the parties was not required before 1929 and consequently in the instant case shall not to be applicable to the pasta deed dated 29.11.1927. He also argues before us that he had agitated the issue of amendment of 1929 and the date of the execution of the pasta deed before this Division while making his submissions during the hearing in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 and further asserts that their submissions were also noted down in the judgment, but that this Division upon an error of law missed out on the legal bar of specific point not being able to give retrospective effect to a new provision of statute under the law. He further attracts our attention to it finding by this Division in its judgment that the land is agricultural land. The learned Advocate strenuously argued that inspire of express submissions made by them on the issue of the amendment of 1929 and the non-applicability of such amendment relating to a deed executed at a prior date, yet the submissions of the appellant-petitioner remained unanswered, not addressed upon by the Court. He also persuades that having obtained knowledge of the adverse remark much later due to circumstances beyond their control, the petitioners finding no other alternative was compelled to file a review application praying before this Division for review of its own judgments.

9. Upon queries made by us as to the legality of filing a review application on the grounds taken by the parties. the learned Advocate for the review petitioners submits that a review application is allowable in this case since this Division in his judgment made an error apparent on the face of the record and therefore according to the learned Advocate. Review will lie in the instant case. Upon further queries the learned Advocate agitated before us that there is an error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment of this Division since this Division by not addressing itself upon an important of law rather remained 'same on the point and thus made a `mistake' and due to which review petition lies.

10. On the other hand, Mr. M. Quamrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate for the respondent-opposite parties submits that this Division cannot sit on its own judgment save for few limited purposes. He points out that no new point of law was agitated and stresses upon the point that in a case where the issue was agitated before the Court but whirls not addressed by it, in such cases review shall not lie. He reiterated the point that this Division cannot review its own judgment on an issue which was already before it and such issue was expressly agitated before it but it was not addressed for some reason. He points out that in this event of an issue being raised even if it is then only it upon a specific point of law can be only subject of an appeal.

11. We have heard the learned Advocates from both sides, perused the application for review, judgments and materials on records. It transpires from the judgment passed in Flea Appeal No.I77 of 1998 by link Division that it is true that the review petitioners had placed their submissions upon a specific point of law, but the Court had not addressed on that point.

12. The situation might have been different if the particular issue was not placed before the Court at all. Bat since in the judgment itself, their Lordships even noted the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant-review-petitioners we do not have any scope to presume that the Court might inadvertently upon an error mistakenly or consciously overlooked the issue. It is obvious from the records that the issue was placed before the Court, but their Lordships decided not to address itself upon the same or did not feel it necessary to address the point same and now ill remained passive and apathetic. Now , in a situation like this whether review petition shall lie against the Court's conscious passiveness and apathy or whether it is a subject of appeal, we must at first examine the provisions of a review application within the scope of order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads under:-

13. Upon a perusal of Order 47 and an analysis of the circumstances under which a review of a judgment may lie, as is quite obvious from the judgment itself, that no new and important matter of evidence was discovered in this case after the passing of the judgment and decree. As we discussed above, it was upon a specific point of law and such point was already submitted by the concerned counsels, as appears from the judgment itself. Hence, it does not prima-facie come within the ambit of any new and hereto before undiscovered or unraveled and important matter of evidence.

14. Another circumstance as provided for in Order 47 for a review to be maintainable is "on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record". Here also we feel it necessary to reiterate that in this case it was not an inadvertent "mistake" or "error" by which the Court might have overlooked a specific issue. It if was, in fact an inadvertent mistake or error, review would lie. But as is obvious, the Court knowingly upon its conscious decision decided not to address the issue, whatever its reason of doing so. Under such circumstances we cannot treat a conscious decision of the Court to be `mistake' or 'error' apparent on the face of the record. Therefore if any person feels himself aggrieved by such decision taken consciously by a Court, not to address itself upon a particular point, in those cases it should be a subject of appeal, and not review.

15. During course of the argument, the learned Advocates from both sides had cited a few decisions before as in support of their respective arguments and had attracted our attention towards them and from which we are mentioning some. Learned Advocate for the petitioner had cited the principle in the case of Hosne Ara Begum —Vs- Anwara Begum reported in 5 BLC (2000) page 111 where the principle of maintainability of review in pars 11 of the judgment is produced here under:-

"A review is permissible only when it is seen that there was an error apparent on the face of the record in recording the judgment and order under review."

16. The petitioner also referred to the case of Rais Ali —Vs- Jabed Ali reported in 19 DLR (1967) page 511 where the principle cited is as follows:-

"What is the face of the record? The judgment which is pronounced by a Court is the face of the record of that Court. It is true that it is not every kind of error which would attract the provisions of Order 47 of the Code.

But them is no doubt that the judgment itself is the face of the record, whatever else may or may not be the face.'

17. The principle in the case of Mathura Mohan —Vs- Hamra Khatun reported in 48 DLR (1996) page 190 was also placed before us in the following terms:-

Order XLVII rule 1

"When there is an omission on the part of a Court to take notice of a provision of law an application for review under Order 47 rule 1 CPC is competent"

18. In the case of Hosne Ara Begum —Vs-Anwara Khatun reported in 5 BLC page the principle enumerates the circumstances under which a review may be permissible and maintains that to make a review application maintainable there has to be an error apparent on the face the record. But as we have discussed, in this case before us we do not find any error which is apparent of the record, rather it is a conscious decision of the Court by which it decided not to dwell upon a particular point raised by the party.

19. In the case of Rais Ali—Vs-Jabed Ali reported in 19 DLR (HC) 1967 page 511, we find an echo of the principle in the case referred to above and therefore our view on it also remains the same. But we would like to draw the attention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and remind him that in the 19 DLR case, the Court also significantly made an observation, stating that "not every kind of error would attract the provisions of Order 47 the Code." Relying upon this observation made in the DLR case we may conclude that just because there is an error in the judgment itself, it shall not make it eligible for a review application under Order 47 of the Code.

20. While drawing our attention to the decision in the case of Mathura Mohan -Vs-Hazera Khatun repotted in 48 DLR (1996) page 191, we find that the petitioner had relied upon the principle that in the event of an 'omission' by a Court to take 'notice' of a particular provision of law, Order 47 will come into play. But as we analyzed above, in the case before us and as it appears from the judgment in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998, the fact remains that in this particular case there are no omissions by the Court to take 'notice' of a specific provision of law. In fact as is evident from the judgment itself, the Court did take notice of the particular provision of law by many of including the submissions of the learned Advocate on the particular point or the judgment itself. It is only that the Court unmistakably noted the particular assertion on a point of law, but knowingly decided not to address the issue and left it at that. It is certainly not an omission on the part of the Court, but a decision by the Court having full knowledge.

21. Therefore use Fled that the petitioner's reliance upon these judgments are misplaced and he has upon misinterpretation of particular circumstances and the provision of law wrongly relied upon these judgment.

22. Parallelly, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties relying upon a few judgments, placed those before us for our appreciation some among which we fund necessary and significant to examine. The decision in the case of Ahmed Safe -Vs-Hamid Box repotted in 42 DLR (1990) (HC) page 209 was cited in the context by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties where in the principle relied upon by him reads as under:-

Failure on the part of a judge to accept properly the submission of the learned Advocate resulting in an erroneous finding is no ground for review.-

23. This judgment concluded that "failure" to accept properly submissions of the Advocate cannot be a ground for review. We feel that the principle enunciated may be applied to the case we are dealing with at present. Since at the case before us also a similar circumstance exists as the one contemplated in the judgment in 42 DLR that we have referred to given that in this review application also the basic contention of the petitioners is that the high Court Division in First Appeal No.177 of 1998 "failed" to accept properly the submissions of the Advocate and which resulted in an erroneous finding. We are inclined to agree with this decision that failure to properly accept submissions cannot be a proper ground of review under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

24. Besides, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties also took us to a decision of our Apex Court in the Case of Fazle Karim -Vs- Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR. (AD) (1996) page 179 where the grounds in Order 47 Rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure was discussed and the Court placing its reliance upon Order 47 concluded in pare 7 of the judgment-

"The Rules provide that review of a judgment or order in a civil proceeding may be made "on grounds similar to those mentioned in Order XLVI1 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure" that is to say, on discovery of new and important !natter or evidence which was not none or could not be produced before, (ii) on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or (iii) for any other sufficient reason. Consistently with the principle that there is to be an end to litigation it is now well-recognised that review is not an appeal nor a rehearing merely on the ground that one party or another conceives himself to be dissatisfied with the decision sought to be reviewed. Unless a prayer for review is based on the grounds mentioned above, the Court will not sit on the matter again for a rehearing or further hearing which is already concluded by decision even if that be erroneous,"

25. In another Para of the judgment in the same case their Lordships finding was-

"No mistake in a considered conclusion, what-ever the extent of that mistake, can be a ground for the exercise of review jurisdiction.

It is not because a conclusion is wrong but because something obvious has been overlooked, some important aspect of the matter has not been considered, that a review petition will lie. It is a remedy to be used only in exceptional circumstances."

26. While drawing upon its own conclusion and opinion our Apex Court in that case also placed its reliance in the case of Mohd Amir Khan --Vs- Controller of Estate Duty PLD 1962 (SC) page 335, part of which we feel significant to repeat hereunder :-

"The indulgence by way of review may no doubt be granted to prevent irremediable injustice being done by a Court of last resort as where by some inadvertence and important statutory provision has escaped notice which, if it had been noticed, might materially have affected the judgment of the Court but in no case should a rehearing be allowed upon merits."

27. The main reason that we also feel that this principle in the case reported in PLD 1962 and which was relied upon by our Apex Court in the case of Fazio Karim —Vs-Bangladesh is significant and applicable in this case is that a ground for review to be maintainable applies to a situation where something obvious has escaped notice or 'overlooked through inadvertence or any other reason whatsoever. But the case in hand does not reveal any such inadvertence or error.

<u>28. As we also discussed elsewhere in the judgment in this particular case there exists no such incident of having escaped notice of the 'overlooking' of any particular point or issue. Rather, the specific assertion and submissions on the point of law was duly noted down in the judgment itself. It is only that while doing so the High Court Division decided not to address it, for whatever its reasons.</u>

29. While deciding discerning upon Use question of maintainability of review when or not a review application may be entertained. We feel it necessary to distinguish and severe between two situations. A situation where a specific point of law was raised, but the Court failed to take due notice of it and a situation where the Court did take notice, but consciously decided to refrain from addressing itself on the point raised. The first situation falls within the category of an inadvertent error or mistake and which is also apparent on the face of the record and in such case a review application may be maintainable. But our case here for reasons we already discussed comes within the scope of the second category and therefore in this case review application under Order 47 the provisions of Order 47 is not maintainable.

30. We might safely conclude that in the case before us no 'overlooking' by any error or otherwise took place. Lastly the learned Advocate for the opposite pasties drew our attention to another decision of our Apex Court in the case of Zenith Packages Limited—Vs- Member Labour Appellate Tribunal Dhaka and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) (2000) page 161 where the principle applicable to the present case reads as follows:-

"Therefore on the grounds urged for review of judgment by the petitioner it seems to as that we are asked to sit over our judgment by way of appeal in a circuitous was addressing a lengthy and repeated submissions which already received our due notice in the judgment sought to be reviewed."

31. From a close reading of the above and upon comparison of the circumstance in the case before as our considered finding is that, in this case submissions of the Counsel did duly receive notice of the Court and which is echoed in the judgment itself and therefore in respectful agreement with the principle set out by our Apex Court, we are of the opinion that we cannot sit upon our own judgment and embark upon a rehearing upon specific a point and therefore the only redress for the petitioner is such cases is the Appellate Forum and not Review.

<u>32. Our finding is that in the case we are dealing with at present the primary aspect which ought to be appreciated in the case, the fact of noting the submissions on a particular point of law in the judgment but yet making a conscious decision of restraining itself from addressing that point of law is discernible and thus distinguishable from a situation where a point was placed but was somehow overlooked or missed out by the Court by an inadvertent error. We therefore feel it necessary to reiterate that what is discernible here is that no such inadvertent "error" occurred in consequence of which Order 47 Rule I could have come into play. Hence in this case the fact of noting the submissions in the judgment itself but yet consciously deciding not to dwell on the point makes all the difference and leaves no scope for a Review under the provision of Order 47 of the Code.</u>

Application for review of judgment-1.(1) Any person considering himself aggrieved —

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred,

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes,

and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order.

(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or order may apply for a review of judgment notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by some other party except where the ground of such appeal is common to the applicant and the appellant, or when, being respondent, he can present to the Appellate Court the case on which he applies for the review.

2. An application for review of a decree or order of a Court, not being the High Court Division, upon some ground other than the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule I or the existence of a clerical arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, shall be made only to, the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed; but any such application may, if the .judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), be disposed of by his successor.

33. Therefore upon hearing the learned Advocates from both sides and upon consideration of the decisions referred to and upon perusal of the judgment in First Appeal No.177 of 1998 against which the instant review application was filed and taking the other materials on record and taking the facts and circumstances into consideration, it is our view that none of the grounds, mentioned in Order 47 Rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure against which a review may be maintainable in this particular case. Therefore, the only forum available to the petitioner could have been way by way of an Appeal before the appropriate forum. Hence we do find any substance in this Rule.

34. In the result, the Rule as to Review is discharged without any order as to costs.

35. Communicate the order at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23.11.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.3496 of 2005 and 3501 of 2005)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J.: Since both these Civil Petitions for leave to Appeal have been directed against the judgment and order dated 23.11.2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division disposing of Civil Revision No. 3496 of 2005 and Civil Revision No. 3501 of 2005 analogously both these Petitions have been heard together and by this single judgment both the Civil Petitions for leave to Appeal will be disposed of.

2. Relevant facts necessary for disposal of these civil petitions are as follows:

3. The respondent Nos. 1 to 3, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 192 of 2000 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur for partition. The plaintiffs case, in short, was that Vagaban Chandra Gope, Debendra Chandra Cope and Rajendra Chandra Cope were the owners of 20.62 acres of land of C.S. khatian No. 86-as described in the schedule to the plaint in equal share. Debendra Chandra Gope died unmarried and consequently his two brothers Vagaban Chandra Cope and Rajendra Chandra Gope became the owners of the scheduled land in equal share. That Rajendra Chandra Gope sold 1.75 acres of land From C.S. Plot No. 605 to Ganesh Chandra and Puma Chandra by registered kabala dated 17.02.1926. Subsequently Rajendra Chandra Gope died leaving four daughters and two daughter's son namely, Paresh Chandra and lonindra Chandra who became the owners of 4.11 acres of land of Plot No. 605 alter the death of three daughters or Rajendra Chandra Gope. Paresh Chandra transferred 1.40 acres of land of this Plot. No. 605 to Shashi Bhushan by kabala dated 26.04.1969. After the death of Shashi Bhushan his three sons Dinabandhu, Pranbandhu and Krishna Chandra Das i.e. the plaintiff Nos.1, 2 and 3 became the owners of the said 1.40 acres of land of Plot No. 605 and the plaintiffs are also in possession of the said land.

4. That Vagaban Chandra Cope transferred 87 acre of land or Plot No. 605 to Joypriya Bairagi by kabala dated 26.04.1937 and thus Vagaban Chandra Cope had 5.07 acres of land in this Plot No. 605. After the death of Vagaban Chandra Cope his four sons became the owners of that land. By a partition deed dated 26.08.1949 each son of Vagaban Chandra Gope got 1.27 acres of land in this Plot No. 605. Haricharan-one the sons of Vagaban Chandra Cope died leaving two sons in Kartick Chandra and Mayan Chandra who became the owners of 1.27 acres of land in this Plot No. 605. That the plaintiffs claimed partition of their 1.40 acres of land in Plot No.  605 to the defendants, but they refused and hence this suit.

5. The defendant Nos.10, 14-20, 21, 30 and 31 appeared in the suit and filed applications for separate saham. The defendant Nos.10, 14 to 20 stated in their application for saham, that Manindra Chandra Gope got 2.14½ acres of land in the Plot No. 605 by virtue of purchase and by partition and sold the same to Nuruddin Bhuiyan. Subsequently Nuruddin Bhuiyan transferred the said land to A. Kadir-the father of the defendant No.  31 at a consideration of Tk. 6,000/- only with an agreement of reconveyance. Thereafter A. Kadir died. Nuruddin Bhuiyan then instituted Title Suit No.  364 of 1980 against the heirs of A. Kadir which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 169 of 1981, for getting the said land re-conveyed and got decree. The heirs of A. Kadir withdrew the money deposited by Nuruddin Bhuiyan from the Court. After getting return of the said land Nuruddin Bhuiyan transferred the entire 2.14½ acres of land to his daughter Golnahar Begum by a registered heba-bi-ewaj deed dated 03.08.1987. Subsequently Golnahar Begum exchanged 1.8½ acres of land from the said Plot No. 605 with the land of one Badaruddin by a registered deed of exchange dated 05.06.1989. She again exchanged .35 acre of land of this Plot No. 605 with the land of Sk. A. Rashid by another deed of exchange dated 31.05.1988. That Sk. A. Rashid subsequently exchanged his said 35 acre of land of Plot No. 605 to Badaruddin by a deed of exchange dated 16.08.1989. Thus Badaruddin became the owner 2.14½ acres of land of Plot No. 605. 13adaruddin died leaving Ills widow, the defendant No. 10, six sons, the defendant Nos.11 to 15 and 20, four daughters, the defendant Nos.16 to 19 as his heirs. That the defendant Nos.12 and 13 transferred .47 acre of land from Plot No. 605 to the defendant No. 11 by a kabala dated 10.06.1998. They again sold .23½ acre of land to, "Sarkari Kurmochari Sonmillito Kallyan Trust" by a kabala dated 16.05.1999. The other heirs of Badaruddin also entered into a contract with the said Kallyan Trust to sell 1.44 acres of land of the said plot. That the defendant No.  31 Abdul Halim son of A Kadir though filed Title Suit No. 128 of 1987 against Nuruddin Bhuiyan but the said suit was dismissed for default on 15.08.1989. The defendant No. 31 filed Title Suit No. 123 of 1998 also in the First Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur against some of the heirs of Nuruddin Bhuiyan, but subsequently withdrew that suit on 09.02.2002. That the defendant No.  31 had no title and possession in the said 2.14½ acres of land of Plot No.  605.

6. The defendant No. 21 Md. Ramjan Ali, Director (Administration) of Sarkari Karmachari Sanmilito Kallyan Trust, Gazipur in his prayer for saham has sup-ported the case of the defendant Nos.10, 14 to 20 and has stated that the Kallyan Trust is entitled to get saham for 2.14½ acres of land from the Plot No. 605 by virtue of purchase from those defendants.

7. The defendant No. 30 also prayed for separate saham for 2.32 acres of land of this Plot No. 605 stating that he acquired that land by way of purchase from the admitted co-sharers of this plot.

8. The defendant No. 31 prayed for separate saham for 2.14½ acres of land out of this Plot No. 605. His case was that Nuruddin Bhuiyan sold out these 2.14½ acres of land to his father Abdul Kadir by registered kabala dated 01.10.1969. That Abdul Kadir was killed during the war of liberation in 1971 leaving his three wives, ten sons and eleven daughters who inherited the land left by Abdul Kadir. That subsequently the defendant No. 31 purchased the entire share of the other heirs of Abdul Kadir and thus he became the owner of 2.14½ acres of land of this Plot No. 605 both by inheritance and by purchase. This defendant No. 31 has pleaded a further case that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 as alleged by the plaintiff was collusive and fraudulent and as such void. That Nuruddin Bhuiyan sold out that 2.14½ acres of land to A. Kadir by a saf-kabala and there was no agreement for reconveyance of that land.

9. The trial court by his judgment and decree dated 31.10.2002 decreed the suit for partition allotting a separate saham for 1.40 acres of land to the plaintiffs. The trial court allotted separate sahams of 2.32 acres of land to the defendant No.  30 and 2.14½ acres of land to the defendant No. 31 also by that judgment.

10. Against that judgment of the trial court the defendant Nos.10, 14 to 20 preferred Title Appeal No. 3 of 2003 and the defendant No. 21 preferred Title Appeal No.  9 of 2003 before the court of the learned District Judge, Gazipur. The appellate court by an analogous judgment and decree dated 1.8.04.2005 allowed both those appeals in part.

<u>11. The appellate court though affirmed the sahams allotted by the trial court to the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 30 but disapproved the saham allotted to the defendant No. 31 and allotted a separate saham of 1.44 acres of land to the defendant Nos. 10, 14 to 20 and another separate saham of .70½ acre of land to the defendant No. 21 out of Plot. No. 605 accepting the case of the defendant Nos.10, 14-20 and 21 that Nuruddin Bhuiyan-the admitted owner of these 2.14½ acres of land of Plot No. 605 transferred this land to A. Kadir with an agreement of re-conveyance and subsequently Nuruddin Bhuiyan got back that land re-conveyed through court by filing Title Suit. No. 169 of 1981 and subsequently Nuruddin Bhuiyan transferred this entire 2.14½ acres of land to his daughter Golmahar Begum by a registered heba-bil-ewaj deed and subsequently Badaruddin acquired this entire 2.14½ acres of land by registered deeds and the defendant Nos. 10, 14 to 20 are the heirs of Badaruddin and the defendant No. 21 is a transferee from these defendant Nos.10, 14 to 20.</u>

12. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the appellate court the defendant No. 31 Abdul Halim preferred Civil Revision Nos.3501 of 2005 and 3496 of 2005 before the High Court Division and obtained rules. A Single Bench of the High Court Division ultimately discharged both the rules by the impugned analogous judgment and order.

13. The defendant No. 31 Abdul Halim then has preferred these two civil petitions for leave to appeal challenging this judgment of the High Court Division.

14. We have heard Mr. Moinul Hosien, the learned Senior Advocate appeared for the petitioner and also Mr. Abdul Quiyum, the learned Senior Advocate appeared for the respondent No. 4.

<u>15. In this suit for partition there is no dispute as regards the sahams allotted to the plaintiffs and the defendant No.  30 The dispute in between the contesting defendant. Nos.10, 14 to 20, 21 and the present petitioner (the contesting defendant No. 31) is with regard to 2.14½ acres of land which Nuruddin Bhuiyan, admittedly, got by virtue of purchase from an admitted co-sharer. The case of the contesting defendant Nos. 10, 14 to 20, 21 is that Nuruddin Bhuiyan sold out this 2.14½ acres of land to A. Kadir the father of the defendant No. 31 by a registered kabala with an agreement of re-conveyance and subsequently Nuruddin Bhuiyan filed Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 against A. Kadir for getting back that land re-conveyed and that suit was decreed on 08.05.1983 and in execution of that decree the decree-holder Nuruddin Bhuiyan got the deed of re-conveyance in respect of that 2.14½ acres of land executed and registered through court. The contesting defendant No. 31 has denied this case of the contesting defendant Nos. 10, 14 to 20 and 21 and alleged that there was no agreement for re-conveyance in between Nuruddin Bhuiyan and A. Kadir and the decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 was collusive, fraudulent and as such void it appears that both the appellate court below and the High Court Division have deeply considered this allegation of the contesting, defendant No. 31 and on meticulous examination of the evidence on record and facts and circumstances found that there was no evidence at all to prove that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 was obtained by practicing fraud. The appellate court below and the revisional, court on consideration of all aspects, clearly held also that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 is binding upon the defendant No. 31 and as such the defendant No. 31 could not have any claim as regards 2.14½ acres of land of this plot No. 605.</u>

16. Moinul Hossain, the learned Counsel for the defendants though has argued to the effect that the appellate court below and the High Court Division have erred in holding the decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 valid and binding on the defendant No. 31 but could not show us any evidence or material from record to substantiate the allegation of the defendant No. 31 that this decree was obtained by practicing fraud.

17. Mr. Abdul Quiyum, the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 4, on the other hand, has made submissions to the effect that the appellate court below and the High Court Division on proper examination of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances and on proper appreciation of the matter and the legal provisions have rightly held that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 is valid and binding on the defendant No. 31 also.

18. We have gone through the judgment of the courts below and considered the sub-missions of the learned Counsels of both the sides.

19. We do not find any error in the findings and decision of the appellate court below and the revisional court. Both the courts, on proper appreciation of the matter and meticulous examination of the evidence and materials on record rightly arrived at the findings and decision dial Nuruddin Bhuiyan got back his 2.14½ acres of land from A. Kadir-the father of the defendant No. 31 as per decree passed in Title Suit No. 169 of 1981 and this decree is valid and as such the defendant No. 31 could not get any saham from the suit land.

20. In view of above it is evident that there is no merit in these civil petitions for leave to appeal.

21. In the result both the civil petitions for leave to appeal be dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2326 of 2009
lawyer:
Abdus Salam Mondal, Deputy Attorney General, instructed by Mr. B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioner 
Ferozur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by Advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent Nos.1 (ka) to 1(gha) and 3-5 
Respondent Nos.2 and 6-11 ------ Not represented.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur ------ Petitioner 
Vs.
Abdul Majid being dead his heirs Mizanur Rahman (Minor) and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated. 19.04.2009 passed by the High Court Division id Civil Revision No. 2789 of 2002 with Civil Rule No.110 (Con) of 1999)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 19.04.2004 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2789 of 2002 discharging the Rule affirming the judgment and decree dated 09.03.1998 passed by the then. learned Subordinate Judge (Artha Rin Adalat), Dinajpur in Other Appeal No. 72 of 1991 reversing those dated 15.01.1991 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge; Dinajpur Sadar, Dinajpur in Title Suit No. 137 of 1986 decreeing the suit.

<u>2. The facts, leading to the filing of this petition, in brief, are that the plaintiffs filed the suit against the Government for declaration of their title to the suit land. The plaintiff’s case is that the suit land along with other land originally belonged to Kasirun Nessa Chowdhury, wife of Sohrab Ali Chowdhury. After death of Kasirun Nessa Chowdhury and her husband, the suit land devolved on their son Mumik Hosan Chowdhury, defendant No. 2 and daughter Hamida Khatun Chowdhury, defendant No. 6, by way of inheritance. By amicable settlement, the suit land fell in the saham of Hamida Khatun Chowdhury. While possessing the suit land, she submitted her return as per provision of P.O. (President's Order) 98 of 1972. Hamida Khatun Chowdhury being issueless used to cultivate her land by bargadar. A portion of the suit land was being possessed by Niltak Barman by way of licence from her. On 02.10.1979, Enam Ali disclosed to Hamida Khatun that his two sons got lease of the suit land from the Government and as such, he would not pay the share of Barga and after the enquiry by her servant, she came to know that in her return she wrongly stated 3.06 acres of land in Plot No. 544 instead of the suit plot. Hamida Khatun filed a petition to the Revenue Officer for amendment and on 16.10.1979, Miscellaneous Case No.  XIII of 1979-80 was started and the notices were served upon the concerned parties. On 28.04.1980, the Revenue Officer, on receipt of the report of enquiry, amended the return inserting Plot No. 561 in place of Plot No. 544. After that, possession was taken over from leases by beating drum. While in possession of the suit land, Hamida Khatun sold the same to plaintiff Nos. 1-5 by registered deed of sale dated 13.04.1981. While plaintiff Nos. 1-5 have been possessing of the suit land, the brother of Hamida Khatun submitted return in the name Monalik Chowdhury, showing Plot No.  561 instead of Plot No. 544. In that return, the suit plot was wrongly written. Against the order of Revenue Officer, defendants filed an appeal to A.D.C (Additional Deputy Commissioner) (Revenue), who allowed the appeal setting aside the order of Revenue Officer. Subsequently, the plaintiffs filed an appeal against the order of A.D.C (Revenue) before the Land Appeal Board, which upheld the order of the A.D.C. (Revenue). Thus the Government leased out the suit land to the leases and as a result, the plaintiffs' title has been clouded. Hence, the instant suit has been filed.</u>

<u>3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filling written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. His case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Hamida Khatun Chowdhury and Momlik Hosan Chowdhury. Subsequently, by amicable settlement, the land in Plot No. 544 fell in the saham of Hamida Khatun Chowdhury and the land in Plot No. 561 fell in the saham of Momlik Hosan Chowdhury. According to P.O. No. 98 of 1972 Momlik Chowdhury submitted return the suit plot No. 561 and the excess land was surrendered in favour of Government and since then the suit land became the property of Government as khash land and the Government leased out the land on yearly basis to Emdadul Huq and Nazubul Islam. While they had been in possession of suit land, Hamida Begum filed a petition for amendment of the return and the Revenue Officer ordered amendment. Against that order, defendants filed an appeal to A.D.C. (Revenue), which was allowed. Against the aforesaid order, Hamida Khatun preferred an appeal before the band Appeal Board, which upheld the order of A.D.C. (Revenue) Hamida Khatun Chowdhury did not have right to transfer the suit land to plaintiff Nos. 1-5 and the document, if any, is produced that would be fraudulent and the suit is liable to be dismissed.</u>

4. Defendant Nos. 3-4 contested the suit by filing a separate written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. Their case is that accepting the statement of surrender, defendant No. 1 on 10.07.1978 leased out 2.90 acres of land to them for the first time for a period of five years and that they had been in possession of the said 2.90 acres of land.

5. The trial Court by its judgment and order dated 15.01.1991 decreed the suit.

6. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, defendant No. 1 preferred Other Appeal No. 72 of 1991 before the District Judge, Dinajpur. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the then learned Subordinate Judge (Artha Rin Adalat), Dinajpur, who by his judgment and order dated 09.03.1998 dismissed, the appeal upholding the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, defendant-petitioner filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2789 of 2002. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 19.04.2009 discharged the Rule without any order as to costs.

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the leave petitioner has preferred this civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

<u>9. Mr. Abdus Salam Mondal, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the leave petitioner, submits that there having been a bar to challenging the order passed by the revenue authorities under Article 17 of the Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order, 1972 and both the Courts below having committed error of law occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the rule and maintaining the judgments of the Courts below. He further submits that plaintiff No. 6 having filed the return/statements on 31.03.1973 and defendant No. 2 having accepted the return/statements on 23.02.1973 as correct and the Circle Officer (Revenue) without authority having corrected the return/ statements filed by plaintiff No. 6 on 31.03.1973 inserting Plot No.  562 with an area of 3.02 acres of land and excluding Plot No. 544 with an area of 3.06 acres from the return, the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule.</u>

10. Mr. Ferozur Rahman, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent. Nos.  1(ka)-1(gha) and 3-5, on the other hand, supports the judgment delivered by the High Court Division.

11. The submissions made on behalf of the leave petitioner merit consideration.

<u>12. Therefore leave is granted to consider the following points:</u>

<u>I. Whether there having been a bar to challenging the order passed by the revenue authorities under Article 17 of the Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Zorder, 1972 and both the Courts below having committed error of law occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule and maintaining the judgment and decrees of the Courts below.</u>

<u>II. Whether plaintiff No. 6 having filed the return/statements on 31.03.1973 and defendant No. 2 having accepted the return/statements on 23.02.1973 as correct and the Circle Officer (Revenue) without authority having accepted the statements filed by plaintiff No. 6 on 31.03.1973 inserting Plot No. 562 with an area of 3.02 acres of land and excluding Plot No. 544 with an area of 3.06 acres from the return, the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule.</u>

13. The petitioner is permitted to prepare the paper-books out of Court in accordance with Rules.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 1087-90 of 2007
lawyer:
Abdul Jabber Advocate instructed by Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners 
Not represented  ------ Respondents.
parties:
1. Shahadat Hossain Mina  ------ Petitioner (In C.P. No. 1087/ 2007)
2. Abdul Khaleque Mollah   ------ Petitioner (In C.P No. 1088/ 2007)
3. Md. Enamul Hoque Mollah.   ------ Petitioner (In C P. No. 1089/ 2007)
4. Champak Kumar Biswas.  ------  Petitioner (In C.P No. 1090/ 2007)
Vs.
Governor, Bangladesh Bank and others.   ------ Respondents (In all the cases)
case_source: (From The judgment and order dated 26.04.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5962, 5963, 4893 & 4894 of 2007)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J : The above petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the judgment and order dated 26.04.2007 of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition. No. 5962, 3876, 5963, 4893, 4894 and 4895 of 2007 discharging the Rules obtained challenging the staff Order No. 226 of 1997 dated 04.08.1997 issued by the respondent No. 2 placing the petitioners under suspension.

<u>2. The petitioners filed the above writ petitions on the averments that they had been working in Bangladesh Bank in various capacities and Mr. Ataur Rahman Miah, District Anti-Corruption Officer, on 30.09.1993 lodged Khulna-P.S. Case No. 45 dated 30.09.1993 and 25 dated 19.01.1994 against them and others allegation that they prepared fictitious bills by creating advice with forged signatures and thereby misappropriated huge amount. The police, after investigation, submitted charge sheet. On coming to know about the aforesaid criminal cases they appeared before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Khulna and obtained bail and had been performing their normal duties in connection with their services in Bangladesh Bank an were never arrested in connection with the aforesaid two cases. Prior to the lodging of the FIR departmental proceedings were initiated against the petitioners and they were also placed under suspension by Bangladesh Bank by departmental Staff Orders which are not in accordance with Regulation No. 22 of Bangladesh Bank's Staff Regulations in terms of which departmental proceedings are he concluded within 4 months from the date of showing cause for disciplinary actions whereas departmental charges were submitted after 8 months and moreover order of suspension can only be passed by a person having authority to make the final order that is the order, of dismissal, and so the suspension orders not being passed by the appointing authority, arc without lawful authority and moreover actions against the petitioners under Regulation No. 22 of the above Staff Regulations should not have been taken before the judgment in the criminal cases and thus the orders of suspensions are without lawful authority.</u>

3. The respondent No. 1 and 2, the Governor, Bangladesh Bank and General Manager, Bangladesh Bank respectively, opposed the rules by filing affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits-in-opposition denying the allegations and contending inter alia, that the petitioners in total violation of the established practice made payment of Tk. 7,25,400/- and Tk.7,69,144/- against 8 forged bills for which Khulna Police Station Case No. 45 dated 30.09.1993 and 25 dated 19.09.1994 were lodged against them an the police after investigation submitted charge sheets under sections- 409/ 467/ 468/471/ 472 / 190 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and since criminal cases were pending against the petitioners for misappropriation of money through the forged bills, they were placed under suspension by various staff orders in accordance with the provisions of Regulation No. 22(IV) of the Regulation read with Rule 73 of the Bangladesh Service Rules and in the departmental proceeding charges have been framed against them for making payment of Tk. 7,69,144/- and Tk. 7,25,400/- in total Tk. 14,94,544/- against 8 forge bills in violation of section 424 of the Banking Department Manual (BD Manual) and other established practice and the inquiry officer, after enquiry, has also submitted his reports and since criminal cases are pending against the petitioners, Bangladesh Bank did not take any further action in the departmental proceeding and after the disposal of the criminal cases the departmental proceedings will be concluded and sine both the departmental proceedings an criminal proceedings are pending against the petitioners, the writ petitions challenging interim orders of suspension are absolutely misconceived and the remedies of the petitioners, if any, lies with administrative Tribunal and further the petitioners were found guilty in Special Case No. 33 of 1997 and Special Case No. No. 1 of 1997 arising out of the above Khulna P.S. wherein they were convicted and sentenced “দন্ডবিধির ২৮৯/১০৯ ধারামতে ৩(তিন) বৎসর সশ্রম কারাদন্ডে এবং ১.৩০,০০০/-(এক লক্ষ ত্রিশ হাজার) টাকা জরিমানা অনাদায়ে আরো ৯ মাস বিনাশ্রম কারাদন্ড এবং দন্ডবিধির ৪৭১/১০৯ এবং ৪৭২/১০৯ ধারামতে প্রতি ধারায় ৩ বৎসর করিয়া সশ্রম কারাদন্ডে এবং প্রতি ধারায় ৫০০/-(পাঁচশত) টাকা করিয়া জরিমানা অনাদায়ে প্রতি ধারায় আরো ১(এক) মাস করিয়া বিনাশ্রম কারাদন্ডে দন্ডিত করা হইল।” and being aggrieved they filed criminal appeals which were dismissed by the High Court Division and so the present writ petitions are not maintainable. The petitioners filed affidavits-in-reply stating that the above criminal cases and appeals were disposed of after the issuance of the impugned orders of suspension and so the result of those criminal cases and appeals should not have any bearing on the legality of the orders of suspension and that the petitioners filed criminal petitions for leave to appeal against the judgments of the High Court Division.

4. The High Court Division, after hearing, discharged the Rules.

5. We have heard the learned counsel of the petitioners, and perused the impugned judgment and orders and other connected papers.

<u>6. As it appears the High Court Division discharged the Rules relying on the case of Junnur Rahman vs. Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others, reported in 51 DLR(AD) 116; Delwar Hossain Mia (Md) and another vs. Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others, reported in 52 DLR(AD) 120, Shamsul Islam Khan vs. Secretary, Ministry of Communication, Roads and Highways, reported in 8 BLT (AD) 120 holding that the Appellate Division in a series of cases has taken a consistent view that a person in the service of the Republic who intends to challenge the vires of a law on the ground of violation of fundamental right may seek his remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution but in all other cases he will seek remedy under Article 117(2) and that on the terms and the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute and that in the instant writ petitions the petitioners did not challenge the vires of any law on the ground of violation of their fundamental rights and the petitioners, being employees of Bangladesh Bank, the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in relation to the impugned orders of suspension of the petitioners. The High Court Division also referred to the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. S.M. Fariduddin reported in 21 BLD (AD) 155 wherein it was further held that when a person in the service of Bangladesh Bank is suspended he is to follow that order of suspension and if by the order of suspension any of the terms and conditions of service is violated his remedy lies before the Administrative Tribunal.</u>

7. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record and the law involved arrived at a correct decision and there is no illegality or infirmity in the above decision so as to call for any interference.

8. The petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1294 of 2010
lawyer:
Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners 
M. A. Jabbers, Advocate, instructed by Mr. MG. Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondents
parties:
Abu Bakkar Lashkar & others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Rostam Ali Mondal being dead his heirs Abu Kalam & others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27.04.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Rule No.1024 (con) of 200)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 27.04.2010 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Rule No. 1024(Con) of 2009 discharging the Rule for condonation of delay of 5791 days in filing the revisional application, challenging the judgment and decree dated 11.11.1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Magura in Title Appeal No. 115 of 1992 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 31.5.1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Salikha, Magura in Title Suit No. 78 of 1989 decreeing the suit.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this petition for leave to appeal, in short, are:

3. The plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 78 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Magura against the defendants for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land or in the alternative for partition.

4. After contested hearing, the suit was decreed in terms of the judgment and decree dated 31.5.1992 (decree signed on 2.6.1992).

5. Defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-7 preferred Title Appeal No. 115 of 1992 before the learned District Judge, Magura and the learned Joint District Judge allowed the appeal on setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 31.5.1992.

6. Feeling aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the appellate Court the plaintiffs-petitioners prepared a revisional application 115 of the ode of Civil Procedure. Since the revisional application was out of time by 5791 days, the plaintiffs-petitioners had to file an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay.

<u>7. It is stated in the application for condo-nation that for filing a civil revision, the plaintiff’s petitioners collected a certified copy of the judgment of the appellate Court on 21.3.1994 and delivered the same to Mr. Md. Lutfor Rahman, a practicing Advocate of Magura District Bar for taking necessary step in this regard. Thereafter in the middle of the year 2004, the said Advocate died, and hearing the news petitioner No.1 went to the house and the chamber of the said Advocate. He tried to collect information from the law clerk and the junior of the deceased Advocate Mr. Lutfor Rahman. But they expressed their inability to return the certified copy of the impugned judgment. Then the plaintiffs-petitioners collected a fresh certified copy of the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court on 23.7.2009 and filed the present application for condonation along with a revisional application.</u>

8. Rule was issued upon the defendants-opposite parties to show cause as to why the delay should not be condoned.

9. Defendants-opposite party Nos. 1-7 entered appearance, but did not file any counter affidavit controverting the statements made in the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act.

10. Mr. Mohd. Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, submits that the High Court Division discharged the Rule on the ground that no satisfactory explanation for the delay of fifteen years was given although the plaintiffs petitioners stated in the application under section 5 of the limitation Act that they could not file the revisional application within time because of sudden death of the learned Advocate Md. Lutfor Rahman. He further submits that the plaintiffs petitioners had no willful negligence and that they are simple, uneducated and poor rural people and that they relied on the assurance of deceased Advocate Md. Lutfor Rahman, who assured them of filing the revisional application within time and that the High Court Division without taking into consideration those facts discharged the Rule.

<u>11. The High Court Division having taken into consideration the statements made in the application filed under section 5 of the Limitation Act came to a finding that the plaintiffs-petitioners were very conscious of the trial and the necessity of timely filling of the civil revision. The High Court Division further found that the explanation for the period from 21.3.1994, to the collection of the second certified copy of the judgment on 16.7.2009 was extremely vague. The High Court Division noticed that the plaintiffs petitioners stated the date of death of Mr. Md. Lutfor Rahman to be in the middle of the year 2004 and that the certificate issued by the General Secretary of the  Bar Association (Annexure-A to the supplementary affidavit) showed that the said Advocate died on 29.11.2004. The High Court Division also considered the four cases, namely, Khairullah Vs. A.D.C. (Revenue) and Another (2002) 54 DLR (AD) 13, Abu Ali Chowdhury Vs. The State (1997) 5 BLT (HCD) 3, Nuru Mia Vs. State (1998) 3 BLC 423 and Momtazuddin and Another Vs Yakub Ali (1994) 46 DLR (AD) 13 cited by the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs petitioners and rightly found that the facts of those cases were different from the instant case.</u>

12. Having gone through the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the plaintiffs-petitioners miserably failed to explain the delay of 5791 days i.e. more than fifteen years.

<u>13. The plaintiffs-petitioners filed the suit for declaration .of title and recovery of possession of the suit land or in the alternative for partition. The cause of action of a partition suit is recurring. The plaintiffs may have recourse to legal measures before the appropriate Court for partition of ejmali property if their claim is not otherwise barred.</u>

14. The findings arrived at, and the decision made by, the High Court Division having been made on proper appreciation of law and facts do not call for interference.

15. We find no substance in this petition which is accordingly dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
A. W. Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, instructed by Mvi. Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant 
Syed Badrul Alam, Advocate instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondents
parties:
Bangladesh ----- Appellant
Vs.
Abbas Ali Munshi being dead his heirs karimun Nessa & ors ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 20th June, 1988 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal From Appellate Decree No. 146 of 1977)
full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdur Rouf J:- This appeal, following leave, by the Government plaintiff appellant, is from the judgment and decree dated 20.6.88 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in second Appeal No. 146 of 1977 dismissing the appeal and affirming thereby the judgment and decree dated 18.9.76 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka allowing Tide Appeal 159 of 1974 and reversing thereby the judgment and decree dated 9.7.74 passed by the learned Subordinate judge, 151 Court, Dhaka decreeing Title Suit No. 202 of 1970.

2. Respondent No. 1 (since dead) as plain-tiff instituted Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration that he is a radiate in respect of 24.67 acres of nut land appertaining to C. S. Plot No. 1474 under khatian 1/29, Touzi No. 133 of kaliakoir Mouza within P.S. Kaliakoir Dist. Dhaka and for further declaration that record-of-right in respect of the said land is incorrect.

3. The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, was that the suit property originally belonged to the then Zaminder of kashimpur, who made a settlement of the same with the plaintiff in 1946 and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the same. The suit property has wrongly been recorded in favour of the forest department of the Government of East Pakistan, who have no right, title and interest therein.

4. The appellant Government and the present respondent Nos. 2-4 the officers of the appellant, as defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff as a raiyat in respect of the suit land and asserting therein that the sun property is a notified forest land as per gazette Notification 3125/. F.O.R dated 13.4.55.

5. On the date of hearing of the suit those defendants having failed to appear, the suit was decreed exparte on 9.9.67. On 1.9.70, the appellant and the plaintiff respondents instituted Title Suit No. 202 of 1970 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a decree to set aside the aforesaid exparte decree alleging inter alia, that the same had been obtained by the plaintiff of that suit fraudulently and collusively. Their case in short is that the cleark of the Government pleader in collusion with the plaintiff of that suit did neither pay the adjournment cost one inform the present appellant and its officers of the date of hearing of the suit, as a result the suit was decreed exparte and thereby the Government have been seriously prejudiced.

6. The respondent No.1 as defendant No. 1 also contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the present appellant had willfully defaulted in making appearance in the suit because there was no gazette notification declaring the suit property as a reserved forest. Considering the oral evidence of one P.W. Two D.Ws and the documentary evidence the trial Court decreed the suit. On an appeal, preferred by defendant respondent No. 1, the lower appellate court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff could not prove the allegations of collusion and fraud as alleged in the plaint. The present appellant then preferred the Second Appeal against the decree of the lower appellate court, which has been affirmed by the impugned judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division.

7. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions made by the learned Additional Attorney General The suit land being reserve forest under Notification 3125-FOR dated id April 1955 issued under Section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927 (EXt.1) Tide Suit No. 160 of 1966 was barred under Section 20(2)(a) (iii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and as such the trial Court had no jurisdiction to try that suit in view of the provision of Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure  and hence the impugned exparte decree passed in the aforesaid title suit being void, abilities ought to have been set aside by the High Court Division;

In the plaint it has been clearly averred that the clerk of the Government pleader in Collusion with the plaintiff of T.S. No.160 of 1966 did neither pay the adjournment cost nor inform the defendants of the suit about the date of its peremptory hearing, which resulted with the passing of an exparte decree adversely effecting the vital interest of the Government in respect of a vast tract; of notified government forest land and as such for the ends of justice the exparte  decree should be set aside.

<u>8. Mr. A. W. Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney General appearing for the appellant, submits that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 the plaintiff admitted that the Suitland has been recorded as government forest and that  the present appellant has proved Ens. the gazette notification in support of the nature of the suit land as the recorded government forest and as such in view of the provision of sub-section (2)(a)(iii) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in not holding that the Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 was i not maintainable and thereby the exparte decree dated 9.9.67 passed in that suit being a nullity is liable to be set aside. Mr. Bhuiyan, further submits that the plaintiffs having proved that they were not informed about the date of hearing of Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 and were also not informed about the requirement to pay the adjournment cost and as a result the plaintiff the could neither pay adjournment costs nor could contest the suit on the date of its peremptory hearing and thereby the plaintiff legally proved the necessary facts and circumstances to substantiate the allegations of collusion in between the clerk of the Government pleader and the  plaintiff of the Title Suit No. 160 of 966, the lower appellate court upon improper assumption of facts wrongly revered the finding of collusion, found by the trial Court on the evidence on record and as such the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in not setting aside  the judgment of the lower appellate court at least in the greater interest of doing justice.</u>

9. Syed Badrul Alam, learned Advocate appearing for defendant respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submits that Abbas Ali Munshi got the settlement of the suit land from the Ex-Zaminder as far back as in 1946 and as such it cannot be the said that the learned Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to try Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 in view of the provision of Section 20(2) (a) (iii) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950.

10. Mr. Alum further submits that the lower appellate court having held that the plaintiff could not prove by producing the gazette notification that the disputed plot is a part of Government reserved forest and accordingly the learned Additional District Judge having rightly reversed the decree of the trial Court upon fresh consideration of the evidence on record the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not commit any error of law in passing the impugned decree.

11. It appears from the plaint of the Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 that the plaintiff could not specify any date of his taking the alleged settlement of such big plot of land measuring 24.67 acres from the Ex-landlord. It was found by the trial court that defendant No. 1 of the present suit as plaintiff could not produce any document supporting his alleged settlement of the suit plot. The trial court on consideration of evidence of P.W. an DWs and the documents of both the parties, produced before it, believed the plaintiff's allegations that the exparte decree of Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 was the result of fraud and collusion in between the plaintiff and the clerk of the Government pleader and accordingly set aside the exparte decree for the ends of justice making a scope for proper adjudication in the matter. The lower appellate court without considering these aspects of the case wrongly observed:

"However, the scope of decision is whether the respondents could establish fraud in the matter of ordering exparte decree but the respondents have failed. The learned Sub-judge is absolutely wrong in deciding the suit en the irrelevant ground which is not based on evidence on record."

12. It appears that a vast tract of land within the reserved forest has been claimed by Abbas ali Munshi as the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 160 of 1966 on the basis of taking pattern from the ex-landlord in the year 1946. But in that suit he could not produce any supporting evidence of title as claimed. Moreover, in view of the statement made in the plaint that the suit land has been recorded as forest land the, trial court committed an error of law in decreeing the suit, mechanically, exparte without considering the effect of the provisions of the S.A.T. Act. as well as the Specific Relief Act.

13. In the facts and circumstances of the case we nee of the opinion that for doing complete justice the appeal should be allowed for having a proper adjudication in the matter of the real dispute, i.e. the title of respondent No. 1 in the suit plot.

14. In such view of the matter this appeal is allowed without, however, any order as to cost. In pursuance thereof the decrees of the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate court are set aside and that of the trial court is restored.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 430 of 2009
lawyer:
Abdus Samad, Senior Advocate instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record.   -------- For the Petitioners 
For the Respondents ------ Not represented.
parties:
Md. Abu Musa Bhuiyan and another ------ Petitioners
VS
Mohammad Ali alias Alimullah and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 02.12.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1340 of 1999.)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin J. This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 02.12.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1340 of 1999 making the Rule absolute and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 31.01.1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 223 of 1997 affirming those of the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka dated 31.07.1997 in Title suit No.160 of 1994 decreeing the suit with direction to hand over possession to the plaintiffs.

<u>2. The facts, in short, are that the plaintiff-petitioners filed Title Suit No.160 of 1994 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka against the defendants: (1) Korban Ali, son of Dhanu Mia, (2) Mohammad Ali alias Alimullah, (3) Salimullah, (4) Habibullah, all sons of Korban Ali of village Nadirpar, Kamrangir Char, Police Station-Lalbagh, District-Dhaka for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of the suit property measuring 10(ten) kathas of land in Khatian No.42(Old) at present khatian No.45 out of total area comprising 1.75 acres of land.</u>

3. The facts of the case of the plaintiff-petitioners are, in short, that land of the original C.S. Khatian C.S. Plot No.45 comprising an area of 1.75 acres of land originally belonged to Sabjan Bibi. She sold the same to Lal Mohammad as a result in the C.S. Khatian Lal Mohammad's name was recorded correctly in the possession column "possession by purchase, that while Lal Mohammad was in possession he died leaving behind his 5 (five) sons namely Dhanu Miah, Tamijuddin, Kamaruddin, Jonab Ali and Samad Ali as heirs. Five brothers were owning and possessing the property in ejmali. Later on, the aforesaid heirs of Lal Mohammad made amicable partition of their ejmali landed property along with other properties among themselves and they were owning and possessing the same, according to amicable partition. Thereafter Kamaruddin died leaving two sons Sultan and Ashraf Ali and one widow Gulmeher Bibi who were owning and possessing .27 acres of land as heirs of Kamaruddin. They sold the said .27 acres of land to one Sabu Miah by registered Deed No.10584 dated 22.10.1956, later on, the said Sabu Biah died leaving behind him Kutu Miah, Badsha Miah and Miajuddin. On the other hand, Abdus Samad, son of late Lal Mohammad died leaving behind him only son Paijuddin as his heir. Later on, Faizuddin sold his .27 acres of land to aforesaid Ktitu Miah, Badsha Miah and Miajuddin by registered sale deed. Thereafter Kutu Miah, Badsha Miah and Miajuddin became owners to the extent of .54 acres of land. While they were owning and possessing the aforesaid .54 acres of land, they sold seven kathas of land on 01.03.1980 by registered deed No.3597 in favour of plaintiff No.1 and on the same day by registered deed No.3599 they sold three kathas of land in favour of plaintiff No.2 and delivered possession to the plaintiffs by the Survey & and the plaintiffs had been owning and possessing the land in suit through a caretaker namely Shamser Ali. In the absence of the plaintiffs, the defendants taking advantage of their absence forcibly took possession of ten kathas of land from the caretaker Shamser Ali. Hence the plaintiffs were constrained to file Title Suit No.160 of 1994 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession.

4. The defendant Nos.1 to 4 contested the suit by filing 2 sets of written statements separately. The defendant Nos.1 and 3 filed one set of written statements and defendant Nos. 2 and 4 filed another set of written statements denying the facts and allegation made in the plaint of the aforesaid suit filed by the plaintiffs contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable. The suit was hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and by the principles of estoppel waiver and acquiescence and also by resjudicata. There was no cause of action for filing the suit and the suit was barred by limitation.

5. The trial court decreed the suit and on appeal the judgment of the trial court was affirmed and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the defendant filed the revisional application before the High Court Division and the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree of the courts below.

6. As against the judgment of the High Court Division the petitioners have filed this petition for leave to appeal.

7. Heard Mr. Abdus Samad, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners assails the impugned judgment. Perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record.

<u>8. The main reasoning of the courts below in decreeing the suit was that the defendants could not prove their document by bringing the volume in respect of the said deed. It appears that in pursuance of an application for calling the volume from the sub-registry office the volume was called for and the High Court Division examined the same and found that the deed No. 3605 dated 16.11.1916 was correctly registered and recorded in the volume and came to a finding that Dhanu Mia purchased the suit land from Sabjan by registered sale deed dated 16.11.1916 and on such finding set aside the judgment and decree of both the courts below.</u>

9. We find nothing to interfere with the judgment of the High Court Division and accordingly this petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Abdus Samad, Senior Advocate (Mr. A. Q. M. Safiullah, Advocate with him) instructed by Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant 
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent No. 1
Respondent Nos. 2-6 ----- Not represented
parties:
Uttara Bank Limited represented by its Managing Director, 94, Motijheel C/A, Dhaka-1000 ----- Appellant
Vs.
Syed Abedur Reza and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 31.07.2004 and 03.06.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3942 of 1991)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin J.:- This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 31.07.2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3942 of 1991 (Dhaka)/No. 122/88 (Sylhet) discharging the rule. 

2.
