The Trial Court having found a good prima facie arguable case, balance of convenience and inconvenience in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner loss and injury to the University granted temporary injunction.

8. The learned Additional District Judge set aside and vacated the order of injunction on the finding that the claim of irreparable loss and injury to the University due to aforesaid appointments does not appear as correct, that the plaintiff has no prima facie arguable case and he will not suffer any irreparable loss and injury personally for such appointments, that the order of injunction denying the salaries of the said employees at this stage does not arise, that the University will suffer inconvenience in morning its routine works, that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is against the plaintiff and that the trial Court gave finding on the merit of the suit in passing the order of temporary injunction improperly, etc.

9. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner in support of the Rule, submits that the plaintiff-petitioner is an Advocate and a Member of Rajshahi Bar Association and being a patriotic and conscious citizen of the country brought the suit and the application for injunction to protest the illegal appointments and to resist drainage of public money in national interest in general and in the interest of Rajshahi University in particular. He submits that the appointments of 546 3rd and 4th Class employees were made by the vested group of the University in an unprecedented manner secretly and malafide without any public notification and in violation of the circulars, decisions, guidelines, rules and procedures etc, of the Government, UGC's and the University itself and without requirement of the departmental and faculties heads, decisions of the Rajshahi University Teachers Association. budgetary provisions, etc, provided for such appointments and violating the principle of natural justice and in malafide with bad motive to remove the existing Master Roll employees of the same nature by the new set of employees. He submits that the trial Court in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the rules and guidelines provided therefore passed the order of injunction on finding a good prima facie arguable case and balance of convenience and inconvenience in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner to prevent the irreparable loss of the University likely to be caused by those appointments made contrary to the rules, procedure and guidelines laid down for such appointment and in breach of the circulars and budgetary provision of Rajshahi University. He also canvassed that the other set of defendants who filed their written objections also admitted the irregularity and illegality, breach and violation of rules and procedures, circulars and the guidelines in making these appointments by the contesting defendant and there was no demand from the departmental heads and they themselves failed to show that the appointments were made in accordance with the same. He urged that the learned Additional District Judge erred in law in setting aside and vacating the order of injunction granted by the trial Court without considering these facts on the documents filed by 'First' by the petitioner in consideration whereof the trial Court granted the order of injunction. Mr Farooqui urged that the documents filed before the trial Court being admitted documents the appellate Court below has erred in law by misreading mis-constructing and non-considering of those documents in setting aside the judgment and order of the trial Court. He submitted that non-consideration of the admitted documents being a question of law the appellate Court below has committed error of law in setting aside the trial Court judgment. He continued that the present suit being an open and shut one for decision of the suit depends upon the documents only consideration of the same in granting relief does not amount to giving decision on merit of the suit, but the appellate Court below has erred in law in finding that the trial Court has touched the merit of the suit in the interlocutory matter. He argued that the appellate Court below has erroneously found no prima facie and arguable case and the balance of convenience and inconvenience against the plaintiff and its finding that the plaintiff shall suffer no personal loss for the appointment of 546 employees, since they will to be provided by the University exchequer is misconceived. Inasmuch as, the appellate Court below failed to find that the instant suit is a public interest litigation (PIL) to safeguard the national interest in general and the interest of Rajshahi University in particular brought by a conscious citizen of the country for the reasons as aforesaid following the provision of Order I, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure although there had been some omissions in complying the procedural provisions of the same which is technical and can be ignored for dispensation of justice. He urged strongly that the appellate Court below has set aside and vacated the trial Court order without reversing its findings and failing to find that the petitioner has brought the suit in public interest as a PIL and not for his personal interest, etc.

10. On the other hand, Mr AF Hassan Ariff, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendants-opposite parties 1-5, controverted the submissions of the learned Counsel of the petitioner, submitting that the suit itself is not maintainable in view of the provision of sections 42 and 56K of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiff-petitioner is not entitled to get relief under Order XXXIX, rule 1 or under section 151 of the CPC. He submits that the civil Court is a creature of law and to be followed by the specific provisions embodied in the Code of Civil Procedure and the trial Court has illegally granted temporary injunction to the petitioner in a suit which is not maintainable and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit. He argued that the suit being not maintainable and the petitioner being not entitled to get relief for aforesaid reasons, non-consideration of the documents filed by him for granting the relief does not arise in view of the fact that the petitioner has no personal right either to the property, office and to any contract with the Rajshahi University and there was no breach of such contract or evasion of right, or threat to office and, as such, the appellate Court below has not committed any error in setting aside the trial Court's order. He argues that the appellate Court below having committed no error this revisional application is not maintainable under the provision of section 115(1) of the CPC. Mr Ariff contends that no breach of contract having been made nor any personal right to property or office of the petitioner having been evaded by the University there does not arise any question of his suffering irreparable loss and balance of convenience and inconvenience in his favour and the question of a prima facie arguable case is far remote and the learned Additional District Judge having properly found the same against the petitioner rightly set aside and vacated the order of injunction. He also argued that section 151 of the CPC has no, manner of application in the instant case where particular procedural provision are available in the said Code. In support of his submission Mr Ariff has referred the cases of Chowmuhani College and another vs Md Ismail Hossain and others, reported in 26 DLR 10 and Prof MA Raquib & ors, vs Prof, Zillur Rahman & ors., reported in 37 DLR 83.

11. In reply Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, strongly rebutted the submissions made by Mr Hassan Ariff, saying that Mr Ariff admits error of law, misreading and misconstruction of the documents had the suit been filed according to the provisions of law mentioned by him which shows that there was a prima facie arguable case in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner causing violation and breach of rule, procedures, circulars, etc. as contained in the documents filed by petitioner and considered by the trial Court in granting temporary injunction. He submits that by non-considering the said documents the appellate Court has, therefore, committed error of law. He contends that section 42 nor section 56K is exhaustive and limited to the status or property to any person and, as such, the suit is maintainable. He also submits that in view of the provisions of section 9, Order I, rule 8 and Order XXXIX, rules I and 2 of the CPC the suit is maintainable having the plaintiff locus standi to file the suit in public interest. He canvassed that Code of Civil Procedure is an Act of 1908 made by the Britishers bringing the concept of PIL under Order I, rule 8 for the first time which is a procedural law and needs to be modified with the changing society but the same cannot over ride the substantive law. He argued that the technicality of procedure to be followed in bringing a proceeding in a Court of law should not stand as a bar in bringing such a suit. He strongly controverts that maintainability of the suit cannot be looked into except incidentally in interlocutory proceeding as a ground for rejecting temporary injunction. Mr Farooqui concludes strongly submitting that, since the petitioner in particular and the nation as a whole does not want to see Rajshahi University to face the unfortunate and saddest fate of Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd, the world's largest Jute Mill, a pride of Bangladesh and the unfortunate fate of ETV channel a most popular private electronic TV channel of the country shut down by the present Government due to crippled economy of the Mill and allegation of graft against ETV. He has brought this suit for justice and equity.

12. Mr Farooqui in support of his submission referred the cases of Ekushey Television Ltd and others vs Dr  Chowdhury Mahrnood Hasan & others, reported in 54 DLR (AD) 130. Md Nurul Haque and others vs Manager, Bangladesh Bank, reported in 39 DLR 310. Dr Mohiuddin Farooque vs Bangladesh. represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Irrigation. Water Resources and Flood Control and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 1, Bangladesh Water Development Board, represented by its Chairman vs Syed Moazzem Hossain and others. reported in 1 BLC (AD) 13. Dildar Ahmed Choudhury vs Farroque Ahmed Chowdhury and another, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 138. Dhaka Match Factory Ltd vs Bangladesh Match Factory Ltd reported in 30 DLR 244, Miah Mohammad Latif vs Province of West Pakistan. reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98. Food Corporation of India, Gorakhpur vs Mohabir Prashad Bhartiya, reported in AIR 1988 (Alia) 160 (on section 34 of Indian Specific Relief Act section 42 of Specific Relief Act of Bangladesh), Ziaul Haque and ors vs Messers Business Resources Ltd & ors reported in 42 DLR (AD) 80. Mvi Abdus Sobhan Chowdhury & ors vs. Fazlur Rahman Chowdhury and others, reported in 9 DLR 467 on the maintainability of the suit are to substantiate the fact that the petitioner is entitled to get, and the trial Court has rightly granted, temporary injunction for protection of community of interest which was the essence of the proceeding.

13. Perused the judgments of the Courts below documents produced and heard the learned Counsels of both the sides at length.

14. Plaintiff filed the suit in the public interest as a conscious citizen of the country to resist and protest the illegal and unfair appointments of 546 3rd and 4th Class employees in Rajshahi University on 15-4-2004. He filed the suit for declaration that such appointments are illegal and for permanent injunction restraining the defendant Nos. 1-5 form confirming such appointments, etc. He also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule I read with section 151 of the CPC for res-training the defendant Nos. 1-5 from confirming the appointments, distributing duties and from giving them salaries. Defendants opposite party Nos. 1-5 contested the application by filing written objections, another set of written objection was filed by some other defendant-opposite parties mentioned above who, however, supported the plaintiff's case and did not contest the application for temporary injunction. Trial Court in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, the written objections filed by the defendants and the documents filed by both the parties granted temporary injunction prima facie finding that the appointments have been made in breach and violation of the circulars, rules and procedures, guidelines, budgetary provision of the UGC, etc, and good arguable case, balance of convenience and inconvenience in favour of the petitioner and that the University will sustain irreparable loss for such appointments. Trial Court also found that the new sets of 546 employees have also been posted to remove the existing incumbents most whimsically against the principle of natural justice and equity without any public advertisement, even without any post, demand and proposal from the concerned departments, etc. The learned Additional District Judge set aside and vacated the order of injunction in appeal. The appellate Court below found that it is not correct that appointments were made for personal interest and there was no necessity that any irregularities if made in the process of appointments the same would be decided in the suit on merit which cannot be considered at the time of passing an order of temporary injunction. The appellate Court below also found that there are official order of the authorities for such appointments and if such a good number of employees are barred from working the normal activities of the University could be hampered and, as such, the balance of convenience and inconvenience is against the petitioner and in favour of the defendants. The appellate Court below also found that there is no arguable prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff, since he will not suffer personal loss for the same and that the trial Court has touched the merit of the case in granting temporary injunction, etc.

<u>15. Admittedly, the instant suit is a public interest litigation brought by the plaintiff in the interest of Rajshahi University. But on perusal of the appellate Court judgment, it appears that the appellate Court has thoroughly misconceived the suit and its spirit. The trial Court complying the guiding principles for passing an order of temporary injunction and being satisfied he granted the temporary injunction arriving at a clear prima facie finding in consideration of the documents filed that the appointments have been made in breach and violation of the circulars rules and procedures, guidelines, without public notification, etc. On the other hand, the appellate Court below has set aside and vacated the same putting much emphasis on the humanitarian ground rather than looking into the merit of rules and procedures, guidelines, budgetary provision, requirements, public notification, etc for making such huge appointments. It also appears that the finding of the appellate Court that the appointments were made in the necessity of the University is also without footing and not supported by any documents filed by the defendants. The appellate Court has totally failed to meet and revert the findings of the trial Court. The appellate Court below erroneously came to the finding on misreading and on misconstruction of the unlisted documents filed by the petitioner that, there is no prima facie arguable case and balance of convenience and inconvenience for the petitioner will not suffer any personal loss, misconceiving plaintiff's case.</u>

16. Mr Ariff, the learned Counsel for the opposite party Nos. 1-5, instead of justifying the above findings of the appellate Court below on the facts of the case, assailed the finding of the trial Court and controverted the submissions of Mr Farooqui, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, has in his extensive submission basically confined himself on the maintainability of the suit itself and locus standi to file the suit by the plaintiff.

17. In support of his submissions, he referred two decisions already mentioned above. The substance of his submissions as aforesaid is that the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit and the same is not maintainable and hence, he is not entitled to set injunction. The decisions referred by him as mentioned above reported in 26 DLR 10 and in 37 DLR 83 are not applicable in the facts and circumstances and the points in issue for decision of the instant case. Both the above cases arose between the officer and the authorities of the institution out of its internal administrative order and decision and, as such, have no matter of application in the instant case.

<u>18. This is a settled principle laid down by our Apex Court as well as the superior Courts of this sub-continent that the question of maintainability cannot be decided except looking into incidentally in an interlocutory matter which should be decreed on merit after taking evidence on trial. Mr Farooqui has referred a number of cases as mentioned above both in respect of findings on the maintainability of the suit in interlocutory mailer while granting and non-granting of an order of temporary injunction and to show that the suit is maintainable. On perusal of the decisions, I shall only say that those rulings are self-speaking on the points urged by Mr Farooqui but I refrained myself from quoting the aforesaid rulings and also from giving my findings and decision on the question of maintainability of the suit as to address his submission except that I am in quite agreement with the aforesaid rulings that the maintainability of the suit is a matter to be decided in the main suit on merit on trial and not in the interlocutory mailer. In agreement with the aforesaid ruling it is suffice to say that I find the suit prima facie maintainable and the petitioner is entitled to get the relief in law and no procedural technicality should stand in its way to get justice for the substance of the prayer has to be looked into rather than technicality. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that it has been held in the case between Abu Taher Chowdhury and others vs State, reported in 11 DLR (AD) 2 that "for promoting the cause of justice, for doing complete justice and for prevention of miscarriage of justice this Court's power is very wide, over riding and exceptional and is not encumbered by any technicality." In the case of Abdul Hamid Kazi vs Abdul Jabbar Jamadar and others, reported in 26 DLR (SC) 68. it has been held that "technicality of form, if adhered to, as the High Court took to be so, then there would be no proper dispensation of justice in the facts and circumstances of the case. In our view the substance of the prayer should be looked into taking an overall view of the facts and circumstances of the case, ignoring the mere technicality of form of the petition. So the views expressed by the learned Munsif in passing the order is in conformity with the substance of the petition filed by the appellant and it is not desired that the technicality of form should prevail causing impediment to dispensation of justice."</u>

<u>19. In view of the matter as above, I find no substance in the submission of Mr Ariff that since the suit is not maintainable and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the same and that the documents filed by the plaintiff being not between him and the University, the appellate Court below has committed no error of law in not finding a prima facie arguable case and balance of convenience and inconvenience and question of irreparable loss of the plaintiff on considering those documents. I am quite unable to accept his submission inasmuch as misconstruction and misreading of document is a question of law. The appellate Court below has thus committed error of law in mis-constructing and misreading those documents. In the instant case, the documents being only reliable documents of facts and evidence for determining the issues involved in the suit non-construction and misreading of the same to find a prima facie arguable case and other principles required for granting temporary injunction, the same cannot be over looked by the Court. The whole submission of Mr Ariff as I have understood and already mentioned above that the plaintiff having no personal interest and right he is not entitled to an order of temporary injunction is, totally misconceived in the facts of the case where the plaintiff himself has disclosed in his plaint that he has filed the suit as a conscious citizen of the country in the interest of Rajshahi University in particular and in the interest of the nation in general. Therefore, where the plaintiff never claimed his personal interest any finding and submission centering round the same is misconceived and not maintainable. The appellate Court below has committed an error of law in failing to find a prima facie arguable case and balance of convenience and inconvenience and of suffering of irreparable loss by the University on the basis of the facts and documents. Humanitarian consideration and emotional thoughts cannot substitute legal consideration and ground for passing a judgment and order by the Court at the cost of the people of the country. The matter in issue has to be decided on merit of the suit on trial but till then the plaintiff-petitioner being able to make out a good prima facie arguable case is entitled to get temporary injunction so that no financial damage is caused to the University till disposal of the suit.</u>

20. In consideration of the above, I find merit in the Rule. The impugned judgment being not sustainable in law is liable to be set aside.

21. In the result, the Rule is made absolute.

The impugned judgment and order dated 14-7-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajshahi in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 50 of 2004 is hereby set aside and that of the trial Court is affirmed.

End.

lawyer:
MA Quyyum with Mozammel Hossain, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
AY Ahmed Ali with Mizanur Rahman, Advocates—For Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Kaniz Fatema alias Beauty ------ Petitioner 
Vs 
Syed Ruhul Amin and others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner was issued calling upon the defendant-opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 28-3-1987 passed in Title Appeal No. 162 of 1986 by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka affirming the judgment and decree dated 28-7-1986 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 905 of 1998 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The plaintiff-petitioner filed the aforesaid suit seeking a declaration of her right, title and interest in the suit land measuring 720 Ajutangsha acquired by her from her foster-mother, proforma defendant No. 5, Saleha Khatoon, out of her love and affection for her by way of oral Heba.

3. The case of the plaintiff-petitioner is that the said suit property measuring 720 ajutangsha originally belonged to one. Shanti Gopal Saha who subsequently transferred the same to Dr Moula Boksha by a sale deed No. 446 dated 23-1-53. Dr Moula Boksha thereafter transferred the said land to Ms Meherunnessa by the sale deed No. 6557 dated 15-12-55 whereupon Meherunnessa had her name recorded in the SA Khatian as owner of 10 annas 13 gandas, 1 kara and 1 kranti out of the total land in the plot measuring 0.80 acres. While Meherunnessa was continuing as owner in possession by paying government rents and dues she transferred the said land to Ms Saleha Khatun (proforma defendant No. 5) by a sale deed No. 207 dated 2-1-62. Saleha Kahtun thereafter mutated her name in the government records and while continuing as the owner in possession by installing electric, gas and WASA connections in her name gifted the same away to the plaintiff-petitioner out of her love and affection.

4. The defendant-opposite party No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations in the plaint contending, inter alias that the entire land in the suit plot measuring 1080 ajutangsha was the khas land of the government. Accordingly, the government settled the same with different persons from time to time and one Nanda Kishore Shah being one of the settlement holders sold his share in the land in the suit plot to one Fazle Rashid by a registered deed No. 7604 dated 16-12-52 and subsequently, the father of the said defendant-opposite party No.1 purchased the same from Fazle Rashid by a registered sale deed No. 5334 dated 14-9-53 and got the same duly recorded in his name and paid rents. The defendant opposite party No.1 inherited the said land after the death of his father and had his name recorded in SA Khatian in respect of the said land and since then he has been owning and possessing specifically one third share of the land in the suit plot. The defendant-opposite party No.1 having subsequently learnt that the suit plot was government khas land prayed for regular settlement of the same and defendant Nos. 2-4 accordingly, settled one third share of the land of the suit plot with the defendant opposite party No.1 on 2-12-81 and since then he has been owning and possessing the same.

5. Both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit mainly on the ground that the plaintiff-petitioner had failed to prove her basic documents of title showing that she acquired 720 Ajutangsha of land out of CS plot No. 126 by way of gift from Saleha Khatun.

6. Mr Abdul Quyyum, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Mozammel Hossain for the plaintiff petitioner, having taken this court through the judgment and decree passed by the courts below and other materials on record contends that although the basic documents of title showing title of the plaintiff petitioner to the suit land were not brought on record in the course of trial but the same were filed before the appellate Court below along with an application for amendment to the plaint, but apparently due to inexperience and negligence of the concerned lawyer of the plaintiff-petitioner and the appellate Court below the appeal was heard and disposed of without the said amendment application and the title deeds having been considered he therefore, submits that non consideration of the same by the appellate Court below before disposal of the appeal has caused miscarriage of justice and this should be rectified by sending the case to the appellate Court below on remand. In this connection he refers to some cases reported in 40 DLR (AD) 101, 54 DLR (AD) 170 and 38 DLR (AD) 6.

7. Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing with Mr Md Mizanur Rahman for the defendant-opposite party No.1, while opposing the Rule strenuously argues that since the impugned judgment is the judgment of affirmance this court would not be competent to interfere with concurrent finding of facts and, for the same reason, this court should not also remand the case for consideration of the application for amendment to the plaint and for admission of the documents of title as additional evidence in the case as that amounts to filling in the lacuna in the case of the plaintiff- petitioner. In this connection he refers to and relied on the case of Hajee Nurul Alam vs Alhaj Abdus Sobhan, 3 BLT (AD) 135, Shah Alam vs Farida Begum, 2 BLC (AD) 92, Abdul Awal Khan vs Md Sadu Miah 1986 BLD (AD) 156 and Bangladesh vs Joynal Abedin Dewan 1 BLC (AD) 26.

8. Careful perusal and scrutiny of the record reveals that no basic documents of title were brought on record during the trial in support of the case of the plaintiff-petitioner as regards her title to the suit land. Certified copy of SA Khatian as well as an attested copy of porcha were filed and brought on record by way of exhibits showing that the plaintiff- petitioner acquired 720 Ajutangsha land in the suit plot by virtue of an Osiwatnama followed by an oral gift from the'proforma defendant No. 5, Saleha Kahtoon. In the premises, the trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff-petitioner failed to prove her title to the suit land in the absence of proof of her basic documents of title to the suit land.

9. Mr Quyyum points out, and it is noted from the record, that the basic documents of title as well as an application of amendment to the plaint were filed before the appellate Court below by the plaintiff-petitioner for consideration before disposal of the appeal. The appellate Court below took note of this and accordingly, fixed a date for consideration of the same. But for some inexplicable reason the appellate Court below disposed of the appeal by the impugned judgment after a lapse of some considerable time without any reference to them. The aforesaid lapse on the part of the appellate Court below has caused failure of justice.

<u>10. Our superior courts in the sub-continent have always preferred admission of additional evidence at the appellate stage not only to pronounce judgment but also for any other substantial cause" which also includes in the interests of justice", 38 DLR (AD) 6 and AIR 1963 SC 1526. The appellate Court below ought to have considered the application for amendment to the plaint as well as the admission of those basic documents of title by way of additional evidence before passing the impugned judgment in the interest of justice. The present case is therefore, considered a fit case for remand to the appellate Court below for consideration of the application for amendment to the plaint as well as for admission of the basic documents of title filed in that Court by the plaintiff-petitioner by a firishti during the pendency of the appeal as additional evidence by giving opportunity to the defendant-opposite party No.1 to adduce fresh evidence, if any, and then dispose of the appeal afresh This view also finds support from the case of Zohora Kahtun and other vs Md Hatem Ali 40 DLR (AD) 101, Superintendent, PDB vs Madumati Cinema Hall, 54 DLR (AD) 170 cited on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner. The cases cited on behalf of the defendant opposite party No.1 do not however appear to be relevant in the facts and circumstances of the case. Accordingly, the contentions raised by the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party No.1 are not acceptable and rejected.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the Judgment and order dated 28-4-87 passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 162 of 1986 is set aside and the case is now remanded to the appellate Court below for consideration of the application of amendment of the plaint filed by the plaintiff-petitioner and. also for admission of the basic documents of title by way of additional evidence to dispose of the appeal within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this order.

End.

lawyer:
Zainul Abedin, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Appellants. 
Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Forest Department & others ------ Appellants 
vs 
Md Shariful Alam and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Rezaul Haque J: This Civil Rule No. 425(f) of 2004 under section 5, Limitation Act (arising out of FAT No. 228/2004) was issued at the instance the defendants-appellants-petitioner calling upon plaintiff respondents opposite parties Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why delay of 279 day (in fact 243 days) in preferring FAT No. 228/2004 against Judgment and decree dated 10-5-2003, decree signed 17-5-2003 in TS No. 108/2002 by Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur should not be condoned or to pass such order or orders as the Court may deem fit and proper.

2. It has been stated that TS 108/2002 was decreed on contest against defendants-appellants-petitioners on 10-5-2003 (decree prepared and signed on 17-5-2003), Application for certified copy of judgment and decree was filed on 31-5-2003, the copy was made ready and delivery was taken on 10-7-2003. Thereafter taking real statement from DFO office/papers including judgment and decree were sent to Senior Assistant Secretary of the concerned Ministry on 29-8-2003 wherefrom the same were sent to the office of Solicitor on 20-12-2003 where from the same were sent to Attorney-General's office on 8-3-2004. Additional Attorney-General then asked Deputy Attorney-General concerned on 11-3-2004 to prepare Memo of Appeal which was prepared and typed on 3-4-2004. The same were sent to Solicitor's office on 20-4-2004 wherein affidavit was sworn on 19-5-2004. By above processes delay of 243 days (not 279 days) occurred.

3. Stating above facts application under section 5, Limitation Act accompanied by affidavit having been sworn on 19-5-2004 as above was filed for condonation of said delay. Subsequently supplementary affidavit was filed on behalf of defendants-appellants-petitioners stating some more facts with regard to appeal itself.

4. Plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties appeared through engaged Advocate and contested the Civil Rule by filing counter-affidavit stating clearly that delay of 243 days has not been properly explained as required under rule.

5. It has been stated that each day's delay has to be properly explained to get order of condonation of delay. It has been stated that the Rule must be discharged.

6. The Rule being ready was taken up for hearing.

7. Learned Advocate for the defendants-appellants-petitioners in support of the Rule relies on the decision in the case Bangladesh vs Jahiruddin reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 180 and submits that in above decision it was stated that "Due to necessity to obtain opinions of various authorities concerned before filing an appeal, sometime may reasonably be expected to elapse which in case of an individual does not happen. Some consideration in appropriate circumstances may therefore, be extended to the government appearing as a litigant. In saying so no rule is being laid down for not observing the strictness of the proof of substantial and reasonable cause in making such delay, standard of acceptance must however remain the same in case of both citizen and state."

8. Inertia in the Government offices wherever exists must be replaced by prompt and vigorous sense of duty and action.

9. Referring to fact and reasons for delay as occurred, learned Advocate shows from the application for condonation of delay, supported by affidavit and supplementary affidavit filed afterwards that the certified copy of the judgment was obtained quite within time. He shows that delay as above mainly occurred due to different processes in between different authorities such as DFO office, Solicitor's office and Attorney-General's office. Defendants-appellants-petitioners are not directly involved in causing above delay. He also submits that if due to above delay the memo of appeal be not accepted the appellants being contesting defendants with the plaintiffs in the suit will be deprived once and for all of the legal right to fight out their claims and right in the court of law and it will operate to the prejudice of the appellants for no direct fault on their own part in the matter, as the delay occurred during processes between different authorities as above. He earnestly submits that the delay of 243 days (not 279 days) as above should be condoned in order that the appeal filed may be admitted for consideration and decision on merit.

10. Learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties cited decision reported in 1994 BLT (AD) 90 as well as cited decision in the case of Government vs Alauddin reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 35 and submits that in the decision reported in 1994 BLT (AD) 90 it was observed that. "There is no good ground for condonation of delay rather these show utter negligence, carelessness, inefficiency or may be connivance of persons/officials of the petitioner Government who handle the matter".

11. "It was either deliberate or due to utter negligence on the part of the petitioner's office. There is no good ground for its condonation. It is better that strong action is taken against the persons responsible for the failure as above".

12. Learned Advocate then refers to the decision cited above as reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 35 wherein it was held that:

"Government stands on the same footing with ordinary litigants. It cannot deserve unlimited latitude in matter of condonation of delay. Though in many cases involving Government delay is condoned upon sympathetic consideration as the file of Government moves through different stages and time consuming procedures. But an inordinate delay of 1340 days arising out of gross negligence of Government officials cannot be condoned. Appropriate action should be taken against delinquent officers for the losses to the Govt."

13. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties argues that delay of 243 days could not be properly explained by the appellants petitioner and, as such, in view of above decisions of honourable Appellate Division the delay as occurred should not be condoned. He submits that the Rule must be discharged.

14. We have perused the application for condonation of the delay as occurred in filing the appeal and also perused the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioners as well as counter-affidavit filed on behalf of opposite parties. We have considered the contentions of both sides. We have also gone through and appreciated the decision reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 180 as cited on behalf of petitioners as well as the decisions reported in 1994 BLT (AD) 90 and reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 35 as cited on behalf of opposite parties.

15. On perusal, it appears that TS 108/2002 was decreed on contest against the appellate petitioners on 10-5-2003, decree was prepared on 17-5-2003. Application for certified copy of the judgment and decree was filed on 31-5-2003, copy was made ready for delivery and the delivery was taken on 10-7-2003. It is thus clear that quite within the time certified copies of the judgment and decree were obtained.

16. The delay started from the subsequent stages and processes.

17. On perusal and scrutiny, it appears that after taking real statement from DFO's office, relevant record with papers including judgment and decree were sent to Senior Assistant Secretary of the concerned Ministry on 29-8-2003 wherefrom subsequently, the same were sent to the Solicitor's office on 20-12-2003 wherefrom the same were sent to the office of Attorney-General on 8-3-2004. Thereafter, Additional Attorney-General asked on 11-3-2004 Deputy Attorney-General to prepare memo of the appeal which was prepared and typed on 3-4-2004 and the same was then sent to the office of the Solicitor on 20-4-2004 wherein affidavit was sworn on 19-5-2004. By above processes delay of 243 days had already occurred.

18. It is not disputed that procedural process has to be passed through in order to prepare memo of appeal to be filed on behalf of Government and in going through such processes concerned file has to be sent to different authorities for opinion, comment, sanction and approval. During such processes time is consumed. It is true that prompt and intelligent dealing with file by office of each authority may save time but from experiences it appears that different authorities do not carefully, efficiently and intelligently deal with such file wherein question of limitation is always involved.

<u>19. Present case is not an exception. It appears that certified copies of the judgment and decree were obtained within time. The unusual delay occurred during aforesaid procedural processes for obtaining opinion and approval of different authorities. The appellants had no direct hand and concern in the movement of above processes. It appears that the record or file moved from the concerned Ministry to Solicitor's office. Then from Solicitor's office to Attorney-General's office and thereafter from Attorney-General's office to the office of Solicitor. In above processes the delay already occurred.</u>

<u>20. In the above respect observation was appropriately made by Honourable Appellate Division in the case Bangladesh vs Jahiruddin reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 180 in the following manner:</u>

<u>"Due to necessity to obtain opinions of various authorities concerned before filing an appeal some time may reasonably be expected to elapse which in case of an individual does not happen. Some consideration in the appropriate circumstances may therefore, be extended to the government appearing as litigant. In the decision in the case Government vs Alauddin as cited on behalf of opposite parties reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 35 it was observed that—</u>

<u>"Government stands on same footing with ordinary litigants. It cannot deserve unlimited latitude in matters of condonation of delay. Though in many cases of the Government delay is condoned upon sympathetic consideration as the file of the Government moves through different stages and time consuming procedures. But an inordinate delay of 1340 days out of gross negligence of government officials cannot be condoned.</u>

<u>21. This decision as above has distinguishing features as there was inordinate delay of 1340 days being unexplained. But the present appeal has only delay of 243 days being explained in the manner that due to movement of the concerned file from the Solicitor's office to the office of Attorney-General time and again the delay occurred.</u>

<u>22. In both decisions reported in 1994 BLT (AD) 90 and 2001 BLD (AD) 35 it was duly cautioned that in appropriate cases the Government officials who are liable and responsible for the delay due to their inefficient, careless handling of the file or deliberate negligence should be dealt with severely in order that others may be careful in future. We have due regard to above observations. We have given anxious consideration to the present case before us. We have also looked to the facts and circumstances of the case itself. We see that on merit the appellants have some arguable points to be fought out in the appeal. We already observed that appellants  themselves had no hand in causing above delay of 243 days in filing the appeal, it is obvious that the delay occurred during procedural processes in between Solicitor's office and Attorney-General's office as discussed above. If anyone is to be held liable for the above delay then the officials of both Solicitor's office as well as Attorney-General's office are to be made liable. But for the fault as above on the part of officials of Solicitor's office and Attorney-General's office the appellants should not be penalised as because if the delay as above in filing the appeal be not condoned the appellants will be deprived once and for all of the chance of appeal to fight out their claim. In above context, we are of the view that the delay of 243 days (not 279 days) should be condoned in order that the appeal may be admitted allowing chance to the appellants to fight out their claim and right before the court of law.</u>

In the result, Civil Rule No. 125(F)/2004 is made absolute, delay of 243 days (not 279 days) in filing the appeal (FAT 228/2004) be accordingly condoned, appeal be admitted and registered.

End.

caseno: FA No. 66 of 2004 with FMA No. 94 of 2004 with FA No. 10 of 2005 and C. Rule 394(F) of 2004
lawyer:
AKM Abdul Hakim with Md Joynul Abedin, Advocates—For the Appellant in FA No. 66 of 2004 and FMA No. 94 of 2004 and for Respondent in FA No. 10 of 2005.
Rafiqul Islam Miah with Md Saifur Rahman, Advocates—For Respondent in FA No. 66 of 2004 and FMA No. 94 of 2004 and for Appellant in FA No. 10 of 2005
parties:
Bangladesh Water Development Board ------ Defendant-Appellant 
vs 
Titas Prokaushali Ltd. ------ Plaintiff Respondent
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: As all the three appeals arose out of the same judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 202 of 2003, subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 7 of 2003, they were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment which will govern all the appeals.

2. These appeals are against the judgment and order dated 16-10-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 2003 refusing to set aside the award dated 14-9-2002 passed by the learned Umpire and making the same a rule of the Court. The Bangladesh Water Development Board as the appellants preferred appeal Nos. 66 of 2004 and 94 of 2004 whereas the Titas Prokaushali Ltd filed appeal No. 10 of 2005 for refusing to grant interest on the awarded sum.

3. After filing of the award in the aforesaid Court the appellant of Appeal No. 66 of 2004 filed an objection under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 (hereinafter called 'the Act') and the self-same appellate also filed an application under section 33 read with section 30 of the Act for setting aside the award which was registered as Miscellaneous Arbitration Case No. 64 of 2000. Both the aforesaid Title Suit along with the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case was heard by the trial Court analogously and by the impugned judgment the trial Court rejected the application filed by the appellant under section 33 of the Act and also rejected the objection filed by them under section 17 of the Act and made the award Rule of the Court by its order dated 16-10-2003. While making the award Rule of the Court the trial Court, however, modified the award by deleting the interest awarded by the Arbitrator/Umpire in favour of Titas Prokoushali Ltd (hereinafter called 'the contractor') and the contractor being aggrieved by that part of the impugned order preferred Appeal No. 10 of 2005 challenging that portion of the impugned decree of the trial Court.

4. The relevant facts, in short, may be stated as follows:

The owner, i.e., Bangladesh Water Development Board, invited tenders on 17-5-94 for construction of Silt Trap at Zero km of the main canal of Teesta Barrage Project under SFD Loan No. 8/221 in Group No. 14. Eight construction companies participated in the tender and after evaluation of the offer made by the participants the contractor's offer was accepted by the owner and in the contract it was expressly stipulated that from the date of placing of the order the contractor will have to complete the entire work within 9(nine) months and there was also a pre-bid meeting held on 25-6-94 wherein the said period was ultimately extended up to 12 months and after completion of all formalities and execution of the contract, work order was issued to the contractor on that very day. After the execution of the contract the owner paid first and second mobilisation advance to the contractor on 15-9-94 and 19-9-94 respectively totaling an amount of Taka 2,08,17,244.00. It may further be mentioned that during the course of execution of the work there were some tender items variation and some non-tender items variation and some part of the land could not be handed over to the contractor. However, the contractor completed the contract work within the extended time granted by the owner. It appears that during the course of carrying out the construction work a series of letters were exchanged between the parties and ultimately a dispute arose between the parties on different counts and as the dispute could not be amicably settled by the parties by mutual discussions, ultimately, the said dispute was referred to the Arbitrators by the parties.

5. This case has a chequered history. Initially, one Mr Abdul Barik Bhuiyan, Member, Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), was appointed as arbitrator on behalf of the owner and Advocate Mr Abdul Quddus, was appointed as an Arbitrator by the contractor but they, within the span of 3(three) years, could neither complete the arbitration proceeding nor took any step to get the time extended. As a result of which through the intervention of the Court the said arbitrators were removed and the present Arbitrators, namely, Mr Serajul Islam, a retired Additional Chief Engineer of BWDB was appointed Arbitrator on behalf of the owner and Mr Luthfe Alam, Advocate, was appointed Arbitrator by the contractor. Jalil was appointed as umpire to finally resolve the dispute between the parties.
